en: (Pariśiṣṭa 1: Nakṣatrakalpa) (AVParis 0.0) Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa!
Oṃ, homage to Vāmadeva, the self of the Atharva, who is Śiva.
Homage to the illustrious Sarasvatī.
(1.1) Now we shall explain the Nakṣatrakalpa.
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, the two Punarvasūs, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā,
the two Phālgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, and Svāti.
Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla,
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā, Uttaraproṣṭhapadā, Revatī, Aśvayujau, and Bharaṇyaḥ.
Six Kṛttikās, one Rohiṇī, three Mṛgaśiras, one Ārdrā, two Punarvasūs, one Puṣya, six Āśleṣās, six Maghās, four Phalgunīs, five Hastas, one Citrā, one Svāti,
two Viśākhās, four Anurādhās, one Jyeṣṭhā, seven Mūla, eight Pūrvāṣāḍhās, one Abhijit, and three Uttarāṣāḍhās.
Śravaṇā consists of five stars; Śraviṣṭhā, one; Śatabhiṣā, four; the two Proṣṭhapadas, one; Revatī, two; the two Aśvayujas, three; and the Bharaṇīs, three.
Thus, Brahman is defined by its numerical measure.
Āgniveśya [is the nakṣatra] Kṛttikā; Rohiṇī [is] Ānurohiṇī; Śvetāyina [is] Mṛgaśiras; Ārdrā [is] Bārhadgavī; the two Punarvasūs [are] Vātsyāyana; Bhāradvāja [is] Puṣya; Jātūkarṇya [is] Āśleṣā;
Vaiyāghrapadya [is] Maghā; the two Pūrva-phalgunīs [are] Pārāśarya; the two Uttara-phalgunīs [are] Aupaśivya; Hasta [is] Māṇḍavyāyana; Citrā [is] Gautamī; Kauṇḍinyāyana [is] (Svāti).
Svāti belongs to Kāpili; Viśākhā to Maitreyī; Anurādhā to Kauśikī; Jyeṣṭhā to Kautsa; Mūla to Hāritayajñī; Pūrvāṣāḍhā to Kāśyapī; Uttarāṣāḍhā to Śaunaka; Abhijit to Ātreyī; Śravaṇa to Gārgī;
Śraviṣṭhā to Dākṣāyaṇī; Śatabhiṣaj to Vātsyāyanī; the two Pūrvaproṣṭhapadas to Āgastī; the two Uttaraproṣṭhapadas to Śāṅkhāyanī; and Revatī to Kātyāyanī.
The two Aśvayujas, the Bharaṇīs, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Āditya, and Candramas—these are the Brahmins among the lunar mansions.
The Kṛttikās have Agni as their deity; Prajāpati resides in Rohiṇī; one should know that Mṛgaśiras belongs to Soma, and the Maruts are the deities therein.
One should know that the two Punarvasus belong to Rudra and Āditi; Bṛhaspati is in Puṣya;
Aśleṣā has the serpents as its presiding deity; and the ancestors are traditionally associated with Maghā.
Bhaga is the deity of the two former Phalgunīs, Aryaman of the latter two,
Savitṛ of Hasta, and Citrā has Tvaṣṭṛ as its deity.
In Svāti, the deity is Vāyu; in Viśākhā, Indra and Agni;
in Anurādhā, Mitra; and in Jyeṣṭhā, Indra and Mahādeva.
Ahibudhnya and Nirṛti are the deities here of the Mūla [constellation];
the Waters are the deities in the Pūrvāṣāḍhās, and likewise the Viśvedevas in the Uttarāṣāḍhās.
Abhijit has Brahman as its deity; Viṣṇu is said to be the deity of Śravaṇa;
Śraviṣṭhā has the Vasus as its deity; and Śatabhiṣaj belongs to Varuṇa and Indra.
Aja Ekapād, the quarters, and Āditya are likewise in the north;
Revatī has Pūṣan as its deity, and the Aśvins are recorded as being in Aśvinī.
The Bharaṇīs are proclaimed as deities whose presiding deity is Yama.
Kṛttikā, Maghā, Mūla, and likewise the three Pūrvās among the dual constellations— these one should know as having their portions in the east, beginning with the day.
Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣaj, Svātī, Āśleṣā, and also Bharaṇī— these,
together with Jyeṣṭhā, they call the "night-portions" of Brahmā.
Punarvasu and Viśākhā, the two Uttarās, Rohiṇī, and the night belong to those who have pairs [of wives], as they partake of both lunar fortnights.
Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Hasta, Citrā together with Anurādhā,
Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Revatī, and the two Aśvayujas— these are the nine.
One should know that these [lunar mansions] have their portions in the latter half [of the month] and begin with the night; the muhūrta is called Abhijit.

Those with their portions in the east belong to the moon as yet to come; those with their portions in the west belong to the moon that has already passed; those with portions on both sides belong to the moon as it is currently present; and those with portions at night belong equally to the moon.
Six are characterized by future yoga, twelve by established yoga, and nine by transcended yoga; thus is yoga perceived.
The seizing spirit harms many newborns while remaining among the Kṛttikās, yet it also grants long life.
Goats, sheep, and mice are distressed; the people of the Brahmanas, along with the barbarians, are likewise afflicted.

The king of the Kaliṅgas is surely distressed; he destroys all the goldsmiths, and he drives away all the smiths, the ironworkers, and those who maintain the sacred fires, along with their heated implements.
Iron, copper, silver, gold, and whatever essence falls mixed with gold;
*kāśa* grass, *kuśa* grass, and whatever is golden-colored or fire-colored—[these are] fruits, roots, and flowers.
Those who are born there [when] the lakes dry up and the rivers recede, both people and animals as well as wild beasts are distressed.
When the heart of Prajāpati is afflicted, the entire world, along with its regions, suffers.
One should know that King Mahābhauma will die when the *chavakā* stars of the single-constellation group appear among the *invakās*.
When the *yojadhānās* descend into the portion of the constellations, it is surely because they were created by the Triṇava.

Thus he was led there for the sight of the treasure; one should know that there was misfortune for them there. Those powerful deer who, having abandoned their former haunts, rise up by force— (AVParis_1,6.6) Thus he was led there for the sight of the treasure; one should know that there was misfortune for them there. Those powerful deer who, having abandoned their former haunts, rise up by force—

By means of the *bhaga* [constellation], they approach the goddess; through the portion of Ārdrā, they become victorious. There, in the portion of the *nakṣatra* Punarvasu, he assigned the grains for both the divine and the human beings.
For thus indeed, the stars knowers of the constellations have declared that the portion of Puṣya belongs to the Brahmins as one; so indeed it is.
The Śatadrus, Kaiśikas, those from the southern regions, and the Āndhras have increased through the application of yoga and laughter.
In that place, those who are accompanied by their companions reside within the portion of Aśleṣā.
They say that the ancestors are the bamboo, and the deity is threefold;
on the eighth lunar mansion, Maghā, it was created by the gods.
There, through the propitiation of the gods, they are united.
For kings, [the rites] are on the full moon of Rākā; then for the Madraka and Kaikeya, they are at the end of the conjunction with Manomāpāyana and Sahaparisunniyoja.
Then, for seven measures, it is equal in the eastern part, during the nine [days] under the Phalgunī asterisms.
The Matsyas, the Māgadhas, the Cedis, and the Śālvas— the Matsyas and both [types of] Phalgunīs—
are joined together there by the grace of the gods.
All the former teachers, desiring [this], join the liver and the pleura together with their portion in the hand;
therein they are united through the grace of the gods.
Those deer that slink away in the eastern half while moving about peacefully, those wild animals and beasts that go aside—they all become your cattle, and they are auspicious in the portion of Citrā.
Therein, for the sake of victory, young women mount a vehicle from which the hair has fallen; here the ox endures them.
It is known that all grasses and plants resort to the ancient Svāti, which was created by the gods.
The trees and the roots of the trees of the Ikṣvākus are joined with the branch Viśākhā by means of prosperity.
When that is seized, there is indeed fear for them; however, if it is afflicted by fate, one must act with force.
Those who were born there.
Those who perish in the western half, the moving Āsavas, the Mṛgas, the northern Āndhras,
and the Magadhas, Vaṅgas, and Matsyas— all these together become powerful there under the constellation Anūrādhā.
There are five peoples who live together as one: the Kāsa, the Saubala, the Dādha, the Auṣyadhā, and the Bāhlīkas; among them, the Jyeṣṭhas approach with devotion.
(AVParis_1,7.9) They say that for the Ikṣvākus, the root is to be churned out;
so too do those who know the constellations understand it, for indeed thus it is.
(AVParis_1,7.10) The Kāmbojas, the Kālamṛṣas, the Krandas, the Ucchuṣmas, the dogs, and the smokeless monkeys resort with devotion to Pūrvāṣāḍhā there.
May all the gods, with the Pañcāla as their chief, and the waters that protect the past and the future,
approach there with devotion under the constellation Uttarāṣāḍhā.
Neither the Arkavindas, nor the Arvvidālas, nor the Sṛṅgāvas, nor the Niṣadhan creatures, nor the Mataṅgas,
having understood the purpose of the Abhijit [conjunction], took their places there.
The Pañcālas have come to hear with devotion; the wise god, while they are pressing the soma, has employed both worlds as his instruments.

The past creator [ordained] the past and future times; likewise, they say that the Kurus, the Śraviṣṭhas, and the Śivas were assigned to their respective portions among the lunar mansions. Thus he distributed the grains.
For thus it is surely:
the Aṅgas and other peoples, those who dwell in caves and those who cast [offerings] into the waters, have partaken of the medicine there under the asterism Śatabhiṣaj.
The Khaḍgas, Hastins, Gavayas, Varāhas, Ahīnaras, and all the Kuntis as well,
approach the two Pūrva-proṣṭhapadas there with devotion.
The Uśīnaras have assigned parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) to the portion of the constellation belonging to the two *proṣṭhapada* stars in the north.
For thus indeed, the Śūdras together with the artisans have been turned back; and having understood the purpose, they have shared the *revatī* star there along with the *yūkās* in the south-east.
Having understood the purpose of the two horses yoked there, the great people from various regions took their places upon the vehicle whose hair does not fall out.

Both the Kīkaṭas and the Kauśalas, and those who wander about in secret while appearing to be fast asleep—having understood their purpose, they shared therein; one should know that for them, his [share] is imperishable.
A Kṣatriya who is about to engage in battle with a rival king should first seek out a Brāhmaṇa who is learned and most proficient in the sacred scriptures.
A king who wishes to live and rule his kingdom should indeed seek to obtain that man who knows the portents arising from heaven, the atmosphere, and the earth.
He who knows the stability of the planets and the prosperity of the lunar mansions should attend upon one who is unanointed and who possesses the same nature as the stars.
A king bearing weapons under the Kṛttikās does not come to harm;
for that constellation is radiant and shines brightly in the sky.
Moreover, the constellation called Kṛttikā is most radiant;
it belongs to Agni, it is the constellation of Agni, for the king prospers under it.
Under Rohiṇī, he should sit together with his wife and have ropes spun;
under Mṛgaśiras, he should maintain his horses, and thus his army shall not suffer harm.
The constellation of Soma is auspicious, for the king prospers under it.
Under Ārdrā, he should go on a hunt and strike fear into his enemies.
One should apply [the ritual] under Punarvasu; one should employ this [remedy] under Puṣya.
Cutting the reed-grass under Āśleṣā, the king suffers no harm.
One should sit together with those under the Maghā asterisms, but one should not undertake any new enterprise;
one should have the gates made of *phalgu* wood and cause attendants to carry out the work.
They should assemble the archways and have the planks carved; ...
and with the two subsequent [verses], one should offer the oblations.
One should desire the acquisition of wealth through the constellation Citrā by means of manual labor;
one may be a witness to many things under Citrā before the Abhiplava sacrifice following Svāti.
Under the asterism Svāti, one should yoke young horses intended for speed to the chariot;
furthermore, if one causes a maiden to fast under this same asterism, she quickly obtains a husband.
A king who causes [the consecration] to be performed during Viśākhā does not come to harm;
a Kṣatriya king should have the consecration anointed during Anurādhā.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should look upon an elephant and have consecrations performed;
... and one should cause the princes to fight.
One should have a moat dug with the *mūla* [mantra] and fortify the city with the *citi* [mantra].
The constellation of Nirṛti is for kings; with this [mantra], one should cause those to be slain to be killed.
Having initiated him for three nights together with the half-night, he should observe the vow during the Āṣāḍhā constellations;
he should apply himself to the rite under Abhijit and perform it under Śravaṇa.
With the Śraviṣṭhās, one should release the juices.
Under Śatabhiṣaj, one should perform medical treatments and administer medicine;
under the two Pūrvaproṣṭhapadas, one may set out on a journey...
Under the two Uttaraproṣṭhapadas, one should employ [enemies]; under Revatī, one should dwell in one's home.
The king should cause his army to march under the asterisms of Aśvinī and Bharaṇī.
The variegated lights together in heaven, the crawling things, the swift ones in the world—
desiring Turmiśa’s favor, I honor the days and the firmament with my songs.
May the Kṛttikās and Rohiṇī be easy to invoke for me, O Agni; may Mṛgaśiras be auspicious and Ārdrā bring peace;
may the two Punarvasūs be gracious, Puṣya be beautiful, Āśleṣā be radiant, and Maghā be my path of progress.
May Puṣya, Pūrvaphalgunī, and here Hasta, Citrā, Śivā, and Svātī be auspicious and pleasant to me;
may Rādha, Viśākhā, the easily invoked Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Sunakṣatra be free from harm.
May the Pūrva-aṣāḍhās grant me food; O Uttarā-aṣāḍhās, bestow strength upon me.
May Abhijit grant me merit; may Śravaṇa and the Śraviṣṭhās bring about well-being.
May the great Śatabhiṣaj come to me with wide space; may the two Proṣṭhapadas bring me good protection.
May Revatī and the two Aśvayujas bring me fortune; may they bring to me wealth and prosperity.
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, the two Punarvasūs, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, the two Pūrvaphalgunīs—these are nine; Agni is the tenth; day and night are the eleventh and twelfth.
"These very lunar mansions kindle for him prosperity, well-being, nourishment, offspring, cattle, food, and the eating of food"—thus one who knows this understands.

Now, regarding him whom he desires: "May these very lunar mansions kindle for him prosperity, well-being, nourishment, offspring, cattle, food, and the eating of food"—for that reason, in this [rite]...
One who knows thus should perform [the rite] under the constellation Citrā:

having laid the fuel-stick pointing eastward, having swept around, sprinkled water, and strewn sacrificial grass, having placed the essences upon the sacrificial grass and taken hold of them, he should then offer [the oblation], saying: "The variegated splendors together in heaven—svāhā!"
Having offered oblations into the fire, having brought the remnants of the offerings into the juices and set them aside, he then causes him to consume those juices.
If he performs [the rite] for him in this manner, these very lunar mansions kindle for him prosperity, success, nourishment, offspring, cattle, food, and the eating of food.

The two *uttare phalgunyau*, *hasta*, *citrā*, *svāti*, *viśākhe*, *anūrādhā*, *jyeṣṭhā*, *mūla*, and *pūrvāṣāḍhā*—these are the ninth; *āditya* is the tenth, namely name and form (*nāmarūpa*); the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight are the eleventh and twelfth.
These very ones belong to him.
(AVParis_1,13.3) Now, that which [is mentioned] at 1,12.3.
(AVParis_1,13.4) The fuel-stick facing eastward at 1,12.4.
(AVParis_1,13.5) In this manner at 1,12.5.

Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, the two Proṣṭhapadas, Revatī, Aśvayuj, and Bharaṇīs—these constitute the tenth [group]. ... The full moon and the new moon nights (AVParis_1,14.2)—these indeed belong to him (=1,12.2). (AVParis_1,14.3) Now, as for whom... (=1,12.3).
(The fuel-stick) facing east—1,12.4.
(The same)—1,12.5.
(AVParis_1,15.1) The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Brahmaveda, phonetics, ritual procedure, grammar, and etymology.
Metre, astronomy, history and ancient lore, dialogue, the current year,
the following year, the full year, the tenth [item], cold and heat as the eleventh and twelfth—
these indeed belong to him.
(AVParis_1,15.3) Now, that which [is stated] at 1,12.3.
(AVParis_1,15.4) The fuel-stick facing east at 1,12.4.
(AVParis_1,15.5) In this manner at 1,12.5.

In-breath, out-breath, diffused breath, equalizing breath, up-breath; sight, hearing, speech, mind—this is the ninth. Name and form are the tenth; the eleventh and twelfth are these very [elements]. (AVParis_1,16.2) These indeed belong to him. (AVParis_1,16.3) Now, that which... (AVParis_1,16.3) ...is as follows. (AVParis_1,12.3)
(AVParis_1,16.4) The fuel-stick facing east—1,12.4. (AVParis_1,16.5) Thus—1,12.5.
(AVParis_1,17.1) The noble was born; nobility was born; glory was born; splendor was born; brilliance was born; power was born; greatness was born.

"Unborn is Brahmā; unborn is the splendor of the Brāhmaṇa; unborn is the sovereign lord born from the birth of all worlds, all gods, all Vedas, all beings, and all rivers—he who knows this becomes unborn. (AVParis 1,17.2) Now, regarding whomsoever one might desire [to be the sovereign lord] of all worlds, all gods, all Vedas...
"May he be born as the lord of all beings and of all rivers, one who is himself unborn. Therefore, one who knows this should perform [the rite] under this very constellation.
(1,17.3) The fuel is placed facing east.
(1,17.4) If he performs [the rite] for him in this manner, he becomes the unborn overlord of the birth of all worlds, all gods, all Vedas, all beings, and all flowing rivers.

"This constellation is indeed named 'Established Renown' (*viṣṭhitaśravas*). He who stands upon it in the forenoon—his holy fame becomes established; holy fame comes to him, holy fame stays with him, and holy fame does not depart from him. He becomes possessed of renown through offspring, cattle, prosperity, houses, and wealth—so he knows."
Now, if one should desire of someone: "May his fame spread abroad; may fame come to him;

may fame abide with him; may fame not depart from him; may he be possessed of fame through offspring, cattle, prosperity, houses, and wealth," then one who knows this should perform [the rite] under that very constellation.
Having placed the fuel-stick pointing eastward and having strewn the sacrificial grass around, he places the juices upon the grass;

then, taking hold [of the ladle], he should offer with "To the all-conquering conqueror, svāhā! Having offered in the fire and poured the remnants of the offering into the juices, and having concluded the oblations, he then makes him eat those juices.

If he acts thus for him, his glorious fame stands firm; glorious fame goes to him, glorious fame remains with him, and glorious fame does not depart from him. He becomes possessed of fame through offspring, cattle, prosperity, and houses.

(19.1) This constellation is indeed named *varcas* (splendor). When one performs [the rite] at midday, splendor goes to him; splendor remains with him; splendor does not depart from him. "He becomes possessed of splendor through offspring, cattle, prosperity, houses, and wealth"—thus he knows.
(19.2) Now, regarding one whom he might desire: "May splendor go to him; may splendor remain with him; may splendor not depart from him."

"Luster might depart from me; may I be endowed with luster through offspring, cattle, prosperity, house, and wealth"—thinking thus, one who knows this should perform [the rite] under that very constellation.
Having placed the fuel-wood towards the east and having strewn sacrificial grass around, he places the juices upon the sacrificial grass; then, touching them, he should offer oblations, saying:

"Thou art splendor; bestow splendor upon me, svāhā! Having offered into the fire and poured the remnants of the offerings into the juices, and having concluded the oblations, he then causes him to eat those juices.

If he performs [the rite] for him in this manner, splendor (*varcas*) goes to him; splendor abides in him; splendor does not depart from him. He becomes possessed of splendor through offspring, cattle, fortune, houses, and wealth.
“This lunar mansion is indeed named *tejas* (splendor). If one performs [the rite] during the afternoon, splendor goes to him;
splendor remains with him; splendor does not depart from him. He becomes possessed of splendor through offspring, cattle, prosperity, houses, and wealth—so he who knows this understands.
Now, regarding whom one might desire: ‘May splendor go to him; may splendor remain with him; may splendor not depart from him’...”

"May the brilliance depart; may he who possesses brilliance be deprived of offspring, cattle, fortune, house, and wealth"—therefore, one who knows this should perform [the rite] under that very constellation.

Having placed the fuel-wood pointing eastward, having strewn the sacrificial grass around, and having placed the juices upon the sacrificial grass, he should touch them and then offer oblations, saying:

"Thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me, svāhā! Having offered into the fire, having poured the remnants of the offerings into the juices, and having concluded the oblations, he then causes him to consume those juices.

If he performs [the rite] for him in this manner, splendor goes to him; splendor abides with him; splendor does not depart from him. He becomes endowed with splendor through offspring, cattle, prosperity, houses, and wealth.
That constellation which is in the forenoon is indeed named Viṣṭhitaśravas.
That constellation which is at midday is indeed named Splendor.
This constellation that appears in the afternoon is indeed named Tejas (Splendor).
But indeed, when performed at the wrong time, they become ineffective.
That lunar mansion which is in the first part of the night is indeed named Viṣṭhitaśravas.
This constellation that is at midnight is indeed named Splendor (*varcas*).
This constellation that appears in the latter part of the night is indeed named Tejas (Splendor).
They become effective when applied at their respective times.
(As for those [verses] which indeed belong to the night, they remain unapplied.)
He who indeed knows the auspicious day of the day becomes possessed of an auspicious day; an auspicious day accrues to him, and he makes it truly auspicious.
The sun is the vehicle and the auspicious day; therefore, one who knows this should perform [the rite] under that very constellation.
Having placed the fuel-wood facing eastward and having strewn the sacrificial grass, he places the juices upon the grass;

then, while maintaining contact, he should offer them, saying "To the all-conquering conqueror, svāhā! Having offered into the fire and poured the remnants of the oblations into the juices, and having concluded the offerings, he then causes him to consume those juices.
If he performs [the rite] for him in this manner, it becomes an auspicious day for him; an auspicious day accrues to him; he indeed makes it an auspicious day.
He who knows the auspicious day of the night becomes one whose days are auspicious; for him there is an auspicious day, and he makes his days truly auspicious.
The moon is indeed the auspicious day of the night; therefore, one who knows this should perform [the rite] under that very constellation.

Having placed the fuel-stick facing eastward and having strewn the sacrificial grass around, he places the juices upon the sacrificial grass; then, having taken hold [of the ladle], he should offer oblations.
Having offered into the fire with "Svāhā to the King," and having poured the remnants of the offerings into the juices, and having concluded the oblations, he then makes him eat those juices.
If he performs [the rite] for him in this way, it becomes an auspicious day for him; an auspicious day accrues to him; he makes it truly an auspicious day.
Whoever knows the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) of the day and night becomes possessed of an auspicious day; an auspicious day accrues to him, and he makes it truly auspicious.
Or a Brāhmaṇa may declare the day and night to be an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).
One should ask him, "By what has it been won?
If he should say, "It must be performed," one should do so accordingly.
He becomes auspicious; for him there is an auspicious day; he makes it truly auspicious.

Whatever constellations are in heaven, in the intermediate space, in the waters, on the earth, or upon the mountains, and whatever the moon traverses as it courses through the quarters— may all these be auspicious for me.
May the twenty-eight auspicious and beneficial [days] grant me union. I resort to union and resort to security; I resort to security and resort to union. Homage be to Day and Night!
May there be well-being for me; may my morning be auspicious, my evening auspicious, my day auspicious, my deer auspicious, and my omens auspicious.
O Agni, having gone to the immortal world of well-being, may you return again with joy, being easy to invoke.
O Savitṛ, drive away all those who seek to seize me from behind, those who seek to seize me from the side, those who revile me, and those who sneer at me— drive them all away like empty jars.
May we enjoy the auspicious sneeze that drives away evil; may your nostrils be propitious, and may the one seeking merit urinate upon us.
O Brahmaṇaspati, those waters which blow forth in all directions—
O Indra, having made them flow together, make them most auspicious for me.
May there be well-being for us; may there be fearlessness for us; homage be to Day and Night.
Having eaten curd-rice, if one should rise while the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikās, he indeed returns having achieved his purpose.

On Rohiṇī, [one should offer] beef; on Mṛgaśiras, deer meat; on Ārdrā, blood; on the two Punarvasus, the food of a householder; on Puṣya, ghee with milk-rice. These, indeed, are the constellations whose gates face the east.

If he should encounter, while heading toward the eastern direction, someone with a weapon in hand, someone with a noose around the neck, or an executioner, he should turn back; for indeed, within a *krośa* of that point, there is no obstacle to his purpose, but beyond a *krośa*, it becomes impossible to avoid.
Having eaten *kṛśara* with oil, if the moon should rise during the *Maghā* asterisms, he returns having indeed achieved his purpose.
Having eaten mutton, if the moon should rise during the two *Phalgunī*s, [he succeeds]; with meat soups during the latter two;
having eaten *praiyaṅgava* rice mixed with sesame in his hand, if the moon should rise during *Citrā*; and having eaten those [grains] that are the largest, if the moon should rise during *Jyeṣṭhā*.
If the moon should rise in Svāti, one should offer cakes during Viśākhā;
these indeed are the lunar mansions that have their gates toward the south. When it has risen toward the southern direction, with a hand for reclining or a hand for spreading out a mat—

If he should meet [someone] with a hand carrying a palanquin, or a hand holding the end of a garment, or a hand on the knee, he should turn back; for indeed, within a *krośa* of that point, there is no obstacle to his purpose beyond one *krośa*. If, after eating at threshing floors, the moon should rise in conjunction with the *Anurādhā* asterism, he returns having surely achieved his goal.
Having eaten the best food, he should rise with the *jyeṣṭhā* constellation; having eaten roots, he should rise with *mūla*;
having eaten juices, he should rise with the *pūrvā-aṣāḍhā*s; having eaten curd-rice with fresh butter, he should rise with the *uttarā-aṣāḍhā*s;
having conquered [the obstacle], he should rise with *abhijit*; having eaten [food], he should rise with *śravaṇa*.

(29.3) These, indeed, are the lunar mansions of the western gate. (29.4) Whenever one encounters a man with a noose in his hand, or a net in his hand, or a fisherman, having set out toward the western direction, he should turn back; for within a *krośa* from here, there will be no obstacle to his purpose beyond that *krośa*.
If one eats split-pea soup and the moon rises while the moon is in the *Śraviṣṭhās*, he returns having indeed achieved his purpose.

If one eats vegetables under *Śatabhiṣaj*, or eats iguana with beef under the two *Pūrvaproṣṭhapadas*, and the moon rises; or if one eats meat broths under the two *Uttaraproṣṭhapadas* and the moon rises; or if one eats the meal of a householder’s wife under *Revatī* and the moon rises; or if one eats unbroken beans under the *Aśvinyas*—[in these cases, he returns having achieved his purpose].

If the sun should rise while one has eaten sesame and rice, or if it should rise during the *bharaṇī* constellations—these indeed are the constellations whose doors face north. Wherever he may encounter someone coming from the northern direction with a drink in hand, or with meal-dough in hand, or with a sieve, he should turn back; for this is within a *krośa*, not beyond.
Within the distance of a *krośa*, the purpose becomes unimpeded.
Then, as the king is about to depart, they bring forward a white goat facing to the right, together with a Brāhmaṇa dressed in white garments.
If a well-established, unswerving bull, horned and tawny,
bellows while mingled with the [other] sounds, they call that the highest accomplishment.
An elephant, a banner, a chariot, a parasol, armor, adorned warriors, all ornaments, and excellent weapons.
All kinds of musical instruments, as well as various banners,
white flowers, parched grain, unbroken rice, and white mustard seeds.
Having honored all the deities with fruits, full vessels, incense, perfumes, water, and sesame seeds, and having likewise paid homage to the Brahmins;
Placing the domestic priest at the forefront, as well as his friends and ministers, one who sets out in this manner attains victory; of this there is no doubt.
And [he should give] an elephant of auspicious name, appearing free from physical defects,
and a well-adorned maiden holding a vessel of curd.
(If it should happen, O wretched Adhigu, that in the house of the sun and moon,
the Aśvins should perform a circumambulation of the carriage drawn by a noble donkey.)

One should circumambulate clockwise the fire, cows, Brahmins, a king, a chariot, and a four-horse, six-horse, or eight-horse wagon; likewise a pond that turns to the right, a rising youth, a basket full of people, and the earth as it rises up.
For one who has been bound as a single sacrificial animal,
the owl, the black bird, the swift falcon, and the quail—
these birds fly from left to right; furthermore, the blue jay is seen here.
One should always avoid the nests of cranes, owls, priyas, and tree-dwelling birds located near sacred shrines.

If one sees anyone lying on their side, face down, or prostrate; someone inverted; someone with missing limbs or extra limbs; someone deformed, naked, shaven-headed, or castrated; someone with variegated skin, dark spots, black teeth, or deformed nails; or someone with matted hair or wearing saffron-colored or woolen garments—one should not go [to that house] upon seeing any of these.
If one should go, let those who seek wealth go for their purpose; let them go to the giver’s bounty.
One should mutter this verse: "They have fulfilled the desire of the thirsty one."
"Seizing the Dasyus, concealing them, O Indra!"— or "Praise the famous one"—
or "The gods generated divine speech; that the animals of every form speak."

"May she, the cow Speech, yielding us joy, refreshment, and strength, come to us with fair praise"— with these words he counters [the opponent] by means of a donkey's bray; thus, through this contrary action, all evil words are rendered ineffective,
as is the sight of ill-clad persons.
For it is for the sake of harm that there is lack of purpose; it is for the sake of seeing that [lack of purpose].
Or rather, it is the accomplishment of those who desire to cast off evil.
Now, regarding the durations of illness:
under the *uttarā-aṣāḍhā*s, under the two *proṣṭhapada*s, and for one month;
under *rohiṇī*, for twenty nights.

Under Punarvasu, there is a period of nineteen nights; under the first two [nakṣatras] for those who live in pairs. Under Mṛgaśiras, there is a period of sixteen nights; under Abhijit and Śravaṇa as well. Under Ārdrā, there is a period of fifteen nights; and under Anurādhā, Śraviṣṭhā, and Bharaṇī as well.

Under Puṣya, one observes a twelve-night vow; under Hasta and Svāti, likewise. Under Śatabhiṣaj, one observes a nine-night vow for a month, performing the rite at the time of speech. Under Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, one observes an eight-night vow.
(On the day of the asterism) Revatī, [one should fast] for seven nights;
on Kṛttikā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, the two Uttaraphalgunīs, Citrā, Viśākhā, and the two Aśvayujas—on these seven [asterisms], for ten nights.

(Now, the offerings: White curd, white rice-porridge cooked with milk, white rice-porridge cooked with seven herbs, eighthly rice-porridge mixed with meat-mince, parched grains, groats, and then a fried cake.
A variegated [cock], a wild cock, a white one, a *kambūka-piṇḍaka*, all kinds of seeds, roots, a vessel of water, and two milk-rice offerings.
For the *paśu* [day] there is ghee and a *kaśīkā* bird; for the *ārdramāṃsa* [day], milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
on the *pathyā* [day], roasted flour of black gram (*māṣasaktu*) and milk-rice; then, on the [next day], rice mixed with sesame (*tilaudana*).

In every case, one should employ perfumes, flowers, parched grain, and ointments; furthermore, one should apply the appropriate lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the door-opening time (*anudvāra*), and the presiding deity (*daivata*) to the occasion.
Lamps should be brightly lit within the mandala, and one should offer a pure oblation with the verse: "He who in this [world]... he who [says] 'you' to your mother," reciting it in reverse order.
A bronze vessel with white barley meal is an auspicious object for the eastern part;
a flowing stream and a piece of meat are auspicious objects for the southern part.
A maiden and a bronze vessel of curd are an auspicious omen for one who seeks to return; a draft-ox and a student of sacred knowledge are an auspicious omen for one who seeks to go forth.
A maiden, well-adorned and holding a vessel of curd, should perform a circumambulation; thus it is held that success will certainly be achieved.
If an army has risen up and a jackal howls toward it, one should know that either the king or a minister will die; in that case, one should mutter the Vāruṇī verse:
"O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond. (RV 1.24.15)
If smoke should follow an army that has risen up from the waters, one should know: "He will be victorious.
One should consecrate it with the mantra: "Radiant is thy smoke."

If the wind blows favorably against an army that has set out, one should know that they will be victorious; one should then consecrate them with the mantra, "May the wind blow [favorably]! (vāta ā vātu).
If a deer should touch an army that has set out, one should know that its purpose will perish;
one should consecrate it with the mantra: "The deer is not terrible, the one who moves on the ground and dwells in the mountains."
If birds should fly across an army that has been mobilized, one should offer meat and rice there;
one should consecrate them with the mantra: "The *aliklavas*, the *jāṣkamadas*, the vultures."
If a *kapiñjala* bird should address an army that has risen up, saying, "Speak what is auspicious," they recite three *kāpiñjala* hymns of praise.
O you who, with a tawny iron mouth, devour the sleeping man as he lies there defenseless—
may Varuṇa protect us all around with a spell of iron and a shield of stone.
Thus he lies down in the open air;
he lies down in the open air.

May the divine Agni, whose path is black, Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, the consumer of the first essence of offerings, the purifier among the stars— may that blazing one be appeased for us by the Kṛttikās, the foremost of the lunar mansions.

Prajāpati, who created these creatures and, having created the gods, assigned them to their tasks— he, the consumer of all, in all applications, together with Rohiṇī, may perform auspicious rites for the accomplishment of the work.
May he who knows the Vidyās, who, being free from affliction, worships Śakra together with the hosts of deities—
may that sovereign king, Mṛgaśiras, perform auspicious rites for us so that our actions may achieve success.
May that Rudra—who is praised as the god Bhava, Paśupati, Hara, Kṛśa, Mahādeva, Śarva, Ugra, and Śikhaṇḍin; who is the thousand-eyed one and the thunderbolt—protect us with his moist [favor].
May she who is worshipped by the wise and the poets, by the Dākṣāyaṇas and by men such as Devapura,
she who is the first-born and the Punarvasu— being praised by us, may she make our rites auspicious for the accomplishment of our actions.
I worship Bṛhaspati, the wise teacher of the gods, by whose Vedic studenthood and ritual action the gods overcame the great Asura through their fierce power; may he, together with Puṣya, protect me.
Those Aśleṣās whom I, being praised, release for us through wisdom— those who were tormented by the seers with the fires of desire—
may they, along with the wise seers, the sons of Jaratkāru, protect us from serpents.

Those who have attained divinity through their meritorious deeds, those others, and the great seers beyond them—I, as a son, honor these ancestors who have gone to the realm of King Yama; may they perform auspicious rites for us and grant us prosperity.

He who, performing his work, sustains the people and traverses the earth, bringing prosperity and pleasing all creatures—him I praise in the two *phalgunī* constellations, which are most auspicious, well-adorned, and presided over by that deity; I seek his favor and his protection in the former of the two.
I praise Aryaman, the god who is extolled by the ancient sages, setting forth my speech within the world;
may the two Phalgunīs, most auspicious and adorned, belonging to that deity, be favorable to us for the sake of the divine assembly.
He whose golden chariot, drawn by dark steeds and white-footed, rolls along easy paths—may that Savitṛ, the golden-eater with golden hands, protect us with his hand; may Savitṛ guard us.
Homage to Tvaṣṭṛ, the creator of the earth, the wise one, the protector of beings, the performer of supreme deeds!
May she, the wondrous goddess who bears forms, being praised along with Yoga, grant us the success of our actions.

May the divine Wind, who, becoming auspicious, sustains the vital apertures of living beings while keeping them alive, who is the consumer of the finest essences, the banner of the intermediate space, and the supporter of all creatures— may he protect us through the constellation Svāti.

May Indra and Agni, the bestowers of boons, who are praised by the wise who know the Self, who together sing at the three libations, and who are honored with salutations— may they grant prosperity for the long life of Viśākha and Yā.
The All-Gods call him a seer, Mitra, Bharadvāja, a seer from of old and a knower of the *prasāma* chants;
him I praise with a *jagatī* verse and a *gāthā*. May he, together with the fierce Anurādhas, protect me—[may Bhṛtakaṇva protect me].

He of a hundredfold power, who slew Śambara and, having slain Vṛtra, released the flowing rivers— may that Puraṃdara, praised by us with a pleased mind and accompanied by the Maruts, protect us with his supreme protection.
She who by her might sustains the station beyond the gods— the Mother Earth, the supporter of all beings—
may she, the Goddess Nirṛti, being praised, provide the foundation for the success of our rites in all undertakings.

I praise those waters, created by Parjanya, encompassed by the three [nights], which satisfy [all] on every side for the sake of growth—those Vāruṇī waters... may the former Āṣāḍhās be present at the station with their own inherent power.
Those thirty-three gods who rejoice, and the many more created from the name of the gods—
may those invincible ones, O Vasu, all of them auspicious and well-disposed, perform for us deeds that bring delight.
He who is all-knowing, the maker of all, the sustainer of all beings, than whom there is nothing else higher;
he who is uncreated, the conqueror of truth, praised by many—may that Brahmā, the victorious one, protect us.

May Viṣṇu, the god, protect with his fame him who, having stepped forth thrice, established Indra’s place for drinking and that of the gods, and who, though fallen from his station, set it right again; may he protect all that heavenly realm, the back of the firmament.
The eight hundred white-marked horses which you and he struck down in great numbers—
may those steeds, though embarrassed on both sides by the lack of instruction, protect us with the Śraviṣṭhās.
The goddess Vājā, Devamṛṇānikā, and both Ākubhau, auspicious through their deeds of subduing, [protect] the vigor of the sacrifice.
We praise your troop, O you who are the food of the gods; may the two physicians, Pratyagbhiṣaj and Śatabhiṣaj, be auspicious to us.
May Śuna and Sīra release us from crookedness; may they, flowing forth, grant beautiful breasts to the ancestors.
May those two, the first-born, the one-footed Aja, and the foundation, establish us for the fulfillment of all desires and for fearlessness.
For the sake of all goals and for the accomplishment of ritual action, I pay homage to the one praised by the cow, who performs manifold deeds.
May that Ahi Budhnya make the two [worlds] superior, auspicious, and firm foundations, for the fulfillment of all desires and for freedom from fear.
May Pūṣan— who knows the peaceful ones from the great golden seer Bharadvāja, who [knows] the two moons and the sun,
and who possesses the two horse-yoked [chariots] for the sake of fear— make for us that which is wealthy and auspicious.
Those two who, through their wisdom, made the aged Cyavana young again, and who were made the drinkers of Soma for the seer—
may those two auspicious Aśvins, the physicians who honor him with their thoughts, grant us offspring through the Aśvin constellation.

May Yama the King, together with the two brindled dogs, Śyāma and Śabala— who guard the funeral offerings, who distinguish between evil deeds and good deeds, and who sustain the various peoples— protect us along with the Bharaṇīs, through the impulse of Savitṛ and by those who walk the path of dharma.
Now I shall explain the complete ritual for the lunar mansion baths (*nakṣatrasnāna*),
as well as the worship of the planetary deities, for each [mansion] and in each case according to the prescribed rule.
One who knows the conjunctions of the lunar mansions and the proper times, having performed the ritual procedure according to the rules,
should worship the planets with sacrificial offerings and the deities with the oblations as prescribed.

The wise one, recollecting the ritual procedure, should prepare a jar possessing auspicious marks, filled with water and the necessary ingredients, having performed the *saṃpāta* oblation while reciting the mantras.
With the Sāvitrī, with hymns of pacification (*śāntisūkta*), and likewise with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*);
with praises of the waters, with purificatory hymns, and likewise with laudations of the constellations.

One who understands the application of ritual characteristics and injunctions should insert the mantras dedicated to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) for each respective mansion, and likewise insert the mantras intended for specific desires.

Then, having performed the *saṃpāta* oblation and consecrated [the water], one who is skilled in the ritual of the *nakṣatra-snāna* should bathe the seeker with auspicious words while it is being consecrated.
This very same rule is prescribed for the sacrificial assistants (*sadasya*) regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):
one should first satiate the body [with food] and afterwards give the sacrificial fee.
Having bathed according to this rite, one should also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here;
he obtains the favor of men and enjoys the fruit of the Vedas.
Having purified oneself and having worshipped the gods as well as the planets,
one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the learned and satisfy the twice-born with food.
One who desires to be honored by kings should bathe [the image] with the leaf-shreds of the *śirīṣa*, the *aśvattha*, and the *vaṭa* under the asterism Kṛttikā.
Under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should cause a Vaiśya to bathe, adorned with all kinds of seeds;
having placed unbroken grains (*akṣata*) between [him and the water], he thus merits good fortune.
When the constellation Mṛgaśiras is joined [with the moon], then bathing is prescribed;
one seeking wealth should bathe with pearls, gems, and gold.
Those merchants who bathe on the day of Ārdrā with *śrīveṣṭaka*, resin of *sarja*, *tagara*, *uśīra*, and *pattraka* obtain excellent gains.
Under the two Punarvasus, one should take the topmost earth from a cow-path;
one desiring cattle should bathe [the image] on a cow-hiding place, and he will quickly become possessed of cattle.
A Brāhmaṇa who has bathed on three Puṣya days, using a thousand seeds of red rice, as many white mustard seeds, sahasravīryā, anantā, madayantī, and priyaṅgu, obtains royal glory.
Under the asterism Aśleṣā, one should have earth brought from both riverbanks;
by bathing a horse with this, it will become a swift runner.
One should bathe with sesame seeds under the Maghā asterism, as well as with blue and white lotuses;
in that month, that maiden quickly obtains a husband.
Now, during the two former Phalgunīs, *śatapuṣpā*, *priyaṅgu*,
and honey as the third [ingredient] shall constitute a rite that increases good fortune and enjoyment.
Then, during the two Uttaraphalgunīs, one should employ this bath consisting of unhusked grains and white mustard seeds; it is the supreme means for establishing progeny.
For all artisans and also for thieves,
bathing with clay from rivers, mountains, and lakes by hand is always the most excellent practice.
On the day of Citrā, one who desires a woman should bathe with variegated garlands and all kinds of perfumes; by that means, he quickly obtains his beloved.
Under the asterism Svāti, she should bathe with perfumes, as well as with blue and white water-lilies;
in that month, that maiden is then quickly given in marriage.
Anointed with the horn of a rhinoceros, an elephant, or a bull at the Viśākhā nakṣatra, the king shall rule over the earth.
Under the constellation Anurādhā, one should have clay brought from a hundred anthills;
by bathing with that, one performs a plowing rite, and through it, one increases in wealth and grain.
In the month of Jyeṣ� juices and mixed grains, one should consecrate the domestic priest who desires preeminence; once consecrated, he should consume the juices.
Seated upon the Sarvatobhadra diagram with the root mantra, the woman of excellent complexion gives birth to a son after bathing with a thousand *śamī* leaves.
Now, she who bathes under the *pūrvā-aṣāḍhā* [nakṣatra] while wearing an unwashed garment,
being beautiful with gold, enjoys prosperity and is dear to her husband.
Now, if one who has fasted should bathe during the later *aṣāḍhā* [nakṣatra],
he prospers with great ponds, *uśīra* grass, and male and female servants.
Having bathed with *vacā*, blue lotus, *kuṣṭha*, *brāhmī*, and white mustard seeds, a Brāhmaṇa who has performed the *abhijit* rite obtains royal glory.
He who bathes at the confluences of rivers that flow upon hearing [the sacred sound] shall unite with gold, bullion, or wealth.
One desiring wealth should have [the patron] bathed with sandalwood under the Śraviṣṭhā asterisms;
by employing this bath, one increases in wealth and grain.
One desiring healing should perform the consecration under Śatabhiṣaj during rites for pacification;
thus consecrated, he is cleansed of evil and liberated from all diseases.
Then, having bathed with the light of the two former Pūrvaproṣṭhapadas, with collyrium,
and with an elephant’s tusk, one shall cause a king to be born as a son.
Then, during the two Uttaraproṣṭhapadās, one should bathe the Gandharva with honey and *prasannāpadmaka*; by that means, he will become a royal vehicle-bearer.
Having bathed on the day of Revatī with the horn of a rhinoceros, water, honey, and clarified butter, a Kṣatriya becomes a king who rules over the earth.
On the day of Aśvinī, a svastika-shaped garland made of madayantī and priyaṅgu flowers constitutes a bath for a courtesan; it increases her good fortune and her enjoyment.
Having bathed with *bharaṇī* flowers, auspicious *musta* grass, cardamom, and white mustard seeds, she may go to her husband’s family home free from rivals and free from thorns.

O all-knowing and omnipresent Nārada, proclaim wisdom that is not inferior to that of others! When a man has attained the world of heaven by means of his body and other [faculties] through those paths,
when he has fasted, is pure in conduct, and possesses a holy fragrance— if he remains constantly untiring before eating until the sun has set— [then he attains it].
The accomplishment of ritual action preceded by the conduct of the traditional rules is praised; one who desires heaven, having passed away, attains that which yields all desires.
One who desires heaven should feed him milk-rice with clarified butter under the asterism of Kṛttikā; having departed from this world, he attains that cow of plenty.
On the day of Rohiṇī, one should bestow upon him unbroken mung beans mixed with ghee, along with rice and milk-based food and drink; thus he remains uninjured even in the abode of Yama.
Under the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should bestow a milch-goat; having milked for him all his desires, she goes on before as a provider of nourishment.
Under the asterism Ārdrā, one who has fasted should offer kṛsara mixed with oil;
under the two Punarvasus, he should bestow unsurpassed honey-cakes.
One should bestow a golden ornament under the constellation Puṣya; he remains unharmed in the abode of Yama.
One sent by the bull should give silver under Āśleṣā.
The serpent that stands as an obstacle to the deceased destroys his happiness through fear;
however, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with honey under the Maghā asterism while remembering the ancestors.
There, those who are Soma-sacrificers attend upon them with their desires.
[One should offer bricks mixed with molasses during the two former Phalgunīs, and with honey during the two latter.
During the two former and latter Phalgunīs, they milk the honey and the molasses.
A man who gives a large elephant-chariot yoked with an elephant by means of his hand attains the station of Savitṛ, a celestial assembly hall that moves at will.
On the day of Citrā, one should give a low-caste woman adorned with all kinds of flowers;
by serving her with perfumes, one attains a fragrant state in the eternal realm.
At the Svāti constellation, one should give away all one's wealth and whatever else is dear to one in the house;
one should go forth without attachment, like the bodiless mind.
One should cause a cow endowed with beauty, or two oxen capable of drawing a load,
to reach the highest station by means of the two Viśākhās, accompanied by a honey-mixture.
Under Anurādhā, one should give a garment; under Jyeṣṭhā, pure food.
And one should give food to the Brahmins along with various kinds of snacks.
Having fasted, one who mixes liquor with its root for non-Brahmin women becomes free from debt to his mother and is released from the mixture of castes.
One should prepare a stirred drink with honey during the Pūrvā-aṣāḍhās, and a superior one during the Uttarā-aṣāḍhās.
One should give one's daughter, preceded by the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*), to an *Abhijit* [bridegroom];
in the highest station of Brahman, he rejoices in all his desires.
Having fasted, one should give a woolen blanket under the asterism Śravaṇa; another garment under Śraviṣṭhā; a pair of garments under Śatabhiṣaj; and perfumes under Śatabhiṣaj.
One should cook goat meat and offer it as boiled rice during the two former Proṣṭhapadas; during the latter two, one should offer it with mutton.

And one should give a cow endowed with beauty—a young cow that has had only one calf and yields a full udder—along with a three-year-old calf, when the moon is in the constellation Revatī; she should be auspicious and accompanied by a bronze milking vessel.
Having bound two oxen together with a cloth, a man should give them during the Aśvayuj festival;
for every single hair, he is honored in heaven for ten thousand years.
One enjoys the milk of a goat-cow for eight thousand years;
one enjoys the milk of a cow-cow for ten thousand years.
But he who gives a bull that is a good draught-animal and a friend to its master attains the status of a hero and a sustainer of his subjects, equal to one who has given ten cows.
(When two feet and also the head of the calf are visible, then the cow should be known as the Earth, as long as she does not release the fetus.
Under the Bharaṇī asterisms, one should give black sesame seeds— a milch cow made of sesame— as a gift.
By means of it, one crosses over difficult places and mountains with edges as sharp as razors.
As Soma is among the stars and the Sun among the luminaries,
so does the pure, supreme, purifying fire shine as a divine light in heaven.

Whoever gives this aforementioned sacrificial fee for the constellations here in the world of the living, having struck away all darkness, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. As it is for the sacrificer, so it is for the student; this is the Vedic promise, this is the Vedic promise.

(Pariśiṣṭa 1b. [The Mantras of the Paippalāda School between Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī]) (AVParis 1b.1.1) Oṃ. When they made King Śakadhūma the constellations, they bestowed upon him an auspicious day; from that, sovereignty was born.
May there be a blessed day for us in the evening; may there be a blessed day for us in the morning.
O Śakadhūma, make every day blessed for us always.
To you who have brought us auspiciousness in the evening, in the morning, and likewise by day— to you, O King of Constellations, whose smoke is dung, we offer perpetual homage.
That which they call the smoke of cow-dung, the first-born light of the great constellations at the beginning—
may that grant us hundredfold prosperity and bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
Whatever consumption has entered this man, impelled by divine power—may Agni, who awakens with clarified butter, leap away from us; may it go far from us and encounter another.
For him we bring forth [this offering].
He who has encompassed you as you were being born from your mother or from your father— he whom we do not cause to perish through you, let him enter into another woman.

Let the *aliklava* birds, vultures, herons, eagles, beasts of prey, winged creatures, fowl, and birds roam upon the funeral pyre of such-and-such a descendant of such-and-such a lineage, the son of such-and-such a woman.
The mantras of Paippalāda are between Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī.

(Pariśiṣṭa 2: The Collection of the Realm) (AVParis 2.1.1) Om! Having paid homage to Brahmā, the knower of the Veda, to Rudra, and to Parameṣṭhin, I shall proclaim the remaining Atharvaṇa ritual procedure.
Fate is the supreme power; human effort is merely an instrument. But when fate is well-guarded, one is capable of conquering the earth.
Between fate and human effort, fate alone is superior;
therefore, a lord of the earth should especially honor fate.
Therefore, the king should constantly maintain the astrologer and the domestic priest— who are both experts in divine rites— by means of gifts, honors, and pleasing attentions.
Just as a child is without a father, so is a king without an astrologer; just as a child is without a mother, so is one who is devoid of the Atharva Veda.
Just as one is alone in the midst of enemies, so is one who is bereft of a physician.
The lord of the earth, intending to conquer the entire world through righteousness,
should choose as his preceptor a descendant of Bhṛgu who is endowed with both learning and the auspicious marks.
For Prajāpati alone determines the certainty of the fourfold action through the true essence of the Veda; he does not regard the three Vedas as sufficient.
That which is peaceful and distinct from the Atharva is peaceful, not by the other three;
through the knowledge of the Brahma-veda, realization arises within the three worlds.
Atharvan creates the terrible; likewise, he pacifies the marvelous.
Atharvan protects the sacrifice; Aṅgiras is the lord of the sacrifice.
Because he knows the Veda of Brahman, Bhṛgu is the pacifier of manifold portents— celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial— and therefore he is the protector.
The Brahman priest shall pacify [the obstacles], neither the Adhvaryu, nor the Chandoga, nor the Bahvṛca;
for the Brahman protects against the Rakṣases, therefore the Brahman must be a knower of the Atharvan.
Therefore, for the protection of the army, for the increase of his own kingdom,
and for the sake of peace, the protector of the earth should appoint a descendant of Bhṛgu as his preceptor.
The king should give ten million as the fee for the selection of a preceptor;
he should give half, a quarter, or a third of his share of the earth.
In this way, one should indicate a ten-millionth part according to the measurement of the ground;
or rather, the teacher should act toward the king in whatever manner he himself may be satisfied.
Divine calamities strike and the god does not send rain;
heroes are not born there in that kingdom which is without a domestic priest.
The deities, the ancestors, and the twice-born do not accept the sacrificial offering of that lord of the earth in whose house there is no teacher learned in the Atharva Veda.

One should appoint as a preceptor the follower of the Paippalāda [recension], whose limbs and minor members are well-composed, who is endowed with the virtues of knowledge and conduct, and who increases prosperity, the kingdom, and health.
Likewise, one should also [appoint] a follower of Śaunaka who is learned in the Vedic mantras,
the constant bringer of prosperity to the kingdom through wealth, grain, and other such means.
Except for one who is an Atharvan, no other teacher learned in the Atharva-veda should be appointed by a king desiring victory, just as the sacrificial fire is prepared at a ritual.
The Bahvṛca indeed destroys the kingdom; the Adhvaryu would cause the Soma-pressings to perish;
the Chandoga leads to the loss of wealth; therefore, the Atharvan is the [proper] teacher.
If one whose teacher is a Bahvṛca should [behave] out of ignorance or negligence,
there will undoubtedly be the destruction of his country, kingdom, city, and ministers.
If the King appoints the domestic priest to perform the duties of the Adhvaryu,
he will quickly be slain by the sword, his wealth and vehicles utterly exhausted.
Just as a lame man cannot travel the road, nor a wingless bird the sky, so a king does not attain prosperity without a teacher of the Sāmaveda.
If one's domestic priest (purohita) is a member of the Jalaḍa or Mauda lineage at any time,
that king shall suffer the loss of his kingdom within ten months from a year.
All this is but straw, established as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman;
the Atharvāṅgirases know the essence of essences to be the grain.
The three worlds, the three gods, the three Vedas, and the three fires—these all go to dissolution in the half-measure; and the Atharva Veda is likewise declared [to do so].
Neither the lunar day, nor the constellation, nor the planet, nor the moon matters;
through the attainment of the Atharva mantras, all success shall come to pass.
Through the Guru Paippalāda, who is an expert in the Vedic mantras, the kingdom will undoubtedly increase in wealth and grain; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires land should not beg from a donor, even if that donor is a king, if he is stubborn, cruel, negligent, lacking in faith, or ignorant of the scriptures.
By reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred thousand times, a priest who sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrifice,
as well as a killer of an embryo and even an eater of the food of a Cāṇḍāla, is purified.
Purification through the renunciation of all possessions has been proclaimed by some;
by others, it is said that the highest purification consists in studying the first verses of the four Vedas.
Whether from performing a sacrifice, a malevolent rite, or any ritual action involving mantras,
they declare that the twice-born are indeed purified, possessing a radiance like fire and gold.
Thus ends the Rāṣṭrasaṃvarga.
(Pariśiṣṭa 3: The First Consecration of the King) (AVParis 3.1.1) Om. Now, one should examine the primary materials for the first consecration of the king.
It is as follows:

One should not employ again chariots, lion-thrones, swords, umbrellas, chowries, banners, elephants, horses, garments, ornaments, astrologers, physicians, domestic priests, and so forth, once they have been used.
"The substances deposited for the deities of the cremation fire," so says that evil-minded Bhāradvāja from the perspective of the teacher, the domestic priest, and the thunderbolt-mouthed one;
for Parāśara says that there is no further utility for [the fire] once it has been used, just like a fire that has already been consumed.
Brahmā is immeasurable like the fire of the cosmic egg;
he is not employed by another family,
nor is his domestic priest employed by another family for rites of pacification, nourishment, atonement, sorcery, occasional ceremonies, or funeral rites.

One should perform the rites prescribed by the Atharva; having become its *pratyaṅgirasa*, he [the king], desiring to bestow elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry upon the leaders of his subjects... (AVParis 3,1.11) ...the king should not appoint another as his domestic priest (*purohita*).
Like a withered floral offering, the king should not employ him again, nor should anyone else.

For the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is the cause for the perpetual [offering] in the fire on behalf of one who is afflicted by disease, fallen, insane, accused, abandoned, ruined, or whose [vow] has been expanded.
Therefore, [one should appoint] a man of noble birth, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a knower of the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* hymns, endowed with discipline, physical form, purity, and conduct;

one who is not greedy, perfected in the qualities of vows, observances, character, behavior, and auspicious marks; a counselor in matters of peace and war, highly skilled in rites such as the *māhendrajāla* and others; one who has mastered standing and sitting postures, who endures cold, heat, and rain, and is possessed of modesty, fortitude, uprightness, tranquility, self-control, compassion, generosity, and power.

The king should choose as his preceptor one who possesses the station, form, and stature of Bṛhaspati or Uśanas, whose qualities are inferable from his complexion, learning, and physique, and who is radiant, profound, endowed with courage, and venerable.
Having prepared the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and other offerings according to the prescribed ritual as required, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
consisting of either the third part from the middle of ten million [gold pieces] or according to the extent of the land.
One should give to the teacher an elephant, a horse, a human vehicle, divine ornaments, a parasol, gold, land, cattle, wealth, grain, jewels, and so forth,
or whatever else by which he might be satisfied.
The consecration has been explained in the ritual procedure for the *saṃhitā*.
One should give an elephant and horse to the teacher, as well as a vehicle for men,
divine ornaments, and likewise a parasol and so forth.
A lord of the earth should not accept anything for the sake of leftovers or for the sake of auspiciousness;
in such cases, mantras and medicinal herbs do not succeed, and the king perishes.
One should never appoint as a domestic priest someone who is excessively tall or excessively short, nor one who is too stout or too thin, nor one whose limbs are deficient or redundant.

A king should never appoint as his preceptor one who has missing or extra limbs, one who is fallen, discolored, a thief, dull-witted, impotent, lacking in capacity, one with a broken voice, one-eyed, deformed in the eyes, or one who is hateful.
If he has a missing or extra limb, there will be the ruin of the city and the kingdom; if he is one-eyed or dull-witted, there will be the destruction of the mounts and the treasury;
if he is a thief or incompetent, all evils will arise; and if he is impotent or discolored, the king shall perish.
If there is a change in voice, a disorder of the limbs arises; they say that a hostile attitude toward the teacher [leads to loss].
If the eyes turn pale or he falls down, he destroys his sons; and if [this occurs] with the Adhvaryu, he destroys his grandsons.
One should know that a black [owl] portends the depletion of the treasury; a red one, the loss of mounts;
a tawny one shall slay the king; but a squinting one shall destroy the kingdom.
For if a king appoints a Bahvṛca to the office of domestic priest,
he sinks along with him, like an elephant in the mud of a river.
For that king who appoints an Adhvaryu priest to the office of domestic chaplain is like one who, wishing to cross over, takes up a stone for his own destruction.
Even one who is devoted to austerity and chants the Sāmans brings about these conditions for his lineage: slaughter, imprisonment, affliction, and the depletion of treasury and transport.

Therefore, a king should appoint as his domestic priest one who is endowed with noble lineage and physical excellence, who is learned in the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* [Vedic texts], and who belongs to the *Gotra* of Aṅgiras or Vasiṣṭha.
In sacrifices, kingdoms, and cities, as well as in the armies of kings and in their own dwellings—
whatever portents of three kinds are of terrible form, a knower of the Veda of Brahman shall pacify them all.

Therefore, a ruler of men should appoint as his domestic priest a teacher who is versed in the secret doctrines of the Vedas, diligent in the fourfold ritual action, tranquil, self-controlled, a master of his senses, and pleasing in appearance.
And it is called "Piyadassana" (of lovely appearance).
Thus ends the first consecration of the king.
(Pariśiṣṭa 4: Duties of the Purohita) (AVParis 4.1.1) Om. Now, the duties of the domestic priest.

When the king has risen in the morning and the rites for his well-being have been performed, then the domestic priest— having bathed, anointed himself, being pure, dressed in white garments, and wearing a turban— recites the verse "Savitā prasavānām," as previously explained.
"O Indra, increase this one"—thus it is said.
Having consecrated the king's garment with the two verses beginning "pari dhatte," he should hand it over.
(Regarding the verse) "When they bound on... [it refers to] ornaments.
"Like a lion, like a tiger"—thus [is described] the lion-throne.
With the verse "That fragrance of yours," [he offers] perfumes.
With the verse, "Come hither, O life-preserving one," he anoints his eyes.
With the words "Having the speed of the wind," [he addresses] the horse.
"Having the splendor of an elephant" refers to an elephant.
"That which your mother [gave], that which your father [gave]"—this is the *naryāna* chant.
"And I consecrate the sword," [he says] regarding the sword.
And I consecrate this sword which shall crush the enemies;
may the enemies crushed by it come under your control forever.
A couch, a seat, a sword, a banner, an umbrella with its fly-whisks;
a chariot, an excellent horse and elephant, a bow, armor, and a quiver of arrows.
One should sprinkle collyrium, perfumes, garlands, garments, and ornaments with all these [substances] using water for pacification, and then consecrate them with mantras.
Having placed *dūrvā* grass and other items upon his head, he should consecrate them with benedictory mantras;
then, having prostrated before the Brahmins while reciting the mantra "Fearlessness, O Heaven and Earth," he should first [proceed].
"Through your grace, I shall attain peace."
Having been told, "So be it," he should depart.
When one has thus performed the rites for well-being, whatever he gazes upon is accomplished.
Regarding that, there are also these verses:
In ancient times, Śakra, the lord of the world, being oppressed by the Asuras,
duly appointed Bṛhaspati to the office of his domestic priest.
Requested by him who was terrified by fear and desiring his welfare,
he performed eight auspicious rites for the sake of securing freedom from fear for Śatakratu.
Eight auspicious things have been proclaimed: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, fire, the earth, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, the Śamī tree, and likewise rice and barley.
Constantly perceiving these meritorious acts and honoring them as well,
a king does not encounter calamity, but attains unsurpassed prosperity.
Now, regarding the royal rites: having bathed during the Viśvāvasu moment and being consecrated with the mantras for royal inauguration, [the king should proceed].
He is anointed with ointments.
According to the previously mentioned procedure, having taken with his left hand a gold *niṣka* or a *kṛṣṇala* coin, along with garments, ornaments, and other such items;
With this mantra, "May it burn all evil— that which is ill-done and that which is variegated"—
one should rub gold upon the body and give it with the right hand to a Brahmin,
as well as a healthy cow.
Having placed sesame seeds of immeasurable merit in a vessel made of gold or copper, one should recite the mantra "yad ajñānāt" and give them to a Brahmin.
"O Lord, whatever has been done by me in a muddled manner, whether through ignorance or through knowledge— may all that be consumed by this gift of sesame seeds."
Land abounding in crops should indeed be given according to one's ability to a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas, in accordance with the words of Bṛhaspati.
Having enjoyed various pleasures and having obtained the earth girdled by the seven oceans,
that lord of the earth shall rejoice like the moon.
One should always provide various kinds of food to the twice-born,
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and having likewise performed rites for well-being.
Having worshipped the household deities, a festival should also be held in the house;
one should personally worship the parasols and other vehicles according to the prescribed rules.

A wise man should also worship with various white flowers and fruits. Therefore, after having bestowed all gifts, the lord of the earth, endowed with faith and surrounded by Brahmins, should eat while remaining silent.
Then, one should place an image made of flour, representing the Night, before him, adorned with perfumes and garlands along with four lamps.
Having paid homage and then honored the Night according to the prescribed rule,
one should worship her with incense, food and drink, and with hymns of praise.
Protect me always, O Goddess, along with my kingdom and my friends; grant us dawn and bestow peace upon me forever. For those who take refuge in you, O Goddess, no fear exists.
I take refuge in the Night, the mother who is the dwelling place of all beings,
the auspicious, blessed, dark-hued night of the entire world.
I have entered this auspicious night, which brings sleep, which binds [all beings], and which is garlanded with planets and constellations; O blessed one, may we reach its end.
"May that Night, whom all beings— both stationary and moving— always pay homage to in the evening and in the morning, protect me."
"O Night, [bring] the earthly [wealth]," "The vigorous maiden," and "The protector"—these are the verses addressed to Night.
Having touched [the water] while reciting the two hymns beginning with "mamobhā" and "mahyam āpaḥ," he should mutter them.
One should offer mustard seeds with the five verses beginning with "yo naḥ svaḥ."
Having circumambulated the king three times with a lamp while reciting "yo 'smin" and "yas tvā mātuḥ," he should hand it over to the one who has issued the command.
With the verse "Fear not," he should throw four pebbles clockwise in each direction.
"Come, step upon the stone"—with these words, he should cause her to step upon the fifth [stone].
With the verse, "May no consumption come to him, O god," one should give guggulu, kuṣṭha, and dūpa.
With the mantra, "The fragrance of yours which is the triple life-span," he should bestow prosperity.
Having tied on an amulet with the mantra, "Dūṣyā, you are the defiler," he should throw pebbles clockwise in each direction with the mantra, "May Agni protect me from the east with the Vasus."
Having gone out, having proceeded along the north, and having emerged by the outer path, one should perform it for a friend; one should perform it for one who has faith.
The son of Musalī, Paiṭhīnasi, declared that an action performed at night brings no fear.
Now, therefore, we shall set forth the procedure for the hymns addressed to Night.
The domestic priest shall be pure and dressed in white garments.
Having performed the evening twilight worship for the king, with *darbha* grass held in their hands as purifiers, they should approach the king and fashion a night out of flour.
Having honored [the deity] with food, drink, incense, lamps, and garlands.
Having worshipped with four blazing lamps.
Having worshipped the night with the two hymns beginning with "O Night, come hither, the vigorous maiden of the earth," (AVParis_4,5.7).
Having circumambulated the Soma king three times to the right with the verses "trāyamāṇe," "viśvajite," and "ahne ca tvā," he releases it at the gate of the royal palace.
One should offer incense of *guggulu* and *kuṣṭha* with the verse, "May no consumption come to him, O God" (AVParis 4.5.10);
having consecrated prosperity with the verse, "That fragrance of yours" (AVParis 4.5.11);
and having performed a protective rite for the king with the verse, "The threefold life-span" (AVParis 4.5.12).
Having consecrated a pebble with the mantra "asapatnam," he should throw it toward each direction, starting from the right, beginning at his thumb.
Having recited "The sky is peaceful," one should lead the king to his sleeping chamber.
Having performed the protection with the *bhūti* hymn and having gone forth,
one should perform this very rite day after day.
In whatever king’s realm an Atharvan who has mastered the *śānti* rites dwells, that kingdom flourishes, free from affliction.
In whatever king's realm that [protection] does not exist, his kingdom is afflicted by various fears and sinks like a cow in the mud.
Therefore, a king should especially and constantly honor an Atharvan who has conquered his senses with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality.
One should constantly perform rites for pacification, worship the planets and constellations,
and carry out acts of "milking the earth" at the temples of the deities.
One should cause the ritual satiation of cows to be performed according to the rules at crossroads, in cow-pens, at sacred fords, and in waters; this destroys all defects.
The king who, having conquered his senses, causes this to be done at all times,
attains infinite happiness and enjoys the entire earth.
Thus the duties of the domestic priest are completed.
(Pariśiṣṭa 5: The Puṣyābhiṣeka) (AVParis 5.1.1) Om. Now I shall declare the complete ritual procedure for the Puṣyābhiṣeka;
a king should have his domestic priest perform that which is joined with virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
The taking up of water is prescribed with a thousand, or even a hundred, jars made of gold, silver, copper, or even earthenware.
Having diligently gathered water from the four oceans and from a hundred rivers for the consecration of the king.
One, two, three, four, or five of the oceans—
one should prepare medicinal herbs in all those jars.
Sahā, Dahadevī, Balā, and likewise Atibalā; Madayantī, Vacā, Śvetā, Vyāghradantī, and Sumaṅgalā.
Śatāvarī, jayantī, śatapuṣpā with candana, priyaṅgu, rocanā, aśīra, amṛtā, and sārikā.
Adorned with the tender shoots of the *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *bilva*, *nyagrodha*, *panasa*, *śirīṣa*, mango, and *kapittha* trees.
The domestic priest, having consecrated with mantras objects scented with gold, gems, medicinal herbs, bilva flowers, and perfumes, and having covered them with white cloths;
One should perform the *Sāvitrī* on both sides, as well as "śaṃ no devī," the hymn beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and the first section of the *Anuvāka*.
The earth shall serve as the footstool, with auspicious roots and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass;
upon that, one should place a seat made of gold or even silver.
One should arrange these four skins— in the order of the ox, the tiger, the lion, and the deer— beginning from the east.
The domestic priest should offer oblations according to the ritual procedure of the Cāturhotra,
while Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences stand in the four directions.
One should subsist on *bilva* fruits, or on other fruits, or even on milk;
for seven nights one should consume only ghee, and thereafter one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
One should perform [the rite] with cow’s milk, using a golden *sruva* ladle,
accompanied by the mantras that begin the Vedas and preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
The Gaṇa Śarmavarmā, as well as Aparājita, Āyuṣya, Abhaya, and likewise the Svastyayana Gaṇa.
Having offered oblations to these five groups, he should cause the best of the twice-born to recite [the benedictions],
with gold, unbroken grains, respectful offerings (*argha*), fruits, honey, and clarified butter.

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, the wise man should cause the commencement [of the rite] to be made during a favorable moment (*muhūrta*) conjoined with the Tiṣya asterism and under an auspicious lunar phase (*karaṇa*).
Having consecrated the musical instruments with the mantra "A loud sound," the domestic priest,
having been consecrated and adorned, [proceeds] amidst the resonance of all the musical instruments.
Having ascended the lion-throne or the footstool in due order,
it was provided with chowries and an umbrella, and adorned by the chamberlain.
And he should arrange four intoxicated elephants in the four directions;
then, having sat down, the king shall promote the welfare of his subjects.
Brahmins, cows, women, children, the mentally infirm, and the sick are exempt from taxes.
Then the king should grant an audience to the Brahmins,
as well as to the guilds and the leaders of the subjects, and he should pay homage to the womenfolk.
"For the people on earth, being satisfied, will grant you blessings; thus the subjects will be delighted and the earth shall come under your control."
The domestic priest, the minister, and likewise the commander-in-chief;
the superintendent of horses, the superintendent of elephants, and the master of the granary.
The king should honor, in due order and with appropriate treatment, the master of the treasury, the physician, and the astrologer.
Having entrusted the kingdom to the domestic priest and the remaining [offices] in their proper order,
