and having assigned other various positions, one shall attain happiness.
The domestic priest should place upon [the king's] head dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, śamī wood, rice, barley, and white flowers.
For this is the ritual prescribed by the Atharva for the consecration under the Puṣya asterism;
having bathed, the king enjoys the earth and goes to the world of Śakra.
Thus concludes the Puṣyābhiṣeka.
(Pariśiṣṭa 6: The Ritual for Piṣṭarātrī) (AVPariś 6.1.1) Om. Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Piṣṭarātrī.
Wearing new clothes, having first smeared a sacrificial mound with cow dung in front of the bed,
and having covered a lion-throne with a new cloth;
One should invoke the night with the verse: "That which the gods welcome."
Having fashioned an image made of flour according to the verse "The counterpart of the year," he should cause it to sit facing the north.
One should give a golden parasol and a golden seat;
one should give bright garments and bright ointment as well.
One should always offer pure food as well as abundant sweetmeats,
and one should constantly provide various types of incense and lamps.
Having performed worship with these verses, "Come to me for prosperity and for nourishment," and so forth.
Having consecrated mustard seeds with mantras that destroy demons,
and having scattered them all around the bed while muttering "āvatas ta," and having tied on an amulet while reciting "ayaṃ pratisaraḥ," he should throw pebbles in every direction.
One should give the remainder of the incense to the king.
Action that bestows fearlessness.
Subsequently, in all the corners, one should place either a two-faced or a single-faced [image] of Sarvatovijayā; or else, one may place a single four-faced [image] of her among them for protection.
Some say that one should recite the Apratiratha hymn with a single voice throughout; others say that there should be the scattering of pebbles everywhere.
Having taken the flour-mixture for the night, one should discard it at the door of the house.
One should offer incense of *guggulu* and *kuṣṭha* with the mantra, "This tree is in the midst," and having consecrated the prosperity (*bhūti*) with the mantra, "That fragrance which is yours."

Having performed a protective rite for the king with the verse "Tryāyuṣam," and having consecrated pebbles with the verse "Asapatnam," he should throw them toward each of the directions, starting from the thumb and moving clockwise.
Having recited "The sky is peaceful," he should lead the King to the bedchamber.
Having performed the protection with the *bhūti* [mantras] and having gone forth,
one should perform this very same rite day after day.
The ritual procedure for Piṣṭarātri is completed.

(Pariśiṣṭa 7. The Ārātrika) (AVParis 7.1.1) Oṃ. In former times, Śakra did not sleep soundly because of the medicinal formulations and applications employed by the priest of the Dānavas, through the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings.
Having prostrated before Bṛhaspati, Atharvan, Purandara said, "I am being overwhelmed by the Dānavas; save me!"
Then, having been addressed thus, he [bestowed] that which increases abundant strength,
grants health, brings prosperity, and destroys minor calamities.
For at that time, an *ārātrika* rite must be performed to protect him;
having prepared a lamp made of flour, provided with a wick and oil.
With the two verses beginning "ati nihaḥ prānyān," he should kindle it,
having placed it in a vessel containing flowers, along with mustard seeds and unbroken grains of rice.
One should place an offering there consisting of *priyaṅgu*, *śatapuṣpā*, *dūrvā*, *śatāvarī*, and *bhūti* which removes all sins.
Surrounded by Apsarases, the Guru went to Purandara,
who was seated on his throne facing east, composed in mind and having attained his true essence.
One hundred and one lamps should be consecrated with the mantra "preto yantu";
then, one should circumambulate them three times for the king with the "sumaṅgala" mantra.
Then his diseases, seizing spirits, obstacles, and Vināyakas are pacified;
may there be well-being for the king and the kingdom, and may there be well-being for cows and Brāhmaṇas.

Then, accompanied by the sound of a conch shell, the priest or the astrologer—being self-restrained—should carry forth the lamp together with a stream of water; or else a nurse, desiring his welfare, may do so herself, having been instructed in the Atharva Veda.
Having sipped water himself, the domestic priest should first cause the king to sip water;
then, at dawn, he should cause him to give gold to a Brāhmaṇa according to his means.
For him, no harm such as root-rites performed by the five Guhyakas shall occur;
he shall have no fear of the king, and his splendor and vigor shall increase.

Thus has this entire ritual procedure been duly prescribed; it has been declared to bring all auspiciousness to kings. No calamities shall ever befall that king for whom the *ārātrika* rite is performed every night.
Thus ends the Ārātrika.
(Pariśiṣṭa 8: Inspection of the Clarified Butter) (AVParis 8.1.1) Om. Now we shall explain the inspection of the clarified butter.

Every morning, awakened by the sound of conchs and drums or by the chanting of the Vedas, the king shall rise from his bedchamber, go out toward the unconquerable direction (the east), and await his preceptor.

Then the domestic priest, having bathed and anointed himself, being pure, dressed in white garments, and having fashioned a turban adorned with auspicious ornaments, shall enter the chamber of peace, offer salutations to the gods, obtain permission for the recitation of benedictions, and sit down in a humble manner.

Having performed a rite for well-being with the mantra "yo na jīvo 'si" (you who are not life), having scratched [the ground], sprinkled [water], and strewn [grass] around the fire, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with ghee while reciting the *śantātīya* hymn from the world of Yama.

Having offered those, one should consecrate the clarified butter—placed in a vessel made of gold, silver, or udumbara wood, filled with ghee, and containing gold—with the mantra: "The impulse of ghee; thousand-horned; stride wide from the world of Yama, O Viṣṇu! (AV Parisiṣṭa 8.1.5).
"Radiance," he says, and then he touches it.
Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin.
By means of clarified butter the gods are satisfied; in clarified butter all worlds are established.
"Whatever impurity has come upon you— whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial—
may it all go to utter destruction through contact with this clarified butter."
In that [mirror], one should indeed see everything situated within a vessel of clarified butter, as well as oneself.
Having touched the head and the heart with curd, he should mutter [the following].
With the two verses beginning "Flying upward" (AVParis_8,1.10),
and having turned clockwise with the verse "The turning of the Sun" (AVParis_8,1.11), he should cause the remainder to be performed;
regarding this, there are these verses.
This procedure for the inspection of the clarified butter has been proclaimed by Atharvan;
it must be performed at all times by a king desiring victory.
One who is restrained and composed should collect all this together;
thus the king conquers the kingdom, and his enemies perish.
The king should give a beautiful, tawny cow to the most excellent of the twice-born;
then, having heard the blessing uttered from his mouth.
Since one who has been recited by a teacher shall obtain long life, he obtains sons, grandsons, and friends; of this there is no doubt.
It is traditionally taught that gazing at clarified butter bestows longevity, luster, good fortune, and the subduing of enemies; it is meritorious and destroys evil dreams.
Thus ends the inspection of the clarified butter.
"O Śrīsāmba,
you have come forth from the world of Yama"— these are six verses; "as a sixteenth part, as a half"— these are six verses.
The verses beginning with "ghṛtasya jūtiḥ" are four; among them, the Pippalāda mantras are for the inspection of the clarified butter.

(Pariśiṣṭa 9: The Ritual for the Sesame Cow) (AVParis 9.1.1) Oṃ. Now I shall proclaim the ritual for the sesame cow, which destroys all sins. There are white sesame seeds, black sesame seeds, and sesame seeds the color of cow's urine.
One should have a cow and a calf made from various kinds of sesame seeds;
the calf should be made from one *droṇa*, while the cow is traditionally said to be made from four *droṇas*.
On clean ground, well-adorned with incense and flowers, it should be performed upon a black antelope skin; or one may have it performed by many people.
One should make the two ears out of jewels, and likewise the two eyes out of lamps;
in the nose, all fragrances, and on the tongue, autumnal ghee.
One should place pearls in the teeth, a copper vessel on the forehead,
madhūśīra on the udder, and ghee and honey in the anus.
One should apply sandalwood to the heart and sugarcane stalks to the shanks;
the sacrificial fee consists of a cow with horns of gold, hooves of silver, and a tail of silver.
It should be given covered with cloth, and the milking vessel should be made of bell-metal;
having consecrated it with the mantra beginning "Prajāpati," one should give it to a Brahmin.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
If one should give a cow and a calf that have not been consecrated with the Atharvan mantras,
without this ritual procedure, the state of divinity does not arise.
All cows are proclaimed to be of universal form when they stand [ready for milking]. One does not attain the true nature of a cow without being consecrated by the *sūkta*;
everything belonging to the virtuous perishes fruitlessly if it is not consecrated.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, in youth, in the prime of life,
in the decline of age, and in other previous births;
Whatever sin has been committed by deed, mind, or speech during the night, as well as at dawn, at midday and afternoon, or during the two twilights— [may it be destroyed].
He who, at the time of childbirth, gives a cow to an eminent Brāhmaṇa,
as well as a black antelope skin, a molasses-cow, and likewise a ghee-cow;
A cow made of gold and jewels, as well as a supreme water-cow,
a milk-cow, a honey-cow, and likewise one of sugar and salt.
All other cows, such as those of flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, are prescribed by this same rule.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood and whatever was committed in youth—
Fraudulent weights and fraudulent scales; falsehood regarding a maiden, falsehood regarding a cow;
spitting into water, and even stepping over a pestle.
The sin of approaching a low-caste woman, of violating the wife of a guru, and whatever sin arises from drinking liquor— all these are pacified by the gift of a cow made of sesame seeds.
That river which is known as Vaitaraṇī in the terrible city of Yama,
where there are iron-beaked crows and terrifying dogs;
There, evildoers are cooked upon sands and dry lands;
there is the Forest of Sword-leaves, as well as the Śālūka and the Śālmalī trees.
Having passed them with ease, one should proceed to the hermitage of Dharmarāja.
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate one! May it be well with you, O great-minded one!"
"This celestial chariot, adorned with jewels and gems, is worthy of you;
ascending it, O best of men, go to the supreme destination."
One should not give it to a soldier, nor should one give it to a domestic priest;
nor to one who is one-eyed, deformed, leprous, or likewise maimed.
It should be given to one who has reached the end of the Vedas, or to the son of one who has reached the end of the Vedas;
it should be given to each one on the full moon day of the month of Māgha.
Whoever recites this constantly, and whoever even hears it,
transcends the world of the gods and goes to the world of the sun.
He goes to the world of the sun.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the sesame-cow.

(Pariśiṣṭa 10: The Gift of Land) (AVParis 10.1.1) Om. Now, having fasted on the entire day of Rohiṇī, Brahmā takes a jar filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and scattered with all kinds of seeds, juices, gems, and perfumes; being authorized, he consecrates the donor with the prescribed consecration mantras beginning with "apām."
With the mantra, "By means of the vow, O Lord of Vows," he undertakes the vow.
They become supplicants and donors, eaters of unsolicited food, and sleepers on the ground;
this is the practice of the vow.
Having observed the vow for one night, five nights, or twelve nights according to his ability,
on the following day, having performed the ritual procedure up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings and having taken hold [of the fuel], he should then offer the oblations.
The priests— all of them— offer oblations with the *kāmasūkta*, the *kālasūkta*, and the *puruṣasūkta*, preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis* repeated according to the prescribed number.

Then, having fashioned a representation of the earth out of gold, measuring the size of a cow-hide, they bring it onto the altar of the pavilion and place it to the north of the altar with the mantra "on which the altar [is established]."
Having established the mountains with the verse, "The mountains are your mountains" (AVParis 10.1.10),

one should adorn them with gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth; then, having fashioned the rivers with the verses, "Those which flow together" (AVParis 10.1.11) and "She, smiling" (AVParis 10.1.12), one should fill them with flavorful liquids.
"You are the foremost of the waters; I release you toward the ocean"—with these words [he releases them] toward the oceans.

"The Lord of the Forest has come to us together with the gods"—with these words [he addresses] Bṛhaspati. "And the other Lords of the Forest"—with these words [he addresses] the other Lords of the Forest.
"In the sacrifice, one should intend for you with the mind"; thus he intends with the mind, and it comes to be here, it comes to be here, it comes to be here.

Having caused [the recipient] to bow with the mantra "Bearing a treasure in many ways" (AVParis 10.1.16), he should have [the recipient] recite the section beginning with "The great truth" (AVParis 10.1.17), as well as the mantras "Those gods who are eleven in heaven" (AV 3.27.1) and "Auspicious day! (puṇyāhaṃ), and then conclude the rite.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, "Nine from heaven by the divine folk," he should give it to the Brāhmaṇas,
saying, "This Rohiṇī shall yield for this giver his desire, whether small or great.
Just as seeds sprout upon the surface of the earth when tilled by the plow, even so do desires always sprout for the mind both in this world and after death.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for all gifts whatsoever, one obtains that very fruit by giving land to Brahmins according to the prescribed rule.
Having bestowed the land according to the prescribed rite.
Thus ends the gift of land.
(Pariśiṣṭa 11: The Ritual of the Tulāpuruṣa) (AVParis 11.1.1) Om. Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual of the Tulāpuruṣa.
(AVParis 11.1.2) This should be performed during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, impelled by faith, or at the time of an eclipse.
The officiating priest and the sacrificer, having had their hair, beards, body hair, and nails trimmed,
and having prepared the ritual materials, perform the eastern rite up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings;
then, having offered the *mahāvyāhṛti*, the *sāvitrī*, the *śānti*, and the verse "brahma jajñānam."

With the verses, "O Agni, with cattle," "O Agni, you who turn back," and "Born from Agni," he should pour the residues from the water-vessels into the consecration jars. Then, with the verse, "Now Indra [is anointed] with the two pressing-stones," he should sprinkle him;
having thus sprinkled him, [he continues] with the verse, "O Waters, as Indra [was anointed] with his two arms."
Having caused [the person] to apply collyrium, ointment, and unguents as prescribed, one should fasten upon them garments, perfumes, and garlands.
Having sprinkled the scales and the gold with purificatory waters, one should cause [the person] to ascend them with the seven verses beginning, "The wealth is commensurate with the man.
One should cause [the person] to descend with the four verses beginning, "The heaven is immovable."
Having turned clockwise with the words "The turning of the sun," and having announced it to the Brāhmaṇas, he should give his own ornaments to the officiant;
a choice village as a gift of a thousand [cows],
and he should satisfy the twice-born with food.
Now, if wealth is acquired through a fraudulent scheme—
whether by weighing it against metals, or with garments, or likewise with liquids, or whatever else may be obtained in the house such as the seven kinds of grain beginning with rice.
Equipped with a sword, wearing a helmet, and adorned with all ornaments,
the king should subsequently be weighed against gold placed upon a balance.
In ancient times, this boon was granted by Indra for the attainment of supreme sovereignty,
for the destruction of all sins, and for the increase of all merit.
Among all great gifts and supreme gifts, this gift is unsurpassed;
it bestows inexhaustible fruit, is most excellent, and increases the welfare of those who give.
Whatever evil has been committed by those born in one's own family through twenty-one generations—
all that perishes quickly, just as cotton is consumed in fire.
Having attained the disease-free state that cannot be transgressed by the gods, and which is won through golden merits,
he— possessing the splendor of gold and liberated from sin— shines like Indra in heaven within the world of the sun.
"Like Indra in heaven, he shines in the realm of the sun."
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa.

(Pariśiṣṭa 12: The Sun-Disc) (AVParis 12.1.1) Om. Now, he who should desire, "May I be the highest among all men," should offer a cake to Bhāskara. (AVParis 12.1.2) Its ritual procedure is as follows.
Having prepared a circular shape with the flour of either barley or wheat,
placed it in a vessel,
covered it, and set upon it a piece of gold along with jaggery and clarified butter, one should worship it with red flowers.
Having consecrated [it] with the mantra "viṣāsahi," one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"Whoever, according to this rite, should give a cake to a twice-born man..."
The wise man should always bestow it; hear now the fruit of his merit.
He shall be healthy and radiant, possessed of offspring and cattle,
as well as wealthy, abundant in food, illustrious, and beloved by all people.
It destroys more than a hundred premature deaths without hesitation;
when properly bestowed, it leads one to the world of the Sun and the supreme state.
One should cause [the disciple] to attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the Ādityamaṇḍaka.
(Pariśiṣṭa 13: The Ritual of Hiraṇyagarbha) (ĀV Pariśiṣṭa 13.1.1) Om! Now we shall set forth the ritual of Hiraṇyagarbha, which removes all sins.
(ĀV Pariśiṣṭa 13.1.2) During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, impelled by faith, or at the time of a planetary conjunction.
The officiating priest and the sacrificer should have their hair, beards, body hair, and nails trimmed.
Then the officiating priest, having placed the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) made of *aśvattha* wood before sunset, consecrates the fire being churned with two verses beginning, "O Agni, be born!
He consecrates the fire that has been produced with the third verse, and he places it upon the altar with the fourth.
Having clothed him in a clean place as prescribed, having caused him to have collyrium, ointment, and unguent applied,
and having tied a golden garland upon him with the verse, "The gold which was born from Agni, which they bound on... and having performed the protection rite with the words,
"May they protect you," they should spread *darbha* grass and lie down facing downward.

On the following day, during the *abhijit* muhūrta, having placed a golden vessel shaped like a disk and reaching to the navel, together with its lid, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), a water-vessel, and the ornaments;

having swept around [the fire], sprinkled water around it, spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) all around, set down the water-vessel, and performed the preliminary service to the clarified butter by pouring water around it; and having offered the regular *purastāddhoma* oblations and the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).
And then he offers the oblation:
"To Hiraṇyagarbha, svāhā!"
Svāhā to Agni!
Svāhā to Brahmā!
Having offered with "Svāhā to Prajāpati" (AVParis 13.2.2),

having caused them to perform a salutation with those same [verses] (AVParis 13.2.3), and having performed the ritual attendance with those same [verses], [he should offer] the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the vessel for clarified butter, the water-pot, and the ornaments.
Having bathed the king in a golden vessel with verses containing the word "gold" (hiraṇyavatī), having poured the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water into it from golden jars,
and having brought together the ritual residues (saṃpāta) with the Hiraṇyagarbha hymn, the Aṃhomuc hymn, the Śantātīya hymn, and the five names;
In the same manner, he should request permission from the officiating priests, both those who are members of the sacrificial assembly (*sadasya*) and those who are not, saying:
"The King desires the state of Hiraṇyagarbha; may you, sirs, grant your consent. Having been so authorized by them, he proceeds.
With the two verses beginning "Come forth, O steed" (*ud ehi vājinn*), he should cause him to enter.
Having focused his mind on the thirty-three deities, he instructs him:
"Restraining your speech and withdrawing your senses from their objects with the mind, meditate upon the Blessed One, the golden one, Hiraṇyagarbha, the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa."
"So be it," he agreed; that is how it is undertaken.
There is an interval of seventeen measures;
Prajāpati, indeed, is seventeenfold.
One should announce, "By the ritual turn of Prajāpati.
In that same manner, having obtained permission from those present in the assembly and those not present in the assembly, one should cause him to rise;
once he has risen, one should cover him with a golden disc.
One should extract [the breath] with the mantra "mā te prāṇa" (AVParis 13.3.10).
Having extracted it and released it from that which has the name "gold" (*hiraṇya*), one should cast it away with the mantra "yas tvā mṛtyuḥ" (AVParis 13.3.11).
Having looked at it with the mantra "saṃpaśyamānāḥ" (AVParis 13.3.12), one should prostrate before the Brahmins, offer salutations, and say: "Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha."
Now, indeed, this [verse] beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha" was spoken for one who is most dear;
then, the Brahmins should say, "Arise, you who are favored by Hiraṇyagarbha! Having offered the Apratiratha oblation, he should bring the rite to a conclusion.
Having praised Varuṇa with the verse, "O King Varuṇa, in the waters... and having bathed with purificatory mantras, they return and worship the sun with the verse:
"Since you are gold in the womb, born from the womb of gold, O Golden Embryo, therefore, being great, protect me from the great [evil]."

Having turned clockwise with the words, "The turning of the sun," and having entered the house with the words, "I am coming to the house," and having worshipped the fire with the verse, "O Agni, you are the guardian," he should then release [the animal].
Then he should give ten thousand [cows] as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born,
as well as an excellent village,
and the *sruk*, *sruva*, clarified butter vessel, water vessel, and ornaments; all else [he should give] to the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*).
Or rather, as much as they may be satisfied with, so much should be given.
The king should give according to his desire; he should serve the Brahmins with food. Regarding this, there are these verses:
If those who have mastered the four Vedas and are most learned in the knowledge of Brahman are satisfied with someone and pronounce blessings upon him, he shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.
Through the grace of the Brahmins, the sun shines resplendently in the sky;
and through their grace, even Indra outshines the gods.
"The fruit of the gift of gold is immortality," so says the Śruti;
for it is heard that he who is its giver attains immortality.
In ancient times, stainless royal seers such as Rāja, Ikṣvāku, and others,
having given gold to the brahmins, became light and dwelt in heaven.
A king who has been thus consecrated according to the ritual by one who speaks the Veda attains sovereign rule, preeminence, and excellence over his subjects in this world.
Having experienced bliss together with that Brahman in that [state],
one indeed reaches the world of truth (satyaloka), which consists of light, and never returns again.
(Pariśiṣṭa 14: The Ritual for the Gift of an Elephant-Chariot) (AVParis 14.1.1) Om! Now I shall declare the sequence of the gifts of elephant-chariots.
(AVParis 14.1.2) Having fashioned one made of gold, beautiful and with a single wheel—
Having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, [one should mount] it yoked with seven elephants.
Alternatively, it may be made of gold or silver, joined with four [components],
or even made of wood, provided it is untouched [by impurities] and filled with all the necessary materials.
Yoked with a pair of elephants or accompanied by a bull,
he enjoys the earth consisting of seven continents for exactly seven births.

When the moon is joined with the asterism Hasta on the full moon or the new moon day, or under an auspicious constellation, one who is pure, in a pure place, should perform the ritual procedure as described.
Having placed the fuel-wood towards the east and having taken hold of it from behind, he should then offer the oblation.
To Savitṛ, svāhā!
Hail to the moth!
To the Purifier, Svāhā!
Svāhā to the one with a thousand rays!
Svāhā to Mārtaṇḍa!
Svāhā to Viṣṇu!
Svāhā to Prajāpati!
Having offered with the words, "Svāhā to Parameṣṭhin," [he says]:
Gold, sesame seeds, cows, a female slave, a house, land, chariots, a maiden, an elephant, and knowledge— these indeed are the ten great gifts.
Therefore, in all acts of giving and in those where no specific ritual procedure has been stated,
one should offer oblations with the hymn beginning "We speak to Agni" according to the *ājya* ritual framework.
The giver of a horse shall go to heaven, as shall the man mounted upon that horse;
he is honored by the gods, gandharvas, as well as by the apsaras and kinnaras.

Having poured the remnants from the ladles into the water-jar with the words, "May the splendor of an elephant spread forth," he sprinkles everything—the yoke, the thong, and the chariot—with the formula, "The yoke, the thong, the chariot."
With the words, "I yoke you with an unwearied mind," he should yoke it.
I yoke you with an unwearied mind, and with that of the first [being].
O Bhava, as one who carries upward, carry upward; having carried upward, run back again.
One should give wealth to her when she is duly engaged.
He whose golden chariot rolls upon easy paths, yoked with dark steeds that have white feet—
may that Savitṛ, who eats gold, with his hand, and Savitṛ, the golden-handed, protect us.
A man who gives a large elephant-chariot yoked with an elephant by the hand attains the station of Savitṛ and a divine assembly hall that moves at will.
(Pariśiṣṭa 15: The Ritual for the Gift of a Horse-Chariot) (AVParis 15.1.1) Om. Now follows the ritual for the gift of a horse-chariot.
(AVParis 15.1.2) Having placed fuel-sticks toward the east in a cow-pen, near water, or in a pure place, and having taken hold of them, he should then offer oblations.
"O steed, being yoked, become one of swift speed"— with this [verse], having brought the ritual residues (*saṃpāta*) onto the horses, he should recite "of the untiring one" as is common.
Having offered the *argha* water to Savitṛ with "Thou art Indra, thou art Mahendra," and having touched himself with "May they purify me," he should mutter [the following].
Having consecrated the sacrificer with the mantra, "May the fires protect you," at the conclusion of the *samṛddhi* oblations,
he should give a choice cow to the performer, as well as a horse-chariot and an excellent village.
Thus, the wise man who gives a horse-chariot to a learned person according to this rite—
He attains here the state of being the eldest, the state of excellence, and sovereign rule over his subjects.
Having gone to the world of light, free from affliction, at the end of the seven worlds, he enjoys supreme bliss as long as the sun exists.
(Pariśiṣṭa 16: The Ritual for a Thousand Cows) (AVParis 16.1.1) Om. Now, therefore, follows the ritual for a thousand cows.
In a cow-pen, near water, or in a pure place, having placed the fuel-wood with its tips pointing eastward and having touched it, he should then offer oblations.
One should offer clarified butter with the hymn beginning "ā gāvaḥ."
Having cooked a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of large-grained rice for Indra and one for Soma in the milk of the thousandth cow, he should offer it with the verse: "The cows indeed are fragrant."
The water from the bathing-places of the five rivers.

To the west of the fire, having placed a jar filled with water from a sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*) and consecrated it with the verse "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," he should bathe ten cows with the ten verses beginning with "Saṃ vo goṣṭhena."
Having quickly sprinkled [the king] with water from the milk of the thousandth cow, saying, "O Indra, increase this Kṣatriya for me," he consecrates the king.
Having performed the application of collyrium, ointment, and unguent as previously described with the six verses beginning "imā āpaḥ," [he should proceed].
Having first adorned the thousandth [cow].
"May the cows attend upon me," with these words he should perform the ritual attendance.
And with the verse, "May you be prolific, from good pasture," he should cause them all to drink.
Having given the favorite food and [offered] grass with the words "O inviolable one," he should touch the thousandth cow and mutter [the following].
Having offered this water for honor with the mantra, "O cows, be united with me, the lord of cattle," [he performs the rite].
Having grasped the tail of the thousandth cow with his hand, he murmurs: "May the earth receive you."
Walking behind the thousandth cow.

Having circumambulated all [the deities] clockwise, having paid obeisance, and having had the Brahmins recite benedictions, he should present ten cows as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the performer; furthermore, he should give the thousandth cow and a pair of garments.
Regarding that, there are also these verses:
The sin committed by seven men that follows one for seven births— a man who gives a cow shall destroy that [sin] instantly by means of this rite.
A man who bestows a thousand cows upon the learned obtains that fruit which has been proclaimed as the result of all gifts whatsoever.
"Whosoever among my sons shall perform the horse sacrifice, the rite of setting a bull at liberty, or bestow a thousand cows— thus saying, the ancestors indeed satisfy him."
"Therefore, a person who gives a thousand cows according to this rite,
having purified his self of all sins, goes to that supreme state."
(Pariśiṣṭa 17: Royal Rites for the Year) (AVParis 17.1.1) Om. Now we shall describe, in due order, the royal rites to be performed every year.
Then, on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.
Of turmeric and barley.
Having bound the protection for the horses with the four verses beginning "May the fires protect you," one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for the elephants and horses.
"You are a horse; you are of swift birth... [he who] would thus bestow [it], being pure in soul, [would merit] the earth with its seven continents.
When the moon is joined with the Hasta constellation, on a full-moon day or a new-moon day, under an auspicious lunar mansion, in a pure place.
It is called "tantra."
Having placed the fuel-wood facing eastward, he should offer the oblation while they maintain their hold on him.
Svāhā to Savitṛ!
Hail to the moth!
To Pāvaka, svāhā!
Svāhā to the thousand-rayed one!
Svāhā to Mārtaṇḍa!
Svāhā to Viṣṇu!
Svāhā to Prajāpati!
Having offered an oblation with the mantra "Svāhā to Parameṣṭhin," one should fasten golden ornaments upon the elephants and horses and perform the *nīrājana* ceremony as previously described.
Then, on the ninth day, in the afternoon, having bathed the vehicles and having prepared a twelve-cubit altar, the Brahman priest, wearing new clothes, [performs the rite].
It is called "tantra."
Having purified the vehicle by means of the rite for pacification (*śāntikṛtya*) and sprinkling it three times, one should circumambulate it.
Reciting the hymn "niḥsālām," he should return and consecrate him.
Having adorned the horse and made its neck variegated, one should present it and offer it.
In the same way, there are vessels of mixed grain and water-bowls in the intermediate directions.
In that very place, one should sacrifice to the deities.
"Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, and the two Aśvins."
Having cooked a mess of rice in milk, he should offer it.

Having offered oblations with the verses "O Agni, [be] our alliance," "O Agni, you are ours," "May they not find us," "With fearlessnesses," "With invincibilities," "With life-prolonging [blessings]," "With auspicious journeys," and "The Apratiratha [hymn]," he concludes the rite.
Having covered [the vessels] with unwashed garments while reciting "Thou art the food of Agni," having filled the Audumbara jars with juices,

and having placed them in each direction, he should offer oblations with the mantras: "O Agni, may there be splendor for me," "Fearlessness, O Heaven and Earth," "Lift up the highest [fetters], O Varuṇa," and "Come, O Aśvins, with sacred prayer."
It has been stated that one should offer oblations with the verses beginning "The full moon is first" and strike the drum.
"Blow upon the earth," with these words, there is likewise the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) right there.
And all musical instruments and vehicles as well.
One should gladden the people and establish them in the fifth [state].
With the verse, "May no consumption come to him, O God," one should offer incense made from guggulu resin.
With the verse, "The fragrance of yours which is the triple life-span," one should bestow prosperity.
Having tied on an amulet with the mantra "dūṣyā dūṣir asi," one should cast it out in each direction with the mantra "ye purastāt."

Having gone out, having proceeded along the north, and having emerged by the outer path, one should perform the rite for a friend, or for one who has faith; it is the rite that grants safety to the mounts.
(Pariśiṣṭa 18: The Annual Royal Rite) (AVParis 18.1.1) Now, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja, in the afternoon, one should perform the consecration of the female elephant.
In a place sloping toward the northeast, or wherever the mind finds delight.
Having demarcated a circle of one hundred cubits or half of that with the verse, "The mountains, those hills," he should sprinkle it with the verse, "With those [waters] by which the sacrifice."
Regarding this, there are these verses:
One should construct an archway made of the *śānta* tree, ten cubits in height and five cubits in width, which increases prosperity.
One should have a bright cave constructed, adorned with white [substances], white garments, banners, and garlands,
and filled with mercury.
I consecrate you with juices; O Earth, be auspicious to me!
Be free from rivals, the slayer of rivals, and the increaser of my sacrifice.
"These two pillars, anointed with ghee, may both protect me with glory;
whoever shall assail me, may these two pillars consume him."
Having joined the two pillars with golden garlands and banners while reciting these two verses, "Rise up" and "O Brahmaṇaspati," [he should perform the rite].
Having constructed a four-cubit altar beneath it, and having offered an oblation and flowers with *darbha* grass purifiers in hand;

Having strewn around the fire honey, parched grain, rice-mash, auspicious figures, mixed grains with molasses, curd, rice-and-pulse porridge, cakes, milk-rice, ghee, various drinks, edibles, and fruits;
Having filled four jars made of udumbara wood with water from a lake while reciting the mantra, "May the waters, our mothers, purify us," (AVParis 18.1.12).
Having established [the offerings] in each direction, one should offer curd; the mantras are those dedicated to Rudra, Agni, Vāyu, and Varuṇa.

Having offered oblations that destroy demons, ward off sorcery, and bestow fame and luster, and having gathered medicinal herbs, one should prepare a circular area two cubits in extent; so it has been said.
On this point, there are these verses:
Bṛhatkaṇṭārī, kaṇṭakā, and lāghukaṇṭārikā are recorded [as synonyms]; likewise, suvarṇapuṣpī, śvetagiri, karṇikā, and udisatrā.
Siṃhī, vyāghrī, hariṇī, amṛtā, aparājitā, pṛśniparṇī, dūrvā, padma, and utpalamālinī.
He addresses her with this mantra.
Having placed a bamboo ring, he should set it on fire.
Having spread out skins of tiger, leopard, and bull.
Then, having offered a bali-oblation to whichever presiding deity it may be, one should also offer the rice-balls.
One should cause the elephant to rinse its mouth.
Having gone in the direction where that enemy resides, one should bring an elephant, [adorned] with gold, silver, diamonds,
pearls, and so forth, as well as conch shells, sandalwood, *bhadradāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *nalada*,
yellow pigment (*rocanā*), collyrium, realgar, and lotuses— *padma*, *kumuda*, and *utpala*.
One should recite the hymn "O Agni, my splendor" over the southern and northern sacrificial pits.
With the remainder, he should anoint his limbs.
Regarding this, there are verses:
In the guarding of elephants, a new staff made of bamboo should indeed be employed;
it should be sixteen cubits in length, with beautiful joints and a pleasing appearance.
With that, one should ward off elephants.
Having placed blades of grass upon the tips of your teeth, you carry the oblation as you swallow it.
One should kindle the fire with the verse: "Well-born is Jātavedas... (AV Parisiṣṭa 18.3.8).
Having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony with the words "so that the oblation [may go]," he should cause [the officiant] to recite, "Well-born is Jātavedas."
Saying, "Bearing a treasure," he should cause her to enter the hall.
Not looking back toward their own abodes, they depart; they become long-lived and powerful.
A thousand cows and an excellent village shall be the sacrificial fee for the performer.

(Pariśiṣṭa 18b. On the Annual Royal Rite) (AVParis 18b.1.1) Now, one who has been increasing [in prosperity] for a hundred years, desiring to cause the king to prosper, should perform [this rite] on his birthday in the course of that year.
It is called "tantra."

Having sprinkled the sacrificial vessels with purifiers using the mantra, "May Vāyu purify me; may Vaiśvānara purify me with his rays," and having likewise sprinkled the patron of the sacrifice with auspicious verses beginning with *puṇyāha*, he should cook the *māhendra* *caru*— excluding floral and other ornaments— with the mantra, "That which they bound [upon him]."
And one should cook a second *caru* offering for the Guardians of the World (*lokapāla*).

Having offered oblations into the third fire with the hymn *mahām indro ya ojasā* and having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapālāḥ*) beginning with "Svāhā to Indra," he should touch the king and offer oblations as before with [the verses]: "Indra who turns hither," "Indra the good protector," and "O Indra, increase this Kṣatriya of mine; may he live for a hundred autumns."
Having performed the protection rite with the four verses beginning "May the fires protect you," one should adorn it with the *rocanā* ointment after tying it with a triple-stranded thread.
Having performed the *saṃpāta* ritual with the hymn beginning "For Manā, the thread" (*manāyai tantum*), he should fasten a protective cord.
With the words, "May Dhātṛ bind your knot," he ties it.
The Uttaratantra [is the ritual], and gold is the sacrificial fee.
On the Mahānavamī day, the consecration of the elephants and horses takes place; from the first lunar day (pratipad) onwards, it lasts for nine nights.
A clash of weapons and arrows.
On the third [lunar day], there is the work of elephants, horses, mounts, and domestic animals; on the seventh, the sight of elephants and horses.
Then, on the eighth day, [one should offer] an image made of flour, and so forth; on the ninth day, there is the worship of Durgā.
Alternatively, the passage beginning with "in the forest" (*vanasyām*) refers to the ninth [day].
Then, on the tenth day known as Aparājita.
In the forenoon, at the moment of victory, the rite for departure has been described.
"These indeed are the eastern doors," and so forth.
Now, it is explained that on the lunar mansion of Śravaṇā, the festival of Indra for kings is to be performed.
Then, on the full moon day, in the afternoon, the full moon ritual is performed.
Then, on the thirteenth lunar day, having bathed during the Śveta muhūrta, one should circumambulate a *apāmārga* plant three times over the king with the mantra.
He performs the bath again with the three hymns beginning "Iśānāṃ tvā bheṣajānām" or with the hymn "pratīcīnaphala."
Then, with the two verses beginning "Wear the lustration lamp," [the procedure] is the same as before.
Now, on the first day of the festival of lights (Dīpotsava), the initiation of the elephants, horses, and other [animals] is performed in the same manner as that of the [human] candidates.
Having performed the rites up to the end of the *abhyātāna* formulas, [he recites]: "Those who are in this eastern quarter... and so forth.

With these hymns, "mā no devā yas te sarpa," one should offer grass-blades together with the *saṃpāta* oblations using a tool for piercing wood; and the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is the same for the group of those who eat the *prātitamita-dhānā* grains, as well as for elephants, horses, and so forth, all simultaneously.
A cow is the sacrificial fee.
Then, on the night of the ninth day of the inexhaustible [rite], there is the final oblation for the arrays of elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as for the chariot.

Then, on the twelfth day of Viṣṇu, the domestic priest, having performed the evening twilight worship and taken darbha grass, approaches the king; and having performed the prosperity-securing oblation (*pauṣṭika-homa*) at night and the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for the elephants and horses.
Now, on the full moon day of Kārttika, or on the Raivatī full moon day of Āśvayuja, the rite of setting a bull at liberty (vṛṣotsarga) is performed.

Then, having performed the ritual procedure on the full moon day of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, he should pour the essence [of the Soma] with the two verses beginning "apād agre," consecrate it, and have the King consume it.
A cow is the sacrificial fee.
Now, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣya, the consecration of Puṣya has been described.
Then, on the night of the full moon of Phālguna, the Holākā festival is performed.
On the Mahānavamī day, one should perform the ritual of kindling the fire as previously described, or the *nīrājana* ceremony.

Now, on the first day of the summer season, having performed the "Life-prolonging" (*āyuṣya*) bath and having immersed himself with the hymns addressed to the waters (*apām sūktaiḥ*), it is said that he should turn his garment from right to left and touch water.
Now, it is said that on the full moon day of Caitra, one should observe the *tejovrata* for three nights, eating [only] once [per day].

Then, on the thirteenth day of the month of Madana, or on the full moon of Vaiśākha, at midday, having thrown all kinds of perfumes into a pit, a pond, a lotus-pool, or a water-jar, and having performed the ritual up to the *abhyātāna* formulas,
[one should sacrifice] with these [verses]: "In the lion, in the tiger, glory is the oblation," "In the morning, Agni on the mountain," and "Among the Aragāṭas, of heaven and earth."
Having poured water together with hymns and consecrated it with mantras, one should bathe the king.
Having entered and performed the ritual sprinkling, one should establish the tantra.
A cow is the sacrificial fee.

Then, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, during the *vijaya* muhūrta, having performed the binding of the protective thread with the four verses beginning "May the fires protect you," and having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), one should go outside— thus says Paiṭhīnasi.
Now, on the day of the sun, the solar disc is explained.
Now, the sacrifice and oblation for the birth-star are explained.

Now, regarding the royal rites that are to be performed under each constellation: one should carry weapons such as the sword and so forth; thus the [rites for] Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and the others have been explained.
The festival of Indra, the great festival of Indra, has been explained.
Every day, there is a sacrifice to the planets.
Every day there is a sacrifice to the lunar mansions.
Every day, the Mahāśānti rite is performed ten times.
The establishment [of images] has been explained under Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī; these are the ritual baths and the sacrificial fees for the constellations.
The royal rites for the year, including the consecration of elephants, horses, and so forth, are completed.
(Pariśiṣṭa 18c: The Release of the Bull) (AVParis 18c.1.1) Now follows the release of the bull.

On the full moon day of Kārttika, or on the Raivatī full moon day of Āśvayuja, having performed the ritual procedure for the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice in a cow-pen up to the point of the Ājyabhāga offerings, one should offer clarified butter with the two Rudra-raudra hymns.
One should offer oblations of the Pūṣan-oblation with the four verses beginning, "May Pūṣan follow after our cows."
May Pūṣan follow after our cows; may Pūṣan protect them on every side;
may Pūṣan win us strength.
O Pūṣan, follow after the cows of the sacrificer who presses the soma,
and also those of us who offer praise.
"O Pūṣan, under your protection we [remain]; Pūṣan is around us from the front."

Having made the bull *Ṛṣabha* accompanied by the *saṃpāta* verses beginning with "The thousandfold belly of Indra, the brilliant one," he should whisper into the right ear of the bull the verse beginning with "He who is like Indra among the gods."
With the words, "With the red axe," he addresses the heifer.
This Prajāpati, the progenitor of creatures, dwells here in the midst of the cow-pen;
as the guardian of the cattle, take your stand over the young cows and the dwelling place of the kine, becoming the protector of the livestock.

Thus he causes the mandalas to revolve: "I release you for the sake of the bestower of seed; I release you for the sake of the bestower of vigor; I release you for the sake of the state of being a herd;
I release you for the sake of the state of being a troop; I release you for the sake of nourishment of a thousandfold; I release you for the sake of immeasurable nourishment."

Having sprinkled water around [the fire], they should drive out—whether it be one-formed, two-formed, or many-formed, or whatever herd covers the herd, adorned with a radiant ornament—toward the unconquered direction together with young cows; they should then conclude the ritual procedure. Then, one should give a milch cow to the Brahman priest; having fed the Brahmins with milk-rice and dismissed them, one obtains all desires and attains imperishable worlds.
(Pariśiṣṭa 19: The Great Festival of Indra) (AVParis 19.1.1) Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for the service of the king’s great festival of Indra.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada.

When the ritual materials have been gathered, both the Brahman priest and the king, having bathed, wearing unwashed garments, anointed with fragrant and well-prepared unguents, fit for the rite and observant of their vows, fast. On the following day, having sipped water three times with the feet, the half-verses, and the verse of the *śannodevī* hymn, and having prepared the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) while touching the King Soma, he should offer the oblations.

Having offered oblations with the verses, "Hitherward Indra the protector, Indra; Indra the good protector; O Indra, strengthen this Kṣatriya of mine; O Bull, slay [the enemy]; Indra shall conquer through Indra," and also with the *Rāṣṭrasaṃvargas* hymns, they then raise up Indra with the verse, "I have brought thee hither from within the firm [heaven]; may all the people desire thee. They should support him on all sides with vigilance.
For a wonder indeed arises from these libations.
If there is danger from fire in the east.
If it is in the south, there is fear of Yama.
If there is danger from Varuṇa in the western direction.
If [the breath] moves toward the north, there is danger from hunger.
If one should know [the mantra] from both sides for the intermediate directions:
"May Agni protect me; may the Agnis reach you, the possessor of wealth."
One should cause them to be placed in each direction, circling clockwise according to their respective characteristics, two by two.
If a vulture alights upon this [corpse], there will be fear of death.

Or, when a black bird flies across the sky, one should mutter the hymn beginning with "yas tvā gṛdhraḥ kapota" at the end; in all cases where [the cause] is unknown, one should perform the Ghṛtakambala rite for three nights.
If the head is broken, it portends for the king; if the middle is broken, for the minister;
if the beginning is broken, for the countryside; and if the root is broken, for the citizens.
When the *indrāṭaka* is split, the royal treasury is plundered;
when the cutting of the rope occurs, the king perishes.

Having consecrated it with the Sāvitrī verse, he should cause the king to turn clockwise while reciting these three hymns beginning with "abhibhūr yajñaḥ"; once the king has taken hold [of him], he should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇahoma*).
Now follows the ritual procedure for the sacrificial animals.
Those who are the king's servants shall have Indra as their deity; all shall be consecrated and remain celibate students (*brahmacārin*).
Having approached Indra, they shall sacrifice.
For three nights or seven nights,
they worship during three courses of days and sacrifice with an oblation.
Having recited "I have turned toward Indra" and "O Indra, the sovereignty," and having offered the oblation,
they cause the Brahmins to pronounce blessings and proceed toward Indra for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

Having bathed with hymns to the waters, having turned clockwise, and having touched water, they return without looking back and honor the Brahmins with devotion by granting whatever boons are desired.
Then, as for this "eṣamiti" [formula]: it is thus.

Day by day his kingdom becomes greater; he becomes the sole king upon this earth; he does not die before old age—this is for one who knows thus, and for one who, knowing thus, performs the Indra-maha sacrifice. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
(Pariśiṣṭa 19b. The Brahmayāga) (AVParis 19b.1.1) Om! Having prostrated before Bhārgava, the venerable Śaunaka said:
"Tell me in full detail the entire procedure for the Brahmayāga."
Thus questioned by him, Atharvan, the best of sacrificers,
established himself in the complete ritual procedure and began to explain it.
This is declared to be the supreme among all sacrifices;
listen now with diligence to this Brahma-sacrifice according to its proper sequence.
In a place that is pleasant to the heart, charming, bright, and free from all afflictions; one that is level and auspicious, and entirely devoid of *śleṣmāntaka* trees, vultures, and the like.
There, the preceptor should have a pavilion constructed according to the prescribed rule,
provided with banners, arches, and various kinds of doors.
Having sprinkled [the site] once with water for pacification or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and having first smeared it with cow dung, the painter should worship each [deity] individually.
The wise one should worship with various white flowers and fruits;
then, at night, the knower of the ritual rules should offer the bali-oblation in the four directions.
One should likewise offer various lamps filled with ghee;
then, in the center of the pavilion, one should draw the divine mandala.
[It may be] square with four doors, or even circular in shape.
In the center of that, one should draw a very beautiful lotus with white powder;
and on the outside, one should fashion various beauties with bright colors.
Having placed a lotus in the center, one should install Brahmā, the Supreme Lord,
and arrange him according to the prescribed rite with the *Brahmajajñāna* hymn.
Likewise, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) properly with the hymns beginning with "tathā imā āpaḥ" and so forth;
one should worship with *rocana*, sandalwood, and the like, as well as with flowers and incense.
One should offer lamps of clarified butter, garlands, garments, and beautiful foods;
one may also indeed offer white sandalwood, camphor, or guggulu incense.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, a person should bow with all their limbs. It is recommended that the altar be situated either to the south or to the west.
Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should then again prepare the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) with the *brahmajajñāna* hymn, and perform worship here;
likewise, one should arrange it for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the *raudra* mantras.
Having offered the Abhyātāna mantras and then those of the Rudra-gaṇa,
the wise and learned practitioner should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the rite with the Nīlarudra mantras.
One should perform the oblation according to the rules with the Kutsasūkta and the Ucchuṣma hymns;
likewise, one should diligently recite the mantras that bestow long life and those that are auspicious.

Having offered the *cātana* oblation there, as well as those with the group of names of the Mothers, one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and likewise with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*).
And one should perform the fruit-bath, being intent upon those who utter auspicious words,
along with bards, Veda-knowers, and delightful songs performed by women.
One should bathe [the deity] with women holding beautiful chowries and variegated staffs together with mirrors,
using the *Brahmasūkta* and likewise worship with the *Raudra*.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, he knelt upon the ground; there, accompanied by those reciting auspicious verses, he offered prayers for his desired fruit.
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and having likewise performed rites for auspiciousness,
he should cause the sounding of drums, filling the air with the blasts of conchs and kettledrums.
One should perform the Uttaratantra and have the members of the assembly recite it;
then, one should feed as many Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas as one is able.
One should especially honor the wretched, the helpless, the blind, and the miserable with various kinds of food and edibles, as well as those who are deprived of food and drink.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should offer the *gaṇabali* at night;
the household deities should be worshipped, and a festival should also be held in the home.
Afterwards, one should feed the practitioners and householders in their homes;
trees should not be cut down, and one should avoid harming living beings.
Those held in bondage should be released, as should enemies bound by anger;
one should proclaim safety throughout the land and worship the Guru.
Having granted fearlessness in every respect and having worshipped the Supreme Lord,
one obtains a long life and enjoys the entire earth.
The entire ritual procedure for the sacrifice to Brahman has been declared by me for the sake of my devotees—
just as it was [declared] by Atharvan to the Lord of the Gods when he bowed down with a desire for what is auspicious.

Having performed his ablutions, completed his sacrifice, finished his daily rites, and established his protection, this Lord of the Gods, having swiftly obtained the grace of the Atharvans, shone resplendent over the three worlds, free from rivals. Thus it is said.
(Pariśiṣṭa 20: The Sacrifice for the Skandas, or the Dhūrtakalpa) (AVParis 20.1.1) Now, therefore, we shall explain the Dhūrtakalpa.
One should perform this regularly every four months, during the first fortnights of the months of Phālguna, Āṣāḍha, and Kārttika.
On the following day, the sixth lunar day, having observed a fast and gone out toward the north-eastern direction,
one should prepare a mandala measuring thirteen *ratnis* on a pure, delightful, and non-saline spot. Having fashioned a garland of all types of forest trees in the center of the pavilion,
and having attached bells, banners, flower-garlands, and protective cords to the back of the [main] garland, one should arrange mirrors in the middle.
There, one should invoke [the deity] with the words: "Those white horses that carry you."
Him whom white horses, ever-yoked and swift as thought,
carry— him, the rogue clad in white armor, I invoke.
Him whom elephants, lions, tigers, and even horned beasts carry— him,
the rogue clad in a lion’s armor, I invoke.
I invoke that rogue, clad in variegated armor, whom peacocks and many-colored winged birds carry.
Him whom all classes carry, ever-yoked and swift as thought—
I summon that rogue, the one clad in every armor.
I invoke that rogue, Śaktisaṃnāha, whose power is always unfailing and who eternally possesses a bell and a banner.
And that youth who is always and eternally surrounded by the hosts of Mothers— him,
the rogue, I invoke together with those Mothers.
And that great one who is always surrounded by a thousand maidens—
I summon that rogue, Siṃhasaṃnāha.
May the god come, accompanied by his hosts, his army, his vehicles, and his attendants, being well-disposed— the six-faced one with eighteen eyes, golden-hued, and possessing swift and full radiance.
May the divine Kārttikeya come to me, together with the Brahmanya-pitṛs and the Mothers, and with his brother Viśākha; O you of universal form, accept this offering along with your attendants.
"Be at rest," he should say, and cause her to lie down.
Lie down in the praise of the Apsarases of the excellent bell, where indeed those with beautiful arms are fashioned;
lying there, O Vināyakasena, grant me long life, progeny, and cattle.
With the words, "These are the waters," he should offer scented water for washing the feet.
"May the Blessed One, the God, accept [this], for he is a rogue."
And six [verses] beginning with "The golden-colored ones," "These divine Gandharvas" for the fragrances, "That fragrance of yours," and "These flowers" for the flowers.
"Dear to the Element... [and so forth].
"You are a tree, worthy of sacrifice," [he says] regarding the incense.
With the mantra "yakṣyeṇa te divā agniḥ śukraś ceti," one should offer a lamp.
"He who has a beautiful countenance on every side"—this refers to the leaflets.

Having washed the sacrificial vessels, he should set out the oblations: rice with curd, rice with milk, rice with molasses, rice mixed with mung-bean porridge, grains, sweetmeats, all perfumes, all juices, and having prepared a vessel full of water, one full of roots, one full of flowers, one full of fruits, and one full of juices;
then, having drawn lines with the verse "Indra [plowed] the furrow," and having carried forward the fire with "O Agni, come forth," he should kindle it and [place it] facing eastward.

Having placed fuel on the fire with the three verses beginning "O Bhaga, this fuel," and having added that fuel with the verse "Well-honored by the Lord of the House (Gārhapatya)," he consecrates the kindled fire with the verse "The fire is kindled."
"Bhadram icchantaḥ," "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," "Mamāgne varcaḥ," "Tvayā manyo," "Yas te manyo," and "Yad devā devaheḍanam"— these six, beginning with the *kāmasūktas*, and ten [others] for Mahīpati,
[are offered] with *svāhā*.

Having offered oblations with the words: "To Dhūrta, to Skanda, to Viśākha, to Pinākasena, to Bhrātṛstrīkāma, to Svacchanda, to Varaghaṇṭa, to Nirmila, to Lohitagātra, to Śalakaṭaṅkaṭa, svāhā! and [with the verses] "To Agni, to Prajāpati," "O gods who are eleven in heaven," and "To Anumati, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
I shall praise the auspicious Śiva, the bestower of boons, who is present in Agni and the Kṛttikās;
praised by me, may he, whose form is universal, grant me all my goals.
Wealth, grain, family, enjoyments, and the sensation of my speech; likewise, male and female slaves, a dwelling place, precious gems, and divine ointment—[may these be mine].
Those who worship with devotion this clever, illustrious, and devoted-to-Brahman man—
may they all be wealthy, possessed of progeny, and renowned.
"Just as the Blessed Lord Indra was formerly pleased after receiving boons, [so may you grant them], saying:
'Grant me vast enjoyments, and especially for my devotees.'"
One should present the offering with the Kāma-sūkta.
O God, having accepted this offering presented by me with devotion according to the proper rite, be gracious and free from anger.
I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In every birth, from the beginningless birth, O Bhavodbhava, favor me; salutations to Bhava.

I take refuge in the God; I take refuge in the Giver of Boons; I take refuge in Skanda, the fierce Kumāra, the son of the six Kṛttikās, the six-faced one, the son of Agni, the achiever, according to the words spoken by the Lord of Beasts.
May that Skanda be gracious to me, whose flowers are red, whose unguent is red, and whose roosters have red eyes.

Some recite [the mantra] as "belonging to Agni, the son of the Kṛttikās," others as "belonging to Indra," and some as "belonging to Paśupati, belonging to Rudra; whoever you are, whoever you are—homage be to you!"
Homage to the Master, to Śaṅkara, the son of Agni; homage to the son of the Kṛttikās.
The Blessed One is incomparable in some respects, svāhā; the Blessed One is incomparable in some respects.
It has the appearance of a supreme jewel-gem.
"Having a form like the finest gold and jewels."

"O God, these are your perfumes, these are your flowers, this is your incense, and this is your garland. Having performed three circumambulations to the right, one should fasten the protective amulet (*pratisara*), a thread spun by the Sun.
"The thread spun by the Sun was tripled by Indra;
its knot was tied by the Aśvins, and the protective amulet was fashioned by Brahmā."
Bringing wealth, fame, and long life, and the destruction of the inauspicious—
I bind this *pratisara*, the subduer of all enemies.
There is no fear from Rākṣasas, Piśācas, or likewise from Gandharvas, nor from humans; and whatever evil deed has been committed [is thereby neutralized].
He is liberated from evil deeds committed by himself and those committed by others;
likewise, that hero shall be released from every sin.
From malevolent magic, from sorcery, from that performed by women, and whatever else is inauspicious—
so long as he maintains this sutra, no harm shall come to him.
"As long as water and cattle exist, and as long as the mountains shall stand,
so long there is no fear for him who shall uphold this sūtra."
Having eaten in accordance with this, one should dismiss the deity.
The Gandharva named Pramoda runs about at nightfall;
O evil one, release [him] from the stone, release, release, and let him go!
"As long as these waters are purified by the wind, golden-hued and of faultless form, so long do I cause this rogue to flow away; once he has been washed away, grant me the boons as promised."
When the stars have risen, having entered his house, he should look at his wife and say: "O wealthy one, grant me wealth."

Whatever desire born of longing that a twice-born man strives for in his mind to enjoy in this world, having enjoyed that very object from the sacrificer who is the army of the Pināka-wielder, he attains immortality in that very manner upon having consumed it.

(Pariśiṣṭa 21. The Characteristics of the Requisites) (AVParis 21.1.1) Oṃ. We shall proclaim the requisites as they are endowed with their defining characteristics, by which indeed the ritual action being performed becomes fruitful for the twice-born.
The wise say that kuśa grass with unbroken tips, whether fresh and possessing a luster like sapphire, or even dry and white in color, brings about peace.
One should prepare fragrant flowers, succulent fruits, and captivating garments among the ritual requisites.
Fragrant seeds and other substances,
as well as the finest items such as water for honorific offerings (*argha*), sandalwood, incense, and the like, along with gold, jewels, and so forth.
And cows that are milch, well-characterized, and intended as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
numbering sixteen, eight, and four, should be given to those most proficient in the four Vedas.
The officiating priests (ṛtvij), however, are said to be endowed with youth, good character, and virtuous qualities;
they should number thirty-two, sixteen, or eight, for rites of pacification as well as for portents.
Those who possess gold, clothing, ornaments,
and calves are declared to be the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) during the recitation of the sacrificial rite.
All those sixteen officiating priests are indeed remembered as Atharvans;
they are pure-souled, free from envy, [purified] by Vedic recitations and burnt offerings.
There shall be a collection of water-jars made of copper, silver, gold, or even clay— provided they are flawless and of uniform color.
Then, the fetching of the sacrificial pots, the fuel— especially of various kinds—
and likewise the bringing of barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth, as well as the clarified butter.
Bladeless, unsplit, straight, long-knotted, and slender in the middle—
these qualities of *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and young grass blades should be known as auspicious for rites of pacification (*śānti*).
Six times sixfold, from a lotus fiber, a cow’s hair, a broken grain, a mustard seed, and a barley grain, is the measure of a man’s finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
The staff should resemble a cow's tail, being even, smooth, and pleasing;
the *sruva* ladle is to be known as belonging to Śāntuka, while the *sruc* ladle is described according to the characteristics of sacrifice.
For a rite of pacification, a sacrificial ladle made of gold is prescribed, or one made of Palāśa or Khadira wood;
however, specifically for a rite of sorcery, one should make the *sruva* ladle out of iron.
One should use bell-metal for the rite of driving away [enemies], and wood from the *aśvattha* tree for the rite of subjugation;
specifically, for the rite of causing dissension, a sacrificial ladle made of *nimba* wood is prescribed.
For rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should know the ladle to be made of silver; for bringing victory, it should be of copper;
but for rites such as the attainment of immortality (*amṛta*), the ladle should be known to be made of sandalwood, which bestows success.
Having understood the scope of the *sruva* ladles and likewise the ritual procedure for the *kīla* pegs,
as well as the rite for the stone at the house in the various directions, one shall attain success in one's undertakings.
In a place free from the śleṣmātaka, arka, and kaṇṭaki trees, and from pungent or bitter substances and the like;
and one that is avoided by the ariṣṭa, vulture, owl, and other birds.
In a place filled with shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants, with delightful and sweet trees—
both young and fruit-bearing— and entirely devoid of the bones of cremation grounds;
In a place resounded by the melodious calls of peacocks, ruddy geese, swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, and other birds, and endowed with delightful sprouts;
On the bank of a river, or especially at the confluence of rivers with the ocean,
in a blameless direction, or in the north which is unconquered.
The performer should purify the ground on an auspicious site sloping toward the east or the north;
having carefully purified the eastern direction, he should have a pavilion constructed there.
It should be a square of sixteen cubits measured on all sides, divided into nine compartments, with four doors or even a single door at the top.
Then, in the northeast corner, one should prepare a bathing altar measuring ten or twelve cubits, or according to the available space.
Furthermore, those which are the main pillars should be four times the height [of the base],
while the supporting pillars on the sides are declared to be half that height.

Water-pots should likewise be offered with pillars; the door is prescribed according to the desires [of the patron], or it is proclaimed to be equal to the height of the sacrificer, or even half of that.

One should construct a house in the shape of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), doubled in size and surrounded [by a wall]. There should be a water-channel in all directions, and one must not cover the top of the pit.
Surrounded by twelve pillars with four columns in the center,
constantly honored and worshipped, it is known as the House of Peace for the sake of pacification.
It is beautified by the upward-swinging of eyes and other features, crowded with banners of various colors—
red, yellow, smoky, black, blue, and pale white.
Indeed, sixteen variegated banners, with the luster of sapphire, are prescribed;
they possess the colors of the rainbow, smoke, black, blue, and pale white.
Sixteen banners—yellow, red, white, and dark—are prescribed;
there, above the sixteen jars, is a great banner.
One should have them covered with cloth, each individually provided with gold,
along with gems, pearls, flowers, and pleasant, sweet fruits.
It was adorned with lamps placed in every direction,
as well as with incense, offerings of oblations, and the shouts of victory from the bards.
Honored indeed by the sounds of conchs and trumpets, accompanied by the resonance of lutes and drums, the king, together with his domestic priest, should enter.
Then, having prepared the water for pacification and having applied the *cātana* [mantras] to it,
one should sprinkle [the fire-drills] according to the rule with the mantras and then bring forth the two fire-drills (*araṇī*).
When the fire has been churned according to the rule, one should perform the oblation with the peace-water accompanied by mantras as prescribed, and then observe the omens.
Resounding like the thunder of clouds and blazing forth on all sides,
with long, uninterrupted flames and being very smooth, it brings about success.

Having the luster of the *kiṃśuka*, the *aśoka*, or the lotus, and likewise resembling the blue water-lily, the fire should be known as a bringer of success within seven nights; of this there is no doubt.
As soon as the oblation is offered, it blazes up and appears as if laughing;
one should know that fire, which resembles the color of a lotus, to be the bestower of success.
A fire whose flames are unaffectionate, accompanied by smoke, black in color, and not moving clockwise— one that is contrary to what has been described— shall not be a bringer of prosperity.
One should declare that great accomplishment is eternally attained there, even before it is completed, whenever the sacrificial fire becomes serene while the oblation is being offered.
One should explain it even before it is finished.
Thus ends the section on the characteristics of the equipment.

(Pariśiṣṭa 22: Characteristics of the Araṇis) Om. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the two araṇis—both their form, their dimensions, and likewise their qualities and defects.
That which was enjoined by the wise Teacher through the science of grammar,
and the characteristic mark seen by the sages in a former aeon;
Having enclosed the domestic fire together with his lawful wife,
he should then perform the Vaitānika rites, beginning with the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), as they have been prescribed.
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, having gone toward a faultless direction,
one should perform the extraction from an *aśvattha* tree that has a *śamī* within it, according to the injunction stated in the Śruti.
But that *aśvattha* tree which is on a *śamī* tree and not joined with any other tree,
and whose root is in the middle rather than on the outside— that is proclaimed as the "womb" (*garbha*).
But in the absence [of a śamī tree], one should fetch [the wood] from a śamī-enclosed aśvattha;
and when a śamī-enclosed [tree] is available, having performed the ritual mounting (*samāropaṇa*), one should release [the fire].
The lower fire-drill (araṇi) and the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi) are twenty-four finger-breadths long, six finger-breadths in width,
and four finger-breadths in height.
According to the Staudāyanas, it is remembered as reaching up to the shoulders or even the chest;
according to the Devadarśas, it is the length of an arm; and according to the Jājālas, it is the length of a thigh.
The Cāraṇas and Vaidyas [state that] the shanks are eight finger-breadths according to the Mauda school; Jaladāyana says they are one span, while Bhārgava says they are sixteen [finger-breadths].
At the height of the head and at the navel, it is indeed twenty-four [finger-breadths];
this measurement has been proclaimed by the teachers Śaunaka and others.
Its lump, however, should be six parts in height and four parts in width; it should be square, smooth, and free from holes or knots.
One that is damp, split, scorched by fire, cracked, struck by lightning,
or possessed of other defects should be avoided with great effort.
A knot at the head destroys the eyes; one with holes brings about the destruction of the wife;
a moist one destroys sons; and one that is cracked brings sorrow.

One should not prepare the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) from wood that is dried upright, nor from wood that is black or rough; furthermore, both should not be from the same tree.
It should be of that same size, half that size, or larger according to one's desire;
however, it must be churned with this [ladle] alone, for one should not cause a confusion of origins.
When there is a confusion and intermixture of wombs, a great fault arises;
that sacrifice is called tāmasa, and no fruit is found therein.
In the *piṇḍa*, however, the solstices and the equinoxes reside in its breadth, while the seasons reside in its length; the half-months and time itself are established therein.
"The sacrificer is the kindling wood," so say some wise men;
for all ritual actions have him as their primary focus, and the sacrifice itself is likewise.
In the first sixth-part of the root, the feet and the shanks are proclaimed;
in the second, the knees and the thighs; in the third, the hips are said to be located.
In the fourth [month], the belly along with its limbs is formed; in the fifth, the neck;
and in the sixth, the head is said to be completed—one should point out these as the constituent parts.
If the feet and shanks are crushed, a piśāca is born;
likewise, from the knees and the thighs, one indeed attains the state of a rākṣasa.
All desires are said to be in the hips; likewise, hunger is known to be in the belly.
Enemies are in the chest; death is in the neck; and pain is in the head.
Therefore, they desire [the gift] specifically on the hip, since it is declared to be faultless;
likewise, [it bestows] wealth, cattle, sons, heaven, long life, and beloved happiness.
The first churning should be performed on the buttocks, especially during the placing of the fire;
the other acts may be done as desired, but one must avoid the neck in all cases.
Having left three finger-breadths at the beginning and likewise four at the end, the gods reside in the middle; therefore, one should churn the fire right there.
The womb should be in natural alignment and there should be no deviation in the sides;
when churned in the direction of the hair, it bestows all desires.
Leaving one finger-breadth from the base and three finger-breadths on each side, that region is to be known as the womb of the gods; there the fire-god is to be churned.
Leaving eight finger-breadths from the base and twelve from the tip, the divine womb should be in between; there the fire is to be churned.
The Vedas were produced for the sake of sacrifice; sacrifices are established in the fire;
and the fire is born from the two kindling woods; therefore, these two are of primary importance.
The two side-pieces should be made of half-araṇya wood, and the two pressing-sticks here should be of khadira;
the thong here is sixfold, and the upper part is recorded as being eight aṅgulas long.

The fire-stirring stick should be eight finger-breadths long, the lower fire-drill twelve finger-breadths long, and the base-block twelve finger-breadths long; this is the prescribed rule for the sacrifice.
Some declare the measurement to be one fathom (*vyāma*), while others know it to be three cubits;
it should be triple-layered, joined with a fist, and made from the bark of sacrificial trees.
The Bhāskaras are said to be in the *cātra*, likewise the Vasus in the *uttara*;
all the hosts of gods are in the *netra*, and Viṣṇu is in the *pīḍaka*.
That which is the second fire-drill is proclaimed as the "upper" one;
having taken a portion from it, that is also proclaimed as the "upper" [fire].
Facing either east or north, the practitioner who performs the whirling motion should face west;
having grasped the pure [substance] with both hands, its tip pointing toward the north, he should press it firmly.
Having joined the root of this [lower] fire-drill with the root of the upper one,
and having placed it upon the fire-pan, one should press it down with the presser.
One should rotate the *cātra* with the *netra* until fire is produced;
for it is endowed with all the gods, and by that it is known as the source of all happiness.
This application of the mechanical device was indeed observed by the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as by the learned ones whose wealth is austerity, for the purpose of performing sacrifices.
The sacrificer himself should churn it, or one learned in his own Vedic branch, or the foremost of the twice-born with that mantra; for this is remembered as the ritual churning.
(Now,) if the two fire-drills should become worn out by insects or by friction, [one should act as follows].

When the two new fire-drills have been brought together, having fetched them on the following day, having split them into pieces on the previous day and cast them into the Gārhapatya fire, he mutters [the mantra] while holding them over the fire.
(AVParis_22,9.2) "Awake, O Agni; enter your womb to carry out the sacrifice for the gods, O Jātavedas!
Move together with the two kindling-sticks; cast off the worn-out skin with the unworn.
