Having prepared the clarified butter, he offers it into the Āhavanīya fire with the *manasvatī* verse. (AVParis_22,9.3)
[One who desires a son] should cause it to be heard.

"May the mind, the light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns that have been sacrificed for and those that have not been sacrificed for—those I unite with the oblation of ghee, svāhā! With these words, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnimat.
He gives a bowl of rice together with a sacrificial fee.
That original sacrifice is thus summarized.
In this very context, the churning of the fire has been explained as a secondary topic;
it includes the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) produced from the limbs [of the sacrificial animal], as well as the drill-wood (*netra*), the base-wood (*ātra*), and the churning-stick (*pīḍaka*).
Whoever shall maintain here this characteristic of the two fire-sticks,
for them nothing whatsoever will be difficult to obtain, both in this world and in the next.
One desiring a son should always cause this to be heard; before long, he obtains a son who is learned, virtuous, well-conducted, long-lived, and possessed of abundant progeny.
Thus has this supreme preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for young and old twice-born ones been fully explained by the wise Pippalāda.
Having studied this, at the end of the body one attains the supreme Brahman.
For such a person there is neither death nor old age, neither sleep nor disease;
there is no hunger, thirst, or fear—he remains established as Brahman.

(Pariśiṣṭa 23: Characteristics of Sacrificial Vessels) (AVParis 23.1.1) Om. Now, therefore, the characteristics of the sacrificial vessels, as well as their origin, form, and dimensions, shall be proclaimed in due order.
The *camasa* cups, the *graha* vessels, and those which are the *homa* vessels,
as well as the sacrificial trees and their branches, are thus described in the *Brahmaveda*.
At the ancestral rice-ball offerings, one should employ the sacrificial ladle and other implements, as well as those used by the Agniṣvātta gods and prescribed for sacrifice;
likewise, in the evening oblations, both the regular and the occasional rites are performed.
The sacrificial vessel (*caru*) is said to be shaped like a *bilva* fruit, made either of copper or of clay;
it is known as a *carusthālī* when its mouth is wide at the neck.
A winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is said to be that which is made from the leaves of *kuśa* grass, mango, bamboo, or *balbaja* grass,
and is four-cornered with its opening facing downward.
*Asi*, *khaḍga*, and *nistriṃśa* are proclaimed to be synonyms for a sword;
that very form which appears when it is drawn is what they call the *sphya* at a sacrifice.

The sacrificial fire-pit is raised like a faggot; its width is equal to the depth of the excavation itself. It is narrower in the middle and has its opening facing upward; that is the "obstructing" mortar.
Due to its thickness, it is the size of a fist, and in measure, it is the size of a shoulder;
it is like an elephant’s tusk, and its lower part is encased in iron.

The *sruva* ladle consists of a handle with its base, and its hollow is the size of the thumb-joint; when these parts are joined together, they form a single unit, but when separated, the hollow is half that size, and the circularity belongs to the handle.

The *dhruvā* ladle prescribed for all sacrifices is said to be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood; likewise, the *agnihotrahavaṇī* and the *sruva* spoon are also traditionally prescribed as being made of that same material.
The base-staff is hollowed out with bark; the cup is four finger-breadths wide, and the tip is twice the size of the cup, described as being like an elephant's lip.
[Devoid of the eyes and other organs, as well as the two nostrils and the teeth;
the excavation from the opening shall be two finger-breadths deep and the pedestal one finger-breadth;
it is traditionally held that it should be either circular or square, and beautiful at its base.]
The exterior of the cavity should be half a finger-breadth in width all around;
the cavity in the middle of the *sruk* ladle is circular, and the thickness of the handle is half that of the cavity.
Some wise men say that the handle should be twenty-four finger-breadths long;
that sacrificial ladle is also proclaimed to be thirty-seven finger-breadths [in total length].
A [vein] that is split, shattered, crooked, moist, cracked,
as well as porous and knotted, destroys the eyes and other faculties.
When [a tree] remains as a charred stump, when it is half-dry, when it has been struck by lightning,
when it has been uprooted, fallen, or broken— one should not even think of it in one's mind.

On an auspicious lunar mansion and under favorable lunar days, having gone toward an auspicious direction, the wise man, with gentle speech, should fell a tree in the morning, ensuring its tip points eastward for the purpose of making a sacrificial ladle.
The mṛga, the hariṇa, the ruru, as well as the one with a black back and head— whatever its hide and skin may be, that is called the kṛṣṇājina.
When kuśa grass is grasped in the left fist and cut once,
or when it is cut with an axe or a sword, that is called "cut once."

The *mekṣaṇa* spoon, however, has its tip shaped like the upper joint of a thumb and is formed like a ladle; it should be made of *vaikaṅkata* or *pālāśa* wood and measure one span (*prādeśa*) in length.
The two dice are said by the seers of old to be made of gourd, or bamboo, or wood, or indeed of bamboo alone, and they should not be circular.
That which is made by craftsmen with two wheels, masses of wood, and other materials—
the cart well-known in the world— is placed at the fire in the sacrificial rite.

One should understand *ājya* to be clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or well-processed fresh butter (*navanīta*); likewise, the collyrium may be that from Sauvīra or other sources, or even that which is divine.
That which is known as sesame oil is declared to be the ointment;
the seat is called the *kaśipu*, and the pillow is the *upabarhaṇa* resting upon the body.
Eight barley grains are taught to constitute one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
twenty-four finger-breadths are defined as one cubit (hasta) by those learned in sacrificial rites.
The *sruva* ladle is one cubit long and shaped like a sword, and it should be made from a single piece of wood;
the *juhū* ladle is said to be one forearm in length, as are the *dhruvā* and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

The *sruva* ladle is prescribed as being made of copper, and the *khaḍga* spoon likewise of *khadira* wood; the *juhū* ladle should be made of *pālāśa* wood, and especially so the fuel sticks (*idhma*).

The *grahas*, the vessels, the *camasas*, and the posts for the sacrificial stake and the fire-places should be made from trees suitable for sacrifice, using whatever is available and not from anything else.

Fuel sticks (*samidh*) measuring one span (*prādeśa*) are prescribed for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*); the measurements for fuel sticks as observed in the technical definitions are given here in their proper order.
The *śamī*, the *aśvattha*, the *palāśa*, the *khadira*, and the *vikaṅkata*;
the *kāśmarī*, the *udumbara*, and the *bilva*—these are proclaimed as the trees for sacrifice.
In the absence of these trees, others should be taken by those performing sacrifices;
they are to be regarded as suitable for the purpose of sacrificial components, especially for the sake of fuel-sticks.
The grains of barley, rice, mahāvrīhi, and priyaṅgu, as well as the grains of śyāmāka and sesame seeds, are to be prepared as prescribed by the revealed scripture.
Whatever substance is used for the evening oblations should be the same for the morning oblations;
however, that which is offered with a different substance is as if it were not offered at all.
Whether at sunrise, before sunrise, or at the time of twilight, as well as at times of hunger— O Kaikasi, one should likewise perform the fortnightly oblation.
For the Yāyāvaras, the performance of the fortnightly oblation has been prescribed by the sages;
a twice-born man should practice whatever is spoken in the Veda in any manner whatsoever.
One who is ill, a traveler, or one afflicted by royal oppression should then perform the fortnightly fire-oblation; having completed it, he should always practice [the regular rites].
The oblation, drawn fourteen times, is offered once;
there is one fuel-stick and a single offering, which suffices for half a month.
Having performed the rite fourteen times with the *sruva* and the vessel as before,
they likewise offer oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire and the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire.
Having offered the morning oblations on the previous day,
they offer the morning oblations on the following day at dawn according to this very same procedure.
In former times, the sages, having perceived [this] in all circumstances during times of distress,
placed [the sacred fires] upon two kindling woods according to the ritual prescribed in the Śruti.
This should be understood to apply even in the case of houses where the sacred fires have been established, for the purpose of performing oblations;
however, there is no fault in using it during periods of birth-impurity, provided it serves that specific purpose alone.

Immediate purification and other rules regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) have been proclaimed by the twice-born; however, because of the scriptural injunction that "one who performs the *homa* himself" is required, there is no fault [in performing it] due to the Vedic command.
For those observing vows, for those engaged in sacrificial sessions, and for great kings who have established the sacred fires—
no fault shall be found in them, provided they remain steadfast in their morning and evening rites.
Fuel sticks made of *pālāśa* wood are prescribed for daily oblations performed at dusk;
alternatively, those from sacrificial trees mentioned by Kauśika may be used.
Having turned it three finger-breadths in circumference, its height also shall be three finger-breadths;
this is declared to be the measure for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for men in all cases.
Having turned sixteen finger-breadths and three parts further upward in a straight line,
the location for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is proclaimed to be in the southern direction.
The Gārhapatya fire-altar is proclaimed to be twenty-eight finger-breadths;
one should cause the Āhavanīya to be made twenty-four finger-breadths square.
The wise describe the sacrificial pit for the southern fire as being thirty-six finger-breadths in the shape of a bow.

In the northeastern direction, according to the procedure for the *gārhapatya* fire, one should establish the *sabhya* fire; however, Māhakī and Kauśika do not desire the *sabhya* fire in the hall-fire (*śālāgni*).
The Maudāyanas and likewise the Śaunakeyas maintain that where the substance [of the offering] is not visible, it is declared to be [obtained] from the mantra itself.
One should know that clarified butter is used there, and the oblation is performed with a *sruva* ladle;
the sprinkling and the sacrificial rite (*haviḥ-karma*) must be carried out by the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrapāṇi*).
The rites of recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and ancestral ceremonies (*pitṛkriyā*) should be performed with *kuśa* grass in hand.
Likewise, at a sacrifice, the officiating vessels, mantras, oblations, and the twice-born priests constitute the constituent parts.
All ritual acts are performed with sacrificial porridges (*caru*); that is what is called the "Fourfold Priesthood" (*cāturhotra*).
But other ritualists say that whatever is offered with four [mantras] is performed by the Brahman, the Adhvaryu, and the Hotṛ— three of them— with Agni as the fourth.
In times of famine, during a period of turmoil, or when the officiating priests are unavailable, a single person may perform the *cāturhotra* rite; this is proclaimed by Āpastamba.
And in the absence of the officiating priests, the Adhvaryu himself should recite that;
for it has been enjoined that if [the text] is recited at an improper place, the officiating priest and others must perform the necessary rites.
Regarding what has been stated concerning digging and cutting by means of the scriptural injunctions for consecration,
one should perform the collection of materials for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice according to the preceding rule.
One should perform the setting down of the vessels and the second [rite] without the sprinkling of water;
in both cases, one should act according to the procedure for cooked sacrifices and *iṣṭi* offerings.
The black antelope skin, sesame seeds, darbha grass, mantras, clarified butter, and the best of the twice-born—no fault is found in these; one should employ them according to their purpose.
Clarified butter is its smoke-offering, the flame is its ripening, and the sparks are its fruit;
when fire comes into contact with wood in a forest conflagration, no fault is found in the fire.

There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] if one has performed recitations, study, austerities, and gifts, along with fasts and burnt offerings, as well as ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha*.

There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] by one who is a paternal uncle, a brother, or a co-wife's son, nor by one who is outcasted, insane, or impotent, nor by one who is blind from birth, mute, or deaf.
Indeed, one who is excessively lustful and one who is without a wife may perform the Vedic sacrificial rites after obtaining permission from these [elders].

Having performed the rites for the Raudra, Rākṣasa, Paiśāca, and Āsura mantras, as well as those used for malevolent magic and the ancestral rites (pitṛkarma), one should touch water after completing them.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the *dhruvā* vessel, the sword, the pestle, the mortar, and the *caru* pot—
these are purified by being thoroughly washed with warm water alone.
The sacrificial vessel, the cups, the chalices, the oblation, the winnowing basket, the *kuśa* grass, the seat,
and any utensil that has been touched by Soma are purified by washing with water.
Everything declared in the Vedas and everything stated by the high-souled Śaunaka must necessarily be performed constantly by the twice-born who desire their own welfare.
In connection with the sacrificial vessels, whatever else has been proclaimed— namely,
that which was formerly seen by the great seers as a constituent part of the evening and morning oblations.
The characteristics of the materials always prescribed by the Guru himself, as well as those approved by the performers of sacrifices, have been fully proclaimed.
Those who constantly remember the characteristic marks upon the sacrificial vessels will certainly obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
This auspicious [work] was proclaimed by the great Pippalāda for the benefit of the Brahmins and for the welfare of his sons and disciples.

Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, he who performs what is declared in the Veda shall attain liberation if he is free from desire, whereas one who possesses desire enjoys the fruit thereof.
Whatever is prescribed in the Veda as a duty to be performed by one free from desire—
all that should be known as bestowing liberation, the supreme bliss that transcends both the higher and the lower.
For him there is neither sorrow nor disease, neither death nor likewise old age;
free from hunger and thirst, he abides as one whose nature is immortal.

(Pariśiṣṭa 24. Characteristics of the Altar [and Characteristics of the Fire-colors]) (AVParis 24.1.1) Om! Now, in the *Ṛṣiputrikā*, I shall clearly declare, in due order, the characteristics of the fire-colors for all ritual acts.
In the rite for building a house, in the case of portents,
in the lustration ceremony for a king, in all fire-offerings to the lunar mansions, and likewise in the ritual for honoring the planets as guests;
In processions, garden excursions, weddings, tonsure ceremonies, and initiations,
as well as in all fire-offerings, learn now the characteristics of the fires that possess the color of flame.
The altar for rites of pacification (*śāntīṣṭi*) is prescribed as having one and a half heads in measurement, three middles, and six faces; it should be made square and without cuts.
This very altar, however, should be constructed inverted for terrible rites;
hereafter, I shall describe the altars that correspond to their respective rituals.
Having wiped it with a cow-hide according to its natural markings, having sprinkled it, and having spread it out, one should adorn it according to the prescribed rule upon a bed of wheels.
All [the bricks] should be smooth, well-proportioned, sloping toward the northeast, and beautiful;
having swept them, sprinkled them, and spread them out according to the rule, one should adorn them.
But that which is curved toward the south would destroy the sacrificial priest;
and that which should be curved toward the north would destroy the sacrificer.
Whether it be in the front, at the back, or even in the middle,
that which is uneven destroys the city, the inner apartments, and the leader as well.
This altar has been described in brief according to its general characteristics; however, its specific details will be explained in connection with those very rituals themselves.
One should purify the ground toward the east for the sacrificial site as prescribed;
the preceptor should be one who knows the characteristics of sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, fire, and colors.
Then, having properly prepared the fire with diligent effort,
one should examine the [signs] as they are fire-colored, according to what the wise Uśanas has said.
One should examine sound, color, odor, form, moisture, radiance, motion, and touch within fire; this is the definitive conclusion.
But when the fire rises up of its own accord at the conclusion of the utterance of "svāhā," desiring the sacrificial oblation, one should know that this portends the accomplishment of one's purpose.
His voice resounded like a bull, an elephant, a mass of clouds, a chariot wheel, or a drum;
his breath bore the fragrance of lotus stalks, lotuses, dūrvā grass, kumuda, and utpala lilies.
Likewise, the great-souled Fire, the destroyer of evil, roared with a luster like that of a water-jar; he was a mass of gathered flames.
Having the form of the *kuraṇṭaka* flower, with the luster of cow’s milk, gold, and reddish lightning;
possessing the radiance of full-blown blue lotuses, *kunda* flowers, jasmine, white water-lilies, and blue lotuses.
Even when fed, the right ear of a brahmin’s cow,
if she is glossy, licking her lips, joyful, and black in color, certainly blazes with fire for the sake of accomplishing one's goals.
For this fire has broad roots, is stainless and blue, with a wide middle;
its tip is blazing, its expanse is pure, and it is wreathed in garlands of flames.
Moving clockwise, with bright and radiant flames, the carrier of oblations— possessing splendor, honored in its brilliance, worthy of worship, and now worshipped by the king— [stood there].
And from the application of the ritual strewing, he anoints the implements belonging to the sacrificial section,
the house of peace with its upward-flaming rays, and the officiating priests.
As the sacrificial fire was being fed with oblations for the meritorious king, it seemed to laugh with its sound and to shine with its brilliance.
At the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the ritual, he [Agni],
as if touching with smokeless, fragrant flames, reaches toward the end of the terrestrial oblation.
Blazing with rays and masses of flames, burning the directions of his enemies—
smokeless, coiled, and moving in a clockwise direction— he brings success.

When the sacrificial fire—resembling the *kuraṇṭa* flower, gold, the dawn-red sun, a conch, jasmine, a string of pearls, and the moon—blazes with a sound like that of lions, bulls, lordly elephants, and the thundering mass of clouds, and the resonance of drums; [then...]
When the fire is broad at the base, wide in the middle, and its tip is now seen to be pressed down,
and its fragrance is like that of lotus stalks, lotuses, and breezes, the earth as far as the three oceans belongs to the king.
The earth, bounded by the three oceans, belongs to that king whose fragrance is like the breeze from a blooming lotus;
this entire world, filled with wealth and kinsmen, has its royal title eclipsed by the network of rays of his prowess.
The sacrificial fire, glowing intensely and endowed with its full radiance, seems to proclaim the king’s victory with its hands;
its pure rays have assumed a crimson hue from the mass of golden lotus filaments reduced to powder by their friction against the sunbeams.
The sound of the chariot wheels, like a mass of pearls scattered from within the shell-cavity of the Ocean of Milk, was white with dust;
and Agni, the giver of the earth to the king, whose ocean waters were illuminated by the moonlight of the one who bears the snowy-rayed moon upon his crest.

Where Vaiśvānara blazes with a pure form, his nature being that of a peak which is beautiful, smooth, rounded, white as a lotus stalk, and a vessel of prosperity— there a king shall attain sovereignty over a hundred kings.

The Fire-god bestows the earth upon the king— a land whose lotus-buds are awakened by the fragrance of the rising sun, which is delightful with the thundering of clouds suspended over the waters, and where the trees on the ocean waves are shaken by the tips of the tusks of lordly elephants.

Upon that sacrificial altar where the king’s form— resembling the orb of the sun in springtime and possessing a full mass of radiance— is established, the earth, clothed in the waters of the ocean encircled by fire and adorned with a garland of pearls, comes under his control.

"The royal fortune of the protector of the earth, whose fire blazes with a brilliance like gold, whose body is set ablaze, and who possesses the fragrance of a lotus bud— she approaches his palace, accompanied by a swarm of bees glowing like a garland and the rays of the sun shorn of their pride."
(Pariśiṣṭa 25. Characteristics of the Fire-pit) (AVParis 25.1.1) Oṃ. Bhārgava questioned Śaunaka as he sat comfortably:
"In what [place] should the fire-pit be, of what kind should it be, in which direction, and what is its fruit?"
He explained it to that Bhārgava who had approached him:
what kind of pit there should be, in which direction it should be, and what its fruit would be.
Square, shaped like a hoof, half-moon, triangular, circular,
pentagonal, lotus-like, and heptagonal.
One should designate these eight pits in the directions starting from the east;
for the ritual of the eight deities of the directions, one should assign each its own respective [pit].
It should be square in the eastern direction for rites dedicated to Indra;
it should be shaped like a hoof in the southern direction for rites dedicated to Agni.
A half-moon shape should be used in the southern direction for rites belonging to Yama;
and a triangle in the southwest is auspicious for the performance of malevolent magic (abhicāra).
In the western direction, a circle is to be known for rites pertaining to Varuṇa;
likewise, in the northwestern direction, a pentagon is for rites pertaining to Vāyu.
In the north, however, it is lotus-like for gentle rites;
in the northeast, it is seven-cornered for fierce rites, as has been prescribed.
In all rites, it should be known that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) which resembles a lotus is [auspicious];
however, one that is square and symmetrical everywhere brings about victory in every case.
The sacrificial pit that brings about all peace is especially lotus-shaped;
for rites of pacification it is square, and likewise circular for rites of nourishment.

For malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), it is triangular; for subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like, it is a half-moon; for killing (*māraṇa*) and the like, it is hexagonal; and for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), it is octagonal.
In all the sacrificial pits, the girdle is prescribed to be twelve finger-breadths wide;
it should rise progressively higher by a measure of four finger-breadths at each preceding pit.
If it is not deficient in the east, the sacrifice is completed in happiness;
but that which is not deficient in the south bestows fearlessness upon the king.
If it is deficient on the western side, it bestows success and is auspicious;
if it is equal on the northern side, it increases the kingdom of the king.
That which is level and pleasant in the center, and likewise level in all cardinal and intermediate directions,
brings prosperity to the king and his people and shall destroy all enemies.
If the aforementioned rule beginning with "not in front" is followed,
it is traditionally held to bring peace in the measurement of pavilions and houses.

A hand-sized pit is prescribed for constant homa; it is remembered as being two cubits for ten thousand oblations, four cubits for one hundred thousand oblations, and eight cubits for ten million oblations.

(Pariśiṣṭa 26. Characteristics of Fuel-Sticks) (AVParis 26.1.1) Oṃ. I shall fully declare the measurement and the auspicious characteristics of fuel-sticks, as well as their inauspicious characteristics, according to reality and in accordance with the distribution of their results.
In sacrificial rites that are to be performed for the sake of pacification or nourishment,
as well as in all other ritual acts, fuel-sticks one span in length are prescribed.
Eight barley-corns across, or three rice-grains upwards, according to the measurement of a finger; a span (*prādeśa*) consists of twelve fingers.
From this point forward, it should not be made long, nor short, nor too tall;
it should certainly not be crooked, nor should it be provided with knots.
But since upward-moving [hair] causes variegated skin diseases, leprosy,
and scabies, and quickly brings these about during a sacrifice, one should therefore avoid it.
Whether it be a *triphalā* that lacks two fruits or even one,
or one that possesses six or seven fruits— it perishes as a "four-ingredient" (*caturaṅga*) preparation.
Having prepared leaves, flowers, and sacrificial fuel sticks, the wise one should perform the rite for prosperity; it will succeed, there is no doubt in this.
Those fuel sticks that possess leaves and flowers and originate from peaceful trees are proclaimed to be highly recommended when used in the middle of a cow-pen.
(26.2.4) Now I shall further declare the characteristics of the sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
One that is shattered, split in two, short, crooked, or double-tipped at the end; one that is thin, long, or thick—such a [sacrificial blade] destroys the success of the ritual action.

Whatever characteristic has been proclaimed for a particular case, at whatever time, and according to whatever rule—it is by that very means that success shall be achieved there; otherwise, in the contrary case, there will be danger.
Listen now to the fruit of those sacrificial fuels that have been thus collected.
If it is shattered, it causes the exhaustion of one's lifespan; if it is split in two, it brings disease;
and as soon as it moves toward [the practitioner], if it is short, it immediately causes a retreat.
A curved [line] makes one unfortunate; one with two tips at the front causes loss of position;
a thin [line] leads to total destruction; and a long [line] destroys prosperity.
But a thick [line] creates an obstacle for a twice-born man in all his undertakings;
therefore, listen now to the various measurements and their corresponding results.
A twig produced from a creeper, twelve finger-breadths in length and anointed with milk, should especially be offered as an oblation in a pacifying fire-sacrifice.
For the sake of accomplishing liberation alone, the twice-born should offer oblations of [fuel-sticks] smeared with ghee;
indeed, in the ritual of mantra, he should offer those measuring ten finger-breadths in length.
For malevolent rites, it should be made nine finger-breadths long and smeared with oil;
for the sake of prosperity, it should be eight finger-breadths long, and one should perform the fire-oblation with ghee and curd.
When combined with honey and split into seven parts, it is excellent for causing expulsion; however, when split into two parts, it is not for the purpose of pacification.

For the rite of causing enmity, the fuel-sticks should be smeared with pungent oil, made of split pulses, six finger-breadths long, and entirely free of knots; such auspicious fuel-sticks are for Brahmins.
That which is joined with a knot at the tip brings victory to Kṣatriyas;
that which is joined with a knot in the middle is the means for achieving prosperity for Vaiśyas.
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) that are prescribed for all three [fires] and are traditionally held to be acceptable shall not be too moist, nor too dry, nor produced from saline soil.
Those trees that have not been burnt, nor bitten by worms, and are free from all defects— I shall now describe such trees as being equal to sacrificial fuel for the *samidh* sticks.
One should offer oblations with dry wood that was previously used for auspicious sacrificial trees;
however, in rites intended to cause strife, one should offer both moist and dry wood.
For dry woods should serve as the fuel, while the sacrificial sticks (*samidh*) should be as previously described.
One desiring prosperity should take [fuel] from the Palāśa tree; for a rite of pacification, from the Udumbara; one seeking wealth, from the Vaṭa; and one desiring sovereignty, from the Aśvattha.
One who desires prosperity should [use] the wood of the *bilva* tree, and likewise that of the *kadamba*.
One should effect enmity with pungent substances; through thorns, death shall occur.
One should know that the *kakubha*, *kaṭabha*, *vṛkṣa*, *kauvirāla*, *kauhaka*, *vaṃśa*, *vibhītaka*, and *śigru* trees are beneficial for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
For the purpose of victory, one should bestow triumph by means of the immobilization of all armies;
indeed, one who desires good fortune should use *apāmārga*, and one who desires long life, *dūrvā*.
The *punnāga* and *campaka* trees, as well as other auspicious milky trees—
whatever characteristics have been prescribed for each, at whatever time, and according to the proper ritual.
In that case, success shall be achieved by that very [method]; conversely, there will likewise be fear.
[The trees are] Arka, Palāśa, Madhuka, Nyagrodha, and Udumbara.
The *plakṣa*, the *aśvattha*, cow dung, and *kuśa* grass are the sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) respectively;
and the sacrificial fuels for the planets beginning with Āditya follow this same sequence.
A hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand oblations of the Gāyatrī constitute the supreme offering;
whatever is being offered, whether it be prepared food or sesame seeds.
When there is affliction from planets or constellations, even an oblation offered with the Sāvitrī mantra becomes a true oblation.
Thus have I declared to you the distinction between what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
As it has been said: "Whoever should perform this shall obtain all fruits."

(Pariśiṣṭa 27: Characteristics of the Sruva Spoon) (AVParis 27.1.1) Oṃ. One should perform the ritual actions in due order using *sruva* spoons made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, wood, or iron, provided they are endowed with all the required qualities.
At a sacrifice, one should offer with vessels of gold or silver; for rites of pacification and nourishment, with copper; and with bell-metal, blood and meat—one should not offer anything else at all.
All [utensils] should be employed in a sacrifice, with the exception of the iron *sruva* ladle;
however, one should employ an iron or *khadira*-wood [ladle] in the performance of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
One should offer an unbroken oblation with the *sruva* ladle while shaking it;
for by shaking it one destroys one's sons, whereas a broken oblation is for the *rākṣasas*.
One should not meditate upon anything else after having extracted the oblation from elsewhere;
one should meditate upon that deity for whom the oblation is being offered.
When the *sruva* ladle is full, one should mutter the mantra while holding the hand palm-upward in rites for pacification (*śāntika*);
however, in both pacificatory and nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) rites, one should avoid using the little finger.
It should be neither too long nor too short, neither too thick nor too thin;
it should measure twenty-eight finger-breadths according to the measurement of the tip of the little finger.
A long [halo] harms the king; a short one may destroy the officiating priest. A thick one leads to the destruction of crops; a thin one is traditionally held to cause ruin.
The staff has the shape of the tip of a cow's tail; they know the *maṇḍalāgra* to be its head.
One should carve a hollow in the head with a measurement equal to the tip of the thumb.
This characteristic of the *sruva* ladle has been specified according to the distinction of its results;

it has been extracted from the *Gopatha* in accordance with the scriptures and the injunctions of the *Śruti*. Listen now to how one performs the ritual action with the *sruva* as well as with the hand.

(Pariśiṣṭa 28: Characteristics of the Hand) (AVParis 28.1.1) Oṃ. When one offers an oblation with the hand, whether with the right or the other, I shall then declare the rule for it, so that the offering may be most auspicious.
Just as his secret ritual action perishes when it is not understood,
so shall I fully explain the *Gopatha* for those who desire its recitation.
Having fashioned a ring from *kuśa*, *balbaja*, or *mauñja* grass and placed it on the ring finger,
one should then perform the fire-oblation, touching the right hand with the left.
One should not offer an oblation with empty hands, nor with the knees unbent;
for the Rākṣasas seize the oblations of one who has not bent his knees.
Having taken up either fuel-sticks or food, the wise man should offer them with five [verses];
and being well-composed, he should gently place the food into the center of the fire.
In domestic rites or in sacrifice, as well as in rites for pacification or nourishment, one should likewise avoid the *kanīnikā* [the little finger] among the five fingers.
One should offer three oblations of food— neither sesame seeds nor rice grains—
at which time one should employ whatever is intended for malevolent purposes.
One should always perform the malevolent rite with the left hand using three equal fingers; this is designated as the *śūla* (trident), and by means of it, one should strike down the enemy.
If one offers with the left hand while using the right as the *apasavya*,
or if one offers with the right while using the left as the *apasavya*— that [is an improper offering].
That which is called *abhicāra* shall, however, result in total pacification.

(Pariśiṣṭa 29: Characteristics of the Flames) (AVParis 29.1.1) Oṃ. Having prostrated before the great officiant Bṛhaspati, who was seated comfortably and devoted to the knowledge of the Self, Nārada questioned him.
"O one of great wisdom, proficient in all scriptures, tell me what the characteristics of fire are, whether they be inauspicious or auspicious."
Being questioned by him, that highly intelligent one related all of that.
When the fire, being offered oblations, is seen with straight flames,
glossy and having the hue of a *kiṃśuka* flower, one should predict success therein.
Wherever the sacrificial fire is seen to possess the luster of the rising sun,
there the sacrificer and the domestic priest quickly obtain peace.
Even when appearing the color of an *aśoka* flower or likewise the color of gold,
the sacrificial fire, if offered at an improper time, brings about pacification.
If it blazes swiftly without smoke after making a clockwise revolution, then one should know there will be peace; likewise, if the opposite occurs, there is danger.
If it hisses and roars, and sparks fly out in every direction,
one should then perform the expiation as taught by Kauśika.
Moreover, if the fire itself should touch the ground or wander about in every direction,
it would signify an inauspicious omen for the *hotṛ* priest there.
Kapila, piṅgala, tāmra, rakta, and that which has the luster of gold should be known as auspicious and purifying; the opposite brings fear.
Whenever some inauspicious sign is observed in the fire, the Hotṛ priest encounters distress; one should therefore perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) therein.
(Pariśiṣṭa 30: The Brief Lakṣahoma) (AVParis 30.1.1) Oṃ. Gautama questioned Śaunaka, who was sitting comfortably, concerning the merit of the lakṣahoma and the deities of the oblations.
To him, Śaunaka, whose eye is knowledge, explained it correctly:
"Listen with focused attention to the Lakṣahoma according to the prescribed rule."
I shall describe in its entirety that ground which belongs to the fire-chamber: it should be pure in its soil, level, smooth, and sloping toward the northeast.
It is declared and praised as being without ashes, bones, charcoal, or chaff;
its measurement is one cubit, or one shank-length, or two aratnis.
One should mark out a square, four-cornered figure, equal on all sides with a cord;
[this should be done by] Brāhmaṇas who are perfected in the Vedas and whose minds are concentrated on the rites of Brahman.
Having fasted for one night, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times;
indeed, having fasted, the wise should likewise recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times.
Clad in white garments, having bathed, adorned with garlands and perfumes,
they were abstinent from food, self-controlled, contented, and masters of their senses.
Seated upon a seat made of kuśa grass, they should perform the supreme oblation,
having scraped the ground, sprinkled it with water, and prepared it according to the prescribed rule.
Having approached the purifying fire with the mantra, "O Agni, go forth with Agni for wealth," he should perform the rite after kindling it, saying, "O Agni, may you be well-disposed toward me."
When the Lakṣahoma is completed, one should give a milch cow;
or a bull, gold, or a garment—whatever by which the twice-born may be satisfied.
Through barley, however, one obtains abundant enjoyments; through grain, longevity itself;
and by offering sesame seeds, one becomes radiant, and both lifespan and fame increase.
The world of Āditya is attained by means of a ladle made of *arka* wood; that of Soma by one of *palāśa*;
the world of Viṣṇu by one of *aśvattha*; and likewise the world of Brahmā by one of *udumbara*.
By this very procedure, the consumer of oblations is sacrificed here;
having offered these four hundred thousand [oblations], he goes to the world of Brahmā.
As long as that doer lives, he possesses sons, wealth, and prosperity;
when his time is fulfilled, he is led by celestial chariot to the supreme state.
(Pariśiṣṭa 30b. The Bṛhallakṣahoma) (AVParis 30b.1.1) Om. Now Kāṅkāyana questioned the blessed Atharvan.

"Blessed One, by what procedure does one who is about to commence a *koṭihoma*, a *lakṣahoma*, or an *ayutahoma* choose the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and how should they perform it for him? He replied:
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a king, a Vaiśya, a village, or a district desiring prosperity or peace,

who intends: "I shall perform a *koṭihoma*, a *lakṣahoma*, or an *ayutahoma*," from the commencement until its completion, you must remain abstainers from meat, celibate, and eaters of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
Having been told "So be it" by them, he should have a pit dug—one cubit, two cubits, four cubits, eight cubits, or [altogether ten cubits] in length—or ten cubits;
and so says Bādari.
In the case of a *lakṣahoma*, however, it should be made eight cubits in size; of this there is no doubt.
Alternatively, one may make it two cubits or even four cubits.
The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be ten cubits [in length], and its width should likewise be twice as much;
provided it is not deficient in the front part, the sacrifice will be successfully completed with ease.
Now, if it is deficient on the south, it causes fear for the sacrificer;
if it is deficient on the west, it will certainly result in the failure of the sacrifice.

That which is indicated in the north is known to severely take away the kingdom from the king; that sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) which is deficient in the center is understood to cause the destruction of the subjects.
However, a sacrificial pit that is devoid of corners will also bring inauspicious results;
the area for the girdle is said to be twelve finger-breadths in measure.
Three girdles are prescribed, each being four finger-breadths wide;
they are raised in height by four finger-breadths, each subsequent one being higher than the preceding.
O Bull-bannered Lord, that first [girdle] is declared to be *sāttvika*, the second is remembered as *rājasa*, and the third is to be known as *tāmasa*. This, O Vṛṣabhadhvaja, is the *mekhalā*.
There, the practitioner should fashion a vulva fourteen finger-breadths in length;
it should be eight finger-breadths in circumference, and its opening six finger-breadths wide.
That altar for Prajāpati is shaped like an elephant’s trunk;
having thus constructed the pit according to the prescribed rule, it should be characterized by the proper marks.
A sacrificial pit that is complete in all its characteristics and perfectly composed in every respect should be known as a bringer of success, increasing both longevity and fame.
Therefore, having dug a pit with effort and sprinkled it with water, one should establish the planets beginning with Āditya in front of the fire;

to the north, the lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā; the world-protectors in their respective directions; and all the deities beginning with Agni on all the corners of the pit. Having thus established them, [one should proceed].

Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for each of those [deities] with their respective mantras, having taken clarified butter (*ājya*) that has been melted and purified, and having cleansed the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles and heated them, he places the fuel upon the fire.

Then, while the patron holds on to him, he prepares the water of pacification (*śāntyudaka*) with the four groups beginning with Vāstoṣpati; thereafter, he causes the performer to sip water and sprinkles him.

Then all the officiating priests offer fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter, or sesame seeds, accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā* and the prescribed number of repetitions, using either the *gāyatrī* verse or the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.

For one desiring prosperity, [the oblation] is mixed with *śrīparṇa* leaves; for one desiring peace, it is mixed with *śamī* leaves; for one desiring rain, it is mixed with flour of *karīra* shoots; for one desiring cattle, it is mixed with fruits such as *badara*.

After the completion of the daily rites, then—whether at the fullness of ten million, a hundred thousand, or ten thousand [oblations]—when the patron has taken hold [of the vessel], they perform the Great Consecration at night and offer the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*).

They use a ladle made of *udumbara* wood: reaching up to the mouth for a Brāhmaṇa, reaching up to the forehead for a Kṣatriya, reaching up to the shoulder for a Vaiśya, and being of no fixed measure for a common person.

At the end of those [oblations], for the sake of providing a path of escape, one should have a trench dug, wash it with warm water, bring clarified butter, and by pouring a continuous stream of ghee (*vasor dhārā*), one attains Vaiśvānara.
Therefore, when he reaches the butter-vessel and the Vaiśvānara [oblation], he then utters [the formula].

Having offered oblations with the words, "May my vigor and my sovereign power [be granted]; those fires which are the gods—O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious for the sake of my life; obeisance! and having presented the guest-offering (*argha*), he places in a vessel a garment, *lodhra* powder, a garland, fruits, and other items, and casts them into the fire with the *svāhā*-utterance while reciting, "Obeisance to you, O Beholder. Whatever desire he wishes for that is to be restrained, that [he attains].
For him, his desire is fulfilled.

The rites beginning with the *samṛddhi-homa* are the same; one should mutter the *svastyayana* formulas and cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made. Having bestowed cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and clothing upon the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and having prostrated, one should dismiss them. When that day has passed, if a woman, with a garland in her hand, anointed with white sandalwood paste, and holding white flowers, should offer them, or if she should ascend the palace while holding white mustard seeds in the hollow of her hands.

If one should mount an elephant, or a heedless horse, or a white mountain, or a bull, or a vehicle yoked with horses during the time of sleep, one should know that it portends the attainment of every success desired by the mind.
Therefore, one should sleep that night with self-restraint.
Having seen a dream, one should report it to the officiating priests.

"Go away, O stranger! You are not the living one; we know you, O dream, for what you are—a mere fraction, a mere hoof-print. Having consecrated the king's face with this mantra, they should depart by the way they came. Regarding this, there are also these verses:
Regarding divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial wonders, there is no doubt; the wise know that a *koṭihoma* consists of one hundred thousand, or even ten million, oblations.
Whatever sin is committed unknowingly and whatever is done impulsively—
all that indeed perishes through the performance of the Lakṣahoma.
Therefore, in all undertakings, and especially in rites for pacification,
he who always acts with self-restraint does not encounter misfortunes.
(Pariśiṣṭa 31: The Koṭihoma) (AVParis 31.1.1) Oṃ. The gods and the sages, being oppressed by great sorcerers, as well as by death and diseases, spoke this to Brahmā:
"By what action, O Lord of Gods, are death and disease overcome?
Or how is sovereignty attained, as well as the supreme station, O Lord?"
Thus addressed, the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds and the Lord,
replied to all the brahmins together with the hosts of gods.
Listen all of you with focused attention to that action by which sovereignty,
long life, health, sons, and even victory are obtained.
For those who always recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, no fear exists anywhere.
One who desires success should constantly perform the fire-oblation with that [mixture],
using barley, sesame seeds, sacrificial fuel-sticks, rice, and likewise mustard seeds.
Now, O best of gods, if you should desire great accomplishment,
have a *koṭihoma*— which yields great fruit— performed by a domestic priest (*purodhā*).
Just as Atharvan previously performed [the rite] for Tryambaka,
so too is the Koṭihoma applied according to that same procedure.
Seeking greatness, Śarva then said to Atharvan:
"Perform for me that rite by which greatness is obtained."
O Lord, [grant] sovereignty, long life, health, and the highest station;
as well as sons, prosperity, fame, intelligence, strength, and manly prowess.
Thus addressed, the highly resplendent Atharvan, the seer of mantras, [taught] the Gāyatrī joined with austerity as the very word of the Ṛgveda: "iti-iti."
(From AVParis_31,3.2): "The word of the Ṛgveda is measured"—thus it is understood in the mantra.
Indeed, the Gāyatrī is the three-footed Brahman, established as the universal form.
"Since she is the giver of life to all beings and their constant sustainer," having thus resolved in his mind, he performed the *koṭihoma* sacrifice.
With fuel-sticks from a tree that pacifies [evil], being well-composed, he performed the rite with a *gāyatrī* verse;
thereupon he attained greatness as well as supreme sovereignty.
And his name, Mahādeva, became renowned throughout the worlds;
whatever calamities and afflictions there were, they all came to rest for him, and he obtained Skanda as a son.
Then the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, being pleased, questioned the highly wise Atharvan: "What is the procedure for the *koṭihoma*?"
The Brahman consists of twenty-four syllables, has three feet, and sustains the world;
by means of that Sāvitra mantra, this oblation of mine has been performed ten million times.
And I shall proclaim its ritual procedure for the benefit of all the world,
by the performance of which there shall be peace and supreme prosperity for human beings.
In times of affliction for living beings and during various kinds of calamities,
as well as upon the appearance of comets, the Koṭihoma should be performed.
In times of fear from calamities, likewise in times of fear from foreign armies,
and in times of fear from drought, one should perform the *koṭihoma* sacrifice.
One should undertake its commencement on a bright lunar day that is auspicious, and specifically during the *vijaya* muhūrta; one should avoid the *tithi*-defects.
A wise man should perform [the rite] under Rohiṇī, Vaiṣṇava, Tvāṣṭra, Pauṣṇa, the Uttarās, Abhijit, Puṣya, or Saumya, or under any other auspicious asterisms.

Now, if one hastens to perform the *koṭihoma*, which yields great fruit, the wise man, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited for him, should cause the commencement to be made.
A pit for the *koṭihoma* is specified as being eight cubits in measure;
for the *lakṣahoma*, it is ordained to be half that size.

Having fasted for three nights and performed the fourfold propitiatory rite (*śānti*), the *brahman* priest should sprinkle the site with the propitiatory water (*śāntyudaka*) for the sake of the success of the ritual.
Having churned the fire with a concentrated mind according to the ritual for the Great Peace (*mahāśānti*),
the wise one should perform everything until the rite for Nirṛti has been completed.
Then, at dawn, having carefully extracted the fire many times and produced it by friction, he, being composed, should offer oblations there with fuel-sticks and feed many Brahmins.
A hundred, a thousand, ten million, or twenty or ten twice-born ones should offer oblations of fuel-sticks from a pacifying tree mixed with clarified butter.
Or else, the Brahmin himself should worship Savitṛ day after day according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*, and the mantra for this occasion is "viṣāsahi."
One desiring peace should perform [the rite] with barley; with sesame seeds, for the removal of evil;
with fuel-sticks, one obtains all desires; and with bilva fruits, one attains gold.
One obtains supreme prosperity by means of lotuses, and splendor by means of ghee;
one obtains sons by means of curd, and Vedic luster by means of milk.
Eating only sacrificial food, self-controlled, wearing white garments, maintaining a cheerful countenance, and remaining restrained, they should all be celibate students.
One who employs forest-dwelling practices may subsist on milk, or even subsist on fruit; such a Brahmin may perform the Koṭihoma sacrifice.
Then, a sacrificial fee must be given to each of the Hotṛ priests individually: a gold coin, a horse, a cow, a garment, or even gold, according to one's ability.
And whoever may be a Brahmin who is the performer of all rites,
to him one's entire property should be given, or else gold of equal value.
When the ten-million-fold oblation (*koṭihoma*) is completed, the wise man should worship the hosts of planets;
he should also cause the *amṛtā* rite and the *ghṛtakambala* rite to be performed.

When there is fear of death from an untimely end, one should perform the *kāryāmṛtā* rite accompanied by a blanket of ghee; when there is the arrival of an enemy army, however, the *aindrī* rite is performed with a blanket of ghee alone.
Raudrī is for the arising of all wonders, joined with a woolen blanket of ghee;
Salilā is for the cessation of water, and likewise the woolen blanket of ghee.
And she who has a back of ghee-wool is Salilā at the time of the drying up of water.
With whatever specific desire one should perform the *koṭihoma* sacrifice.
The wise man should perform at the conclusion whatever rite has been prescribed therein;
this very rule is seen to be ordained for the practice of *abhicāra*.
When a journey goes contrary [to one's wishes], there is an oblation with sesame and mustard seeds accompanied by the Sāvitrī mantra;
its commencement should take place under formidable lunar mansions and on formidable days.
One should always have [the rite] performed during the intercalary days (*tithichidra*) of the dark fortnight;
likewise, one should always avoid the asterisms Maghā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, Revatī, and Ārdrā.
One should use *śara* grass in place of *darbha*, and oil is prescribed in place of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
In place of the utterance *svāhā*, the word *phaṭ* is used; these, beginning with the braid (*veṇī*), constitute the fourteen [mantras].
One should cause oblations to be offered into the fire of a *caṇḍāla*, or into a funeral pyre, or even into the fire of a woman who has recently given birth,
using fuel-sticks from formidable trees mixed with oil.
Wearing a red turban and red garments, or else wearing black robes,
he should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks with his left hand while facing the south.
Having fashioned an image of the enemy out of beeswax over a fire of *khadira* wood,
one should heat it while mentally reciting the *Sāvitrī* mantra in reverse order.
Having fixed it upon a stake at the throat, one should heat it day after day;
as long as the enemy does not come under control, [the victim] perishes once it has melted away.
By this aforementioned procedure for the *koṭihoma*, Śaṅkara is said to become pleased; therefore, he bestowed that auspicious material reward.
Then Atharvan, having received the Bhautika [Veda], gave it back to his disciples—
the auspicious, merit-bestowing, and beloved vow of Paśupati that brings about liberation.
Having understood this correctly, whoever performs the *koṭihoma* attains all desires and goes to the world of Brahmā.
The wise person who always causes this to be heard and likewise recites it obtains the fruit of ten million fire-offerings (*koṭihoma*) and is glorified in the world of Rudra.
From the Gopatha [Brahmaṇa], this renowned text known as the Koṭihoma has been extracted for the benefit of humanity, in order to delight those who dwell in the midst of men.
(Pariśiṣṭa 32. Gaṇamālā) (AVParis 32.1) *Oṃ bhūḥ*, *tat savituḥ*, *śaṃ no devīḥ*, *śāntā dyauḥ*, *śaṃ na indrāgnī*, *śaṃ no vāto vātu*, *uṣā apa svasus tamaḥ*—this is the Śāntigaṇa.

(1) AVParis_32,2: You are the repeller of witchcraft, the defiler of the defilers; you are the sovereign light, and you are the maker of kinlessness for those who [plot] from the front. (2) "The fair-winged one [takes] you"—[this is] that which they have fashioned against you, with its fruit turned backward. (3) "Whatever evil has been done"—this amulet is the counter-spell.
(4) "That which they fashion"—these are the repellers of witchcraft.
Thus ends the group of Kṛtyās.
The *cātana* [mantras]: "This oblation for the one who praises; those who have approached the new moon night; out from the house, the destruction of the *arāyī* demons;
may the goddess *pṛśniparṇī* look upon us for our welfare; those of true power; with you as the first, yoked in front, offer in the midst of the forest;
to Agni, the slayer of demons"—this section consists of the *cātana* mantras.
Thus ends the section on the *cātana* group.
The divine Gandharva named Mātṛnāman gazes upon this; "O Agni, those two mothers of yours"—these are the names of the Mothers.
Thus ends the group of Mothers.

The Vāstoṣpatīya [section consists of]: "To Vāstoṣpati," "Of the quarters," "To the guardians of the quarters," "Right here, the firm one," "The mantra, the womb, and the son," "And the father," "Thou art the house of Indra"—these four; "To the sky, svāhā!"; "May there be peace for my armor"; "To the earth, to the sense of hearing"—these two; "Carrying strength"—these six; and the section beginning with "Truth is the great. These are the Vāstoṣpatīya formulas.
Thus ends the group of site-plan types.
"O gods, drive away evil; burn away our sin that is enveloped by old age; protect me from evil—thus [is] the 'Evil-Dispeller'. (AVParis_32,6) "The Evil-Dispeller."
Thus ends the Gaṇa that destroys evil.
The first-born from the womb, the destroyer of *takman*, when Agni rose up—O ten-trees, release him!
From *kṣetriya* disease I release you; [I release you] from the swift-gliding deer. I release you; I invoke Bhava and Śarva, you two. To him who is in the mountains, to heaven, Svāhā!
Agni [drives away] the *takman* as if from fire; let us cast away evil like a bowstring. Let Varuṇa ward it off; [ward off] this one.
The two verses beginning with "yavaṃ vidradhasya" and "balāsasya namo rūrāya," as well as "śīrṣaktiṃ śīrṣāmayam," are the hymns for the destruction of fever.
Thus ends the group [of mantras] for the destruction of fever.

(These are) the destroyers of bad dreams: "O evil dream, O misery of life, go away to the other [world], you who are not the living one! I turn myself away from the bad dream; [I turn away] that food which I eat in sleep; [I turn away] him who, being a thief, seeks to harm us; [I turn away] that which, while we are sleeping or waking, is the evil dream of my mind. O Desire, having slept the sleep, may we know thee as a dream!"—these are the three sections.
These are the destroyers of bad dreams.
Thus ends the group for the destruction of bad dreams.
"Life-giving as heaven; you are the out-breath and in-breath, the vital force. To you alone I release [this] from your two eyes.
And may the gods protect you. Seize what is dear for the sake of Antaka, for Death. Homage to breath! To the subduer!"—these are the life-bestowing formulas.
Thus ends the group of verses on longevity.
Those which are the three-times-seven [verses] for splendor, in this wealth; at dawn, [one offers] to Agni, who possesses the splendor of an elephant;

glory in the lion and the tiger; the oblation is glorious; may Indra be glorious on the mountain and among the *aragarāṭa* trees; as Soma is at the morning pressing; and whatever splendor is in dice, by which the great inviolable [cow] strikes her hindquarters—these are the verses for splendor.
Thus ends the Varcasya group.

May Svastyayanī protect us on the further shore; O Indra and Pūṣan, protect us! May Tvaṣṭṛ grant me divine [favor], O Soma, by which [means] there may be homage to the divine slayers and freedom from fear. O Mitra and Varuṇa, he who is thousand-eyed has come toward us; may he drive away our enemies from below. May Yama and Mṛtyu [be held at bay]; may Bṛhaspati protect us around. Him indeed as the protector—Indra is the good deliverer; he is the good deliverer.
"O Indra, [protect] my vital organs with pleasant [songs]; may Heaven and Earth be my armor; the armor of Indra and Agni is yours, O mountains;
that which is your center, those which are your eastern [directions], and [those behind]—do not [assail] us from behind. These are the formulas for well-being (*svastyayana*).
Thus ends the section on the collection of auspicious rites.
Fearless, bestowing well-being upon the people, you have been invoked by the Brahmin. Let not the dust-raising hoof-strike reach them; O Mitra and Varuṇa, grant him fearlessness;

O Heaven and Earth, grant this village fearlessness. Pūṣan has struck down the devourer; Indra the Good Protector has guarded these quarters. May he not go upon this path; may the Lord of the People, the Bestower of Well-being, protect the clans. Homage to your noisy ones; let this kingdom be yours.
"O Indra, that from which we fear—may there be freedom from fear," thus [he says], for the sake of security.
Thus ends the section on the Abhayagaṇa.
"Unconquered, we know thee as the arrow; do not strike us, O thou who art not one to miss the mark! Thou art the giver of well-being. By thee, O Manyu, is my [weapon] sharpened.

O Manyu, these divine armies of thine, irresistible and crushing, having struck down the arrogant, move along their paths; Indra, the overcomer, conquers. 'Over thee, O Indra!'—thus are the invincible [verses]."
Thus ends the section on the Aparājita group.
"Śarmavarman is he who is the rival; from here and from there, O Indra, drive away those who hate us.
Do you [protect] us; O Agni, lead this man forward for life. The three goddesses, wide-extending, may they protect us; 'Thou art the protection of Indra'—[reciting thus], omitting the last [verse];
'That by which the gods [conquered] the Asuras'; 'For the oxen, thee'; these two [verses]; 'Thy two bodies, O steed'; 'In the impulse of strength, of the gods'."

"Speak for the wives; [speak for] the Rakṣas-slaying, vigorous one who is sharp-edged. May Heaven and Earth be my armor; may the armor of Indra and Agni be manifold armor for me. This Mitra has stepped forth from the earth; [he is] the protector, the one without a rival, in front"—thus [says] Śarmavarma.
Thus ends the group [of names] beginning with Śarma and Varma.
Those who are the city-gates of the gods in front, the Brahman born [in the beginning], the thousand-streamed; may Agni protect me.
"Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, Mitra, and the Earth have stepped forth; they have cast down the human weapon; it has been conquered for us"—thus [is] the Devapurīya [chant].
Thus ends the Devapurīya gaṇa.
Rudra is the one who is in this eastern direction; he is the host of Rudras.
Thus ends the section on the host of Rudras.

O Rudra, the fierce one, whose medicine is cooling water! Those three who have stepped forth from here toward this eastern direction—Bhava and Śarva, I meditate upon you both; the Brahman that was born, those who are unattainable in their thousandfold streams. Even so, the summer and the winter [are yours];
for the oxen, for me, O Waters, Vaiśvānara, Yama, and Death. That Rudra of yours who is in the fire, Bhava and Śarva, Rudra—be gracious!
"O Bhava and Āśarva, we say this for that serpent or scorpion of yours from the intermediate direction of the eastern quarter"—this is the group of Rudras.
Thus ends the group of the Raudras.

(Citrāgaṇa: "May they not find us; may he who does not move through the house be the giver of well-being to the people, the unerring one; far away [be] those hated by the wicked—O Agni, that heat of thine..."—these five hymns; "O Rudra, with thy cooling medicine"; "Those gods who are in this eastern quarter";
"And the gods of Agni's mind"—beginning with these, the Mṛgāra-hymns, excluding the last; "May he burn away evil from us... (apa naḥ śośucat).
Agham pṛthivyām; Agnaye; Mamāgne; Brahma jajñānam; Anāptā ye; Sahasradhāre; Savitā prasavānām; Nava prāṇān; Pātaṃ naḥ; Tvaṣṭā me; Yena soma; Namaḥ devavadhebhyaḥ; Abhayam mitrāvaruṇau;
Upa prāgāt; Sahasrākṣaḥ; Siṃhe vyāghre; Abhayam dyāvāpṛthivī; Grīṣmo hemantaḥ; Anaḍudbhyaḥ.

Thou art mine; O Waters, Vaiśvānara, Yama, Death—overcome him, O Indra, Conqueror of All! For Trāyamāṇā; this for me, O Agni; the two verses beginning with *viṣāṇā* and *pāśān*; Śakadhūma; the two verses beginning with *somārudra*; Bṛhaspati for us; that famous one; the Protector;
Indra the Good Protector; with the delightful [songs], O Indra; thy vital organs; for Antaka, for Death; seize it; this is the amulet, this...
May Varuṇa, Bhava, and Śarva be gracious; homage to the vital breath! We address Agni—this is the *arthasūkta*. "Truth is great" (RV 10.190.1)—these two [verses].
"Those mountains of yours... (RV 10.145.2). "That which is your middle... (RV 10.145.3). "Those [streams] of yours that flow eastward... (RV 10.145.4). "Do not leave us behind from the west...

(RV 10.145.5). "Summer is yours, O Earth... (RV 10.145.6). "The rains shall stand upon you, O Earth... (RV 10.145.7). "O Mother Earth, the thousand-horned bull... (RV 10.145.8). "Jātavedas... (RV 10.145.9). "May we not stray from the path... (RV 10.145.10).
The Citrā-gaṇa, which belongs to him who [performs] the sacrifice, consists of the successive recitations beginning with "From the intermediate region of the eastern quarter."
Thus ends the Citrāgaṇa.
The three hymns beginning with "patnīvanto aditiḥ," "dyauḥ," "sinīvālī," and "kuhūṃ devīm" are the *patnīvantaḥ*.
Thus ends the group [of hymns] ending with the *patnīvanta*.
"May there be well-being for you, O Mother! Indra, take pleasure in this station; may your two feet be auspicious to us;
may your head be united with the calf; [the verse] 'The Virāj' is one; 'Flying upward' are two; 'Indra is greater than the subduer, the conqueror'—this is the Āditya-group."

May the Goddess be auspicious to us; may Indra and Agni be auspicious to us; may the wind blow auspiciously for us; may the sky be peaceful; and may the group of pacifiers beginning with Pippalādi be auspicious.
Thus ends the group of pacifying mantras beginning with Pippalāda.
In the *gaṇa* "yad" there are five hymns; thus there are five offspring, they belong to the five peoples (*pāñcajanya*), and the *gaṇa* consists of five offspring.
Thus ends the group of five offspring.

The two hymns beginning with "The two who go to the auspicious one" (*yanti śambhu*), "The Brahman born from the two world-creators" (*mayobhubhyāṃ brahma jajñānam*), "Of this lovely one" (*vāmasya*), "He who is red" (*rohita*), "Upward his deeds" (*ud asya krtavaḥ*), "I am the head" (*mūrdhāham*), and the two hymns beginning with "The all-conquering one" (*viṣāsahim*) constitute the *salilagaṇa*.
Thus ends the section on the group of liquids.
"Those who are thrice-seven"—this is the Viśvakarman troop.
"aghadviṣṭā devajātā," "śaṃ no devī," "varaṇo vārayātai," "pippalī vidradhasya," and "yā babhravaḥ"—this is the *gaṇakarma*; it is both a *gaṇa* and a healing remedy, thus it is the *bhaiṣajyagaṇa*.
"‘This is your womb’ (ayaṃ te yoniḥ), ‘Bring to us with devotion’ (ā no bhara dhītī), and ‘Or he who [is]’ (vā yaḥ)—this is the Arthasūkta; the Gaṇa is the Utthāpana."
Thus ends the section on the arousal [of the deity].

The two that go toward well-being, the bestowers of prosperity, golden-hued, the fires that have emerged from the dwelling; "The Brahman was born first"—these are the *mṛgāra* hymns of the gods, excluding the last one: "May [the fire] burn away our sin," "May they purify me," "The flowing waters flow forth from the Himalayas," "Purified by the wind through the filter," "May there be peace for us and bliss for us," and "To the oxen."

"Thou art for me, O Waters; Vaiśvānara with his rays; Yama; Death; the All-conqueror; our consciousness. Whatever [is lost] in the intermediate space, may that power return to me again. May the auspicious blow upon us; may the wind blow for our peace. We invoke Agni and the lords of the forest"—this is the group of pacifying mantras.
Thus concludes the collection of the Bṛhacchānti rites as taught by Kauśika, consisting of all these hymns (sūkta).

(“The two mothers who go toward auspiciousness, the bringers of well-being, golden-hued, and even the gods—if they have gone into the intermediate space, may they return again with vital power; may they be gracious to us.
“May the wind blow auspiciously for us; we invoke Agni and the lords of the forest. This is the *Śāntātīya*, the *Laghuśānti* group.)

The group of verses for radiance (*varcasyagaṇa*) consists of three verses beginning with: "Those who are thrice-seven," "O Agni, my radiance," "In the morning, Agni on the mountain," "Among the *aragarāṭa* trees," "The radiance of an elephant from heaven and earth," "In the lion and the tiger," "Glory, the oblation," and "That fragrance which is yours. (AVParis_32,28)
"Those Asuras and humans who may find us—homage to those who slay gods!"—this is the group for safety.
"Become one among beings"—thus [the officiants] address the king during the consecration ceremony.

(For those who desire offspring: the seven hymns beginning with "To the guardians of the quarters, of Agni, Manva," "The plants whose king is Soma," "May Vaiśvānara come to us," "The beautifying Heaven and Earth," "That which is near to Agni," "We speak of the trees," and "May Bhava and Śarva release them"— these four [beginning with] "The goddesses" and "When Mātali bought the chariot."
Excluding the group of signs of misfortune.
