If one uses a pill containing the *kalāpa* mantras under that person's name, made from beef due to a connection with a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), the loss of wealth will occur for him.
By performing a fire-oblation with three-colored mustard seeds together with the three sweets (*trimadhu*),
a son is born to him who is intelligent and a retainer of what he has heard.
Some, however, maintain that from that same oblation there arises, without a doubt, madness.
Sesame seeds, *dūrvā* grass, and the three sweets, when offered in the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), bring about the subduing of disease;
so too does the casting of rice grains.
Having offered fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood smeared with three substances, having given a milch cow and eight cakes,
and having subsisted on alms for one day— or for a month combined with the [observances of] the Aṣṭakas.

Having offered an oblation in the evening on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who offers a bilva tree measuring a span in height, complete with its roots and branches, becomes a possessor of gold.
When oblations of reed fuel-sticks (*vaitasī*) are offered into the fire with *arka* wood,
Parjanya becomes a giver of abundant rain through the performance of the daily (*ahorātrika*) homa.
Having subsisted on alms for three hundred thousand [repetitions] and recited this rite, one should undertake it.
Having offered mustard seeds smeared with milk as an oblation, one should cast that ash into the mouth;
in all legal proceedings, he becomes unconquerable.
Having recited the mantra over a weapon and taken it up, one who is seized in battle shall not be defeated;
the mantra "khanakhanāya" is taught for the purpose of preliminary service.
Or, because of the specific nature of what follows, hereafter [is stated] this further [instruction]:
the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) consists of one thousand unpeeled *khadira* fuel-sticks;
likewise for *atasī* fuel-sticks, so says the wise master of the learned.
One should smear a sacrificial mound the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung;
having kindled a fire there upon three potsherds and having paid homage, [one should proceed].
Or else, one should have a monkey perform a mouth-instrument on its head;
wherever that sound is heard, beautiful women come there.
With the terrifying roar of bells upon their fangs and mouths ablaze with flames,
we shall grant you, O son, whatever it is that you desire.
Speaking thus, they were all touched by the ashes from where the oblation had been offered; by the power of that, the Chāgalīs were restored.
After completing more than one hundred thousand recitations, having gone to a river flowing toward the ocean,
one should fashion a linga made of that same substance upon a sand altar in a dwelling produced from it.
Having gathered eight hundred lotuses and worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, one should again recite the mantra at dawn while standing in water reaching up to the navel.
Then the regional king, having bowed with faith, should give him a hundred gold coins and a hundred cows, saying, "Lift me up!"
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one becomes invulnerable to beasts with fangs and horns;
for other types of beasts, however, the number should be increased to three hundred thousand.
By giving away the remains of offerings to Śiva after they have been consecrated with mantras, one shall fall into madness.
For the sake of pacification, one should offer sandalwood consecrated by these three mantras.
A cow’s horn consecrated with mantras by means of meditative concentration, when buried in the enemy’s palace,
will immediately set that palace ablaze.
Sharp oil is said to be pungent; likewise, the *darvī* and the village-spoon (*srūva*) [are used].
Here, however, the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*) should be understood as consisting of honey, ghee, and sesame.
Meditating on a mental image facing him, one should perform auspicious rites;
however, for rites such as destruction, a person attains success by meditating on an image turned away.
An oblation of one thousand and eight is prescribed for this;
and whatever else there may be, such as stakes, missiles, and so forth, that should be consecrated with a thousand recitations.
Thus ends the ritual manual of Ucchuṣma.
Thus ends the first half of the Pariśiṣṭa.
(Pariśiṣṭa 37. Expiations for Combined Offenses) [Resembling the form of the 13th Adhyāya of the Kauśikasūtra] (AVParis 37.1.1) Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, who assumes the forms of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras.
Now, when the pestle falls while it is being struck, that is a terrible occurrence; concerning this, too, a verse has been spoken.
The falling mallet kills the *ulūlhalas* and the eldest son in the wife's family;
the crops, offspring, and cattle perish, just as the thunderbolt hurled by Indra would fall.

Having sprinkled that vajra with water for pacification, having scraped it with the verse "Of the enemy," having washed it with the verse "What [harm] thou [didst]," and having placed it upon the sacrificial grass, he offers the oblation.
The fallen thunderbolt indeed destroys that which is excellent; we, however, have warded off that terrible one from you.
May he be auspicious to us for the slaying of our enemies; may he destroy all my rivals who hate me.
Just as [the gods] led away the creatures from the hand or from the mortar, so do thou protect my rivals; do thou thus protect us.
Whether you are in the intermediate space or high above, whether you are a thunderbolt hurled by the gods or by mortals,
though great and widespread mantras have been employed— terrible is the thunderbolt, the falling of the mace.
"Thou art a thunderbolt, a slayer of rivals"—these three [verses].
You are the thunderbolt, the slayer of rivals; through you may I overcome Vṛtra today.
O Lord of the Forest, we have today risen up with you, the best among trees.
May he, whose priest is Indra, protect us from the *rakṣas* on every side.
The cows have lowed in response; they have lowed toward the glory, O Bṛhaspati.
"O Prāṇa, protect my breath; be gracious to this life-force.
O Nirṛti, release us from the snares of destruction."

(With the verses: "Him indeed as the protector," "Indra is the good protector," "He is the good protector," and "O Indra, with pleasant [songs] I cover your vital parts with armor"—having brought together the falling drops upon the mortar and pestle and having completed the oblations, one should fill the mortar with food and set it back in motion; one should give the mortar, the pestle, a garment, and a cow to the performer; that is the expiation in this case.
Now, that which a crow touches is to be feared as death.
This very point has also been stated in a Rigvedic verse.
...saying "O End-maker, seize death! Homage to life! and having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā," that is the expiation in that case.
Now, therefore, if the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī) falls or moves, what is the expiation for that?
One should offer oblations with the Saṃnatī, the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, and the Kūṣmāṇḍa verses; that is the expiation in that case.
Now, if the strainer should be lost from the midst of the ritual through negligence,
one should cut another [strainer], consecrate it with mantras, and commence the remainder of the ritual.
One should cause the self, conjoined with the senses, to be performed by means of that mantra.
"Purified by the purifier of Vāyu, whatever flaw is in me, let my sensory power return;

O Waters, do not take away our wisdom, nor our intellect; protect us, O Aśvins!"—with these verses of propitiation (*saṃnati*) and with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should offer clarified butter as an oblation and give a cow to the performer; that is the expiation in this case.
Now, if the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should catch fire while the ritual is not yet completed, one should extinguish it and then offer an oblation.
When Agni burned the sacrificial grass on the altar, the garment [was cast] into the waters;
from that, O Jātavedas, protect us alone from misfortune.
May our enemies be utterly consumed, just as this sacrificial grass is;
utterly destroy the splendor and prosperity of those enemies.
O Lord of the People, may that which we desire as we offer this oblation to you be ours;
may those gods who come to the sacrifice protect us on every side.
Burnt away is the evil dream; burnt away are the enemies and all the sorceresses.
Let not the sorcerers harm you, nor let the wild beast seek the peaceful one.
May Darbha, the king of the ocean, protect us on every side.
Having prepared other sacrificial grass from this [supply] and sprinkled it with water, he spreads it again.
"This sacrificial grass, sprinkled here with nectar, golden and green, I spread for you.
Spread it out as something ancient yet ever-new; accept from me this excellent garment. Having said this, he covers it over with another layer of sacrificial grass.

If, once the oblation has been taken up, the remnants of the offering are spilled through negligence, one should set that oblation down, sip water with the verse "śaṃ no devīḥ," offer a second oblation with the half-verse beginning "brahmāparam," and then offer another with the verse "brahmajyeṣṭhā. This is the expiation for that case.

If the oblation is contaminated by hair or insects, one should offer it into the ashes with the formula, "To Śambhu, svāhā!"; then, having purified the sacrificial material, one should offer it into another fire—this is the expiation in that case.
Now, if one should initiate a boy whose teeth have become loose or whose teeth have fallen out, the expiation for that is stated:

either in the house or on sacrificial grass, the father or the teacher should undergo initiation for twelve nights; the performer [of the rite] should remain purified and pure for three nights, having bathed with white mustard seeds, clarified butter, and milk, wearing white garments, and [performing] the full-moon ritual up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
He should cause him to recite the Sāvitrī; with that water of pacification, he makes him sip water and sprinkles him.

One should offer oblations with the *sāvitrī*, the *śānti* hymns, "brahma jajñānam," and the verses beginning with "ye triṣaptāḥ," "agniṃ brūmaḥ," and those for long life, luster, well-being, fearlessness, invincibility, protection, and armor.

Having poured the remnants together, one should cause [the victim] to bathe with the verses: "He who [protects] from fatigue, from heat," "yo vetasam," "yo bhūtam," "ūrdhvā asya," "idāvatsarāya," and "yady antarikṣe" and "punar maitv indriyam. This is the expiation in that case.
If the honey-stone should perish, or if the fire produced at the wedding should be extinguished—
these two extraordinary events portend the destruction of the couple.
In that case, an amulet of *pūtudāru* wood should be bound on, as well as mantras that bring intoxication;
if one cannot find *pūtudāru*, one should employ barley instead.
"May the two long-lived ones, possessing good offspring and brave sons, may Dhātṛ and Pūṣan bestow wealth upon us.
May they release from us all impurity and sin; may Savitṛ grant us a long life. Having sprinkled his finger with this water of pacification (*śāntyudaka*), he should tie it [on the patient].

He should place fuel sticks on the fire, worship [the deity] with the *saṃnati* verses, offer oblations with the *vyāhṛti*s, and give a cow to the performer; this is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in this case.
Now, if in one's ritual system the fire, though not yet formally established and not yet offered to, should go out;

Then, having led Agni forward with the verse beginning "O Ādityas," he should offer oblations with the *saṃnati* and *vyāhṛti* formulas, as well as with the two hymns beginning "Homage to thee, O Agni," and perform the enumerated sacrifices.

Now, when this wedding fire goes out, one should lead forward the fire pertaining to Prajāpati with the mantras for leading the fire, and having led it forward according to the previous ritual procedure, one should offer clarified butter with these hymns: "O gods," "What the wise ones [know]," "That which was borrowed and not returned," "That which was taken by the hands," and "That which was not staked while gambling. One should also place fuel sticks upon the fire or perform a rite of worship; one should give a garment to the officiant.
Now, when the ritual acts have passed their time and the northern solstice has passed, one should— at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings— recite the mantra, "That which of mine has spilled,

that which [has been done] through forgetfulness," and offer twenty-one oblations with the successive formulas beginning, "From that intermediate region of the eastern direction. This applies also to a rite that has exceeded its proper consecration.
Now, when this fire, having been carried forward, goes out.

If [the fire] has gone into the intermediate space, one should lead forth the fire again with the mantra "May Indra's power come back to you; may the Ādityas [bring it back]," kindle it, place a fuel-stick upon it with the mantra "O Agni, may splendor be mine," and complete the remainder of the ritual procedure.
Now, if one's *upayāma* should fall from the hand, he should pick it up with the verse: "That *upayāma* of mine which fell from the hand, that which is adorned with life—that I take back again.
"That *upayāma* of mine which fell from the hand, which is encompassed by life—that I take back again."

"Indra again, Bhaga again, and Brahmaṇaspati again have given me back my life-bringing *brahman*"; with these words he should take it up. He should offer an oblation with the verse: "Whatever breach is mine, whatever through forgetfulness..."
"That which fell from my hand, the sacrificial ladle"—this has been explained by means of the *upayāma* formula.
If the girdle and other such items should float away, one should perform the initiation ceremony again.

Having performed the *vimocanīya* oblations, he should seat another Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas; then, having gone out by the *aparājita* direction with a water-pot, having given a garment, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth, having sprinkled [the student], and having sipped water, he should sprinkle him with the hymns of the waters and purificatory verses.

Having given the sacred thread with the mantra "Make me dear among the gods," he should face eastward with the two mantras beginning with "The one who removes the deer" (*vimṛgvarī*) and "Do not leave us behind" (*mā naḥ paścāt*).

Having sat down, one should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, the Śāntisūkta, the Brahmajajñāna, and with the verses beginning "yad asmṛti," "anumati," and "sarvam," as well as with the Abhyātānas.
Now, when this girdle falls off or becomes worn out, one should remove it with the Sāvitrī verse, bring the rite to a conclusion,

and sprinkle it with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*). Then, with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, the Śāntisūkta, the *brahma jajñānam*, the *ye triṣaptāḥ*, the *idāvatsarāya*, the *ghṛtena tvā*, and the *agnim br̥hama* verses [one should perform the ritual].

If, on the fourth day before the oblation has been offered, the water in the jar should be lost, one should bring fresh water in the same manner, consecrate it with the verses "śaṃ no devīḥ" and "iha devīḥ," pour it together with the verses "āpo yanti" and "āpo hi ṣṭhā śaṃ no devīḥ," and offer it with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *saṃnatī*. One should then consecrate the water-jar with the mantra: "The waters are the form of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases; they are the flower of the waters."
A garment is the sacrificial fee.
(37.19.1) Now, if a water-vessel should move while his ritual action is not yet completed, he consecrates it with this mantra:
(37.19.2) "That great water-vessel which moves, established by the *brahman*,
displaced from its place and set in motion— may that carry away my sin."
Thus he establishes [it].
Having filled it with the *pūraṇa* [verse], one fills it again with this [verse]:
"This vessel is full once more; we establish it with the Brahman, praised by all the gods."
"May it bestow upon us vigor, nourishment, increase of wealth, prosperity, and long life;
may my ritual action be successful."

If, however, the earth should split apart, one should consecrate [the site] with the mantra, "The earth has gone to the earth," and having brought another [piece of earth], one should consecrate it with, "May power return to me again. Then, one should offer an oblation with the verses, "Vaiśvānara for our aid" and "Vaiśvānara has risen up with his rays. This is the expiation in that case.
(Pariśiṣṭa 38: The Brahmakūrca Rite) (AVParis 38.1.1) Oṃ! I shall describe, without doubt, the meritorious rite of the Brahmakūrca in brief;
for it is the supreme purifier among purifiers, and the highest austerity among austerities.
Having bathed and become pure, in a clean place sprinkled with cow dung,
and likewise covered with a cloth and honored with white flowers;
Having fasted for a day and night, patient, pure in soul, and purifying; dressed in white garments, fragrant, and seated facing east upon a seat of *kuśa* grass.
One should bring cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kuśa* grass;
however, the dung and urine should be placed in a copper vessel that has been set upon the ground.
One should take the urine of a blue-colored cow, likewise the dung of a black cow,
the milk of a copper-colored cow, and one should fetch the curd from a white cow.
Clarified butter from a tawny cow should be taken; if that is unavailable, however, [the ghee of] a five-year-old cow may be used.
One should take one *pala* of cow urine and a thumb-tip of cow dung;
seven [palas] of milk, three of curd, and one each of ghee and water.
Having taken cow's urine with the *gāyatrī* verse, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."
"Thou art brilliance, thou art pure"—with these words [he offers] clarified butter; "Thee for the God"—with this [he offers] water from *kuśa* grass.
As for the seven-leaved *darbha* blades, which have uncut tips and are joined together:
Having drawn them up with those [ladles], one should offer them to the deities according to the ritual procedure:
"Svāhā to Agni," "To Soma," and also "To Prajāpati."
Then one should offer oblations with the verses beginning "O Bṛhaspati, that which transcends this," "Viṣṇu," and "Mā nas toke," as well as with the Gāyatrī.
One should drink with the *praṇava* alone, and indeed offer into the fire with the *praṇava*; one should drink with the *praṇava* alone, and indeed offer into the fire with the *praṇava*.
One should drink the remnant of the oblation for the sake of purification with a middle-sized leaf of the *palāśa* tree, or with a lotus leaf, or even with a copper vessel.
Whatever sin resides within the bodies of embodied beings, even if it has reached the skin and bones,
the Brahmakūrca destroys it all, just as a blazing fire consumes fuel.
On the four days beginning with the thirteenth, one should bathe three times and eat food prepared without salt;
on the fifteenth day, consuming the five products of the cow while fasting yields great fruit.

In the eating of the food of those whose food should not be eaten, of forbidden food, or of a Śūdra; in the selling of the Veda; in receiving gifts at an improper time or without the prescribed mantras; in performing a fire-oblation without the proper timing or mantras; and in sexual intercourse by day—[these are causes for loss of caste].
Whatever was done in childhood, as well as in youth and old age, and even whatever was done toward one's mother and father— that he would burn away in an instant.
By practicing this month after month, one shall attain the world of the gods;
and by practicing it every half-month, one shall attain the supreme world of the ṛṣis.
By practicing this for six nights, indeed for six nights, one reaches the healthy world of Brahman;
by practicing it day after day, one attains the supreme Brahman.
Having performed the sacrifice according to this very rule, preceded by the libation to the deities,
one should know that this supreme purifier, created by Brahmā, is indeed beneficial.
(Pariśiṣṭa 39: The Rite for Tāḍāgas and Other Works) (AVParis 39.1.1) Oṃ. The great seers spoke thus to the highly wise Pippalāda:
"Tell us truly the procedure for the purification of a dug-out pit in the ground."
Having stayed for a day and night by wells, large oblong ponds, tanks, lotus-pools, or houses, one should then commence the ritual action.
Then the Brahman priest consecrates that previously mentioned water for pacification with which Agastya [performed the rite], using the two verses beginning with "pari prāgāt."
One should offer the *caru* for the earth according to the ritual procedure of the *Carutanttra*.
The preceding ritual up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings is remembered as being "Truth" (*satya*) and "The Great" (*bṛhat*).
The sacrificial offering, the clarified butter, and the fuel sticks, as well as the ritual salutation, should be performed in their proper order;
moreover, with a concentrated mind, one should mutter the mantras in the vicinity of wells and other such places.

The three verses beginning with "O Waters, you who go," "For you are indeed waters," and "May the goddesses be auspicious to us," as well as "The gold-colored ones purify me," "The flowing ones," and "Those from the Himavat in the waters."
Having recited [the mantra], one should consecrate the cow that has been brought and is drinking with the hymn beginning "ā gāvaḥ"; in the same manner, one should cause the cow to cross over.
One should consecrate [the water] near wells, ponds, and tanks; then, reciting "I summon [you] from the well-watered pasture," one should give a beautiful cow to the performer.
One should take [the materials] with the Kāma-sūkta and then complete the ritual;
thereafter, the wise man should have images of fish and so forth made from gold, silver, and other substances.
The tortoise and the makara are made of gold; the fish and the mallet are made of silver;
the crab and the shrimp are made of copper; and the porpoise is made of iron.

One should pour the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) into that very water; then the performer and the donor should bathe with the verse "From the pillar, as if purifying" (*drupadād iva śumbhanī*).
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should then cause them to pronounce an auspicious day;
for this is the correctly prescribed rite proclaimed for wells and the like—
a meritorious act for the twice-born who desire imperishable heaven.
(Pariśiṣṭa 40: The Pāśupata Vow) (AVParis 40.1.1) Om. Now follows the instruction for the Pāśupata vow:
(AVParis 40.1.2) One should not bestow it upon one who is not a śrotriya, nor upon one who has not performed the vows of the Vedas, nor upon one who has not undergone the tonsure.
The lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika*) may last for two, three, four, five, twelve, or even twelve years;
now, its bases (*āyatana*).
In the sanctuary of Mahādeva, near the waters.
In a mountain cave, in a cow-pen, or in a fire-sanctuary,
or at the resting place of many rivers, [one should perform this] at each of the three libations.
Bathing with ashes, bathing after the *raudra* oblation, and bathing with clarified butter, milk, and scented water;
[the offering of] perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, boiled rice, milk-rice, barley-gruel, parched grain, and so forth, ending with circumambulation from left to right.
Having offered the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*), perfumes, laughter, song, instrumental music, and other offerings, he worships the third [liṅga] with his right hand:
"Homage to the one who wears bracelets and armlets; homage to the Bull; homage to the one whose banner is the bull."

"Your face is monkey-like, fierce, and blameless; I give you a beautiful sacrificial animal, a terrible living being born of birth itself, like a golden ornament. Having spoken thus, he should give garments that are single-layered, stripped, or devoid of color.
Having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, having scraped it, and having sprinkled it with water, he leads forward the fire with the words "O Agni,
go forth," kindles it, and spreads grass around it. Having appointed a *brahmán* priest,
and having placed a vessel of water to the south of Rudra— not in the direction of another deity— he sets down [the fire] in the fire-pit with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) and invokes Rudra.
Rudra, whose face is like the wrathful thunderbolt, the supreme lord of the gods,
white and tawny— the Great God of the gods.
Having come for refuge, I take refuge [in you].
"I invoke that auspicious god, the lotus-eyed one, upon whose chariot are yoked lions and tigers with fierce faces"— having thus invoked him and worshipped him...
One should offer guggulu resin and incense with the mantra: "O Deva, let consumption not come upon him."
Let us know that Puruṣa; let us meditate upon Mahādeva;
may that Rudra inspire us.
To that god we know, to Mahādeva we meditate;
may Rudra grant us his approval for this.
Having thus recited the Rudra-sāvitrī.
One should consecrate with the mantra "yo agnau rudraḥ," and [recite] "namo astu" up until "devadevasya āvāhayāmy aham" during the invocation.
In the [chapter on] crushing, for the destruction of all asuras, he utters "Oṃ Phaṭ!"
At the time of the offering, one who has matted hair, a shaven head, or five tufts of hair should say, "I offer such-and-such."
Having caused [the disciple] to recite: "I, a Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such a lineage, shall observe the vow of the Blessed Maheśvara," [the teacher should proceed].
Then he gives him the girdle made of muñja grass.
But Sāvitrī [carried] a staff made of palāśa, bilva, or aśvattha wood, or a sword, a club, a khaṭvāṅga, or an axe.
"From those who are non-terrible, from those who are terrible, and from those who are more terrible than the terrible;

from all sides, O Śarva, from all thy forms, O Rudra, salutation to thee!"—having first paid homage to Śarva with this verse and having sat down, he kindles the fuel within the clarified butter, saying: "O Jātavedas, for these well-kindled fuels, do thou increase us with progeny, with cattle, with prosperity, with houses, and with wealth."
One should offer two oblations of barley and two portions of clarified butter, saying:
"Svāhā to Vāyu!"
Svāhā to Śarva, to Rudra!
To Paśupati, the Terrible, Svāhā!
Svāhā to the deity Śāntāyādhipati!

In this very manner, one should offer for the wives silently for the overlord; likewise, in all offerings for the announcement of vows, one offers the oblations to the lords of the host (*vrātapatīḥ*).
Having offered the five oblations to Rudra with the verses beginning "By the vow, you" and "The one who grew from both," he performs a bath with the ashes at the conclusion of the oblations.
I shall first take the ash-bath, which destroys all sins;
for by the ash-bath Rudra himself became bathed and purified in his very self.
Rudra bathes with ashes; Viṣṇu bathes with ashes. With that same bath by which Maheśvara is bathed, I too bathe.
By that [water] with which the goddess Umā was bathed, and Rudra, the Great Lord, as her husband;
by which all the Gaṇas were bathed, and by which the twice-born were bathed.
By that [water] at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Śiva, Śarva, and Śaṃkara, whose banner is the bull, were bathed; all beings were bathed there.
I have bathed in all the sacred fords and in rivers and springs;
yet the ash-bath belonging to Varuṇa, Agni, and Soma is the supreme bath. With that bath by which Maheśvara was bathed, I now bathe myself.
Prosperity is Piṅgala and Babhru; prosperity is Viṣṇu, the eternal;
prosperity is Brahmā and Mahendra; prosperity is the gods together with the ṛṣis.
May prosperity drive away my misfortune; may prosperity bring me fortune. May prosperity bestow upon me long life, wealth, splendor, and sacred knowledge.
Constantly moving about smeared with ashes, meditative and deeply contemplative,
they go to the station of Pāśupata, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to find.

The optional rite is performed when there is a conjunction of a specific lunar day, a substance, and a Brāhmaṇa.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite begins from the collection of the bones (*saṃcayana*) up until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
In that regard, for the obligatory rites, one should invite an even number of Brāhmaṇas for the offering to the gods.

With the *pavitra* grass in hand, seated upon *darbha* grass, he should mutter the hymn beginning with "The winds [bear] honey" (*madhu vātā*).
He should recite the *Pavitra*, the *Dharmaśāstra*, the *Apratiratha*, the *Prāṇasūkta*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, an *Upaniṣad*, or some other text concerning the supreme self (*adhyātmika*).

Having ascertained that they are satiated, he should scatter food and, having given water, he should offer the *vikira* oblation with the verse, "Those who were not cremated by fire... (*ye 'gnidagdhāḥ*), while scattering food once for each [verse].

(Pariśiṣṭa 47. Chapter on Phonemes) (AVParis 47.1.1) Oṃ. We shall first explain the phonemes, both those that are natural (*prākṛta*) and those that are modified (*vaikṛta*).
Regarding their various manifestations, all authorities dispute based on the etymological explanations found in the revealed scriptures (*śruti*).
The manifestation of phonemes is their instrument, just as hearing is the instrument for the two ears;
yet, due to the location of that hearing, it is mistakenly regarded as the phoneme itself, just as the phoneme is said to be [located there].
The homogeneous vowels, the semivowels, the sibilants, and the aspirates—by these others are not seen; such is the collection of phonemes.
And those for whom there would be a dissimilar division within the collection of their revealed scripture (*śruti-saṃhitā*).
Those very same castes [are assigned] to Virudraka and the others in the directions.
Those phonemes which are heard through the two [organs] and those whose distinction does not exist,
as well as those mental ones to be grasped, one should apply according to the instruction.
One should pronounce those [consonants] which have been moved outside the placement, as well as those which are non-nasalized,
by means of instruction, with a lateral displacement of the articulators.
Thus the vowels have been declared; of these, the first fourteen are called *samānākṣaras*, while the remainder are the *saṃdhyakṣaras*.
That which lacks color and sound is called a vowel (*nāmin*); the consonants (*vyañjana*) are known as those beginning with *ka*.
Of these, there are twenty-five initial ones; they are the "contacts" (*sparśa*), and they consist of five groups (*varga*).
The four beginning with *ya* are the semivowels (*antaḥstha*); the group of eight sibilants (*ūṣman*) begins with *śa*.
The *ayogavāhas* occur [as variants]; their initial members are of various kinds.
The *visarjanīya*, the *anusvāra*, the *jihvāmūlīya* [as noted below],
and the *upadhmānīya*— these four, as well as the *yamas* that follow, [are produced].
There exist the nasalization and the placement [of the voice] by which the completion [of the recitation] occurs;
such is this mass of speech, numbering sixty-five, which exists in both the Vedas and the world.
Those phonemes which are produced through the mouth and nose are called nasalized (*anunāsika*).
Those which possess the same effort within the oral cavity are traditionally known as homogeneous (*savarṇa*).
A short vowel followed by a sound other than *a* denotes both itself and its homogeneous counterparts;
however, when a long vowel follows a short one, it denotes only that [long vowel] from which it follows.
A letter at the beginning of a varga is considered the marker of that varga;
furthermore, the letters of the vargas are intended to correspond sequentially as the first [consonants] and so forth.

When a letter is preceded by the vowel *a*, it is understood as including that which follows it; this should be understood as its inclusive designation, with the letter *ka* serving as the illustration here.
A consonant is defined as that which possesses sound; the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) and *ha* are followed by the two *yama*s;
the three [consonants] at the end of each group of five and the three [nasals] are also included; the remainder is said to be "without sound" (*agoṣa*).

The sibilants *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*, the two [nasals] *y* and *m*, and those which are second [in their respective classes] as well as the firsts, are voiceless; the remainder of the consonants are seen by the wise to be voiced.

Therefore, the places of articulation for the phonemes are as follows: the throat is prescribed for the vowels *a* and *ha*; the chest for the visarga (*visarjanīya*); and the root of the tongue for *ai* and *au*, which belong to the first and second morae respectively.
The remainder should be understood as produced by the palate and the lips; it is held that this occurs according to their respective order.
Furthermore, for the *yama* sounds and for the final letters of each class (*varga*), both places of articulation are prescribed.
The jihvāmūlīya is said to belong to the vowel ṛ and the guttural class (kavarga);
it is also traditionally known as the letter following y and the letter l.

The palate is said to be the place of articulation for the *ya*, *śa*, and *ca* classes [of consonants], as well as for the *i*-vowels; likewise, the head (*mūrdhan*) is considered the place of articulation for the *ṣa* and *ṭa* classes.

The *t*-group [consonants] are said to belong to the teeth; the vowel *u* is said to belong to the lips. The *upadhmānīya*, the vowel *o*, and the *p*-group are likewise considered to belong to the lips.
For sounds produced in the nose, the nose is the place of articulation; likewise, the anusvāra is held to have the same [place].
The *yamas* and the final letters of each class (*varga*) are also considered to be as previously described.
"The root of the teeth is the place of articulation for the letter *r*, or it is held to be posterior to them.
Thus have the places of articulation of the phonemes been proclaimed in their proper order.
Another says:
"The *repha* should be at the root of the jaw, or again, at the roots of the teeth;
or it is behind the roots of the teeth, according to others, as a *mūrdhanya*."
The sound produced in the chest is struck against the region of the throat;
from that, the resonance (*nāda*) spreads forth, and its modification is the syllable (*akṣara*).
The guttural syllable is attended by the preceding minute measures (*mātrā*), while the subsequent measures are said to constitute the modification of the mouth.

Furthermore, for the sake of practical application, the conjunction of a vowel arising from various phonemes (*nānāvarṇa*) is maintained together with the consonant, provided it is not separated by another syllable.
In the second [set of consonants], one should proceed with the sibilants; in the third, with the voiced sounds;
and in the fourth, with the combination of voiced sounds and sibilants, according to the instruction.
In the case of the final consonants, however, the nasalization (nāsikya) is prescribed; for the semivowels, it is traditionally taught as a voiced sound.
One should apply the voiced sibilant (ghoṣoṣman) to the letter *ha* according to the traditional instruction.

In the case of the two syllables containing the letter *ṛ*, one should apply the *repha* [the *r*-sound] as minute as an atom throughout; when a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel undergoes division, one should proceed according to the traditional instruction.

When there is doubt as to whether [a sound] belongs to the region of the *ṛ*-vowels, it may be without a vowel, or it may follow immediately after, or even precede; know that it is indeed the letter *r*.
The letter *a*, the letter *i*, the letter *u*, and the letter *ṛ*—all of these may be short, long, or protracted; however, in the case of the *l*-vowel (*lṛ*), there is no length.
The letter *e*, likewise the letter *ai*, the letter *o*, and the letter *au*—
these, in their long, short, and protracted measures, are designated as the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*).
The wise perceive shortness in vowels that are acute, grave, circumflex, or tremulous, as well as those that are nasalized or pure.

The Moon’s Lunar Day) (AVParis 50.1.1) Oṃ. If the moon should be seen in the west after sunrise on the new-moon day, one should observe its color, its course, its form, its position, and its height or lowliness.
One should observe the waning and waxing of the horns, as well as which lunar mansion they are conjoined with;
from these one may discern the moon's signs of rain or drought, and of danger or safety.
At the first appearance of the moon,
when it has reached its full orb, the northern horn increases in height while the southern horn sinks downward.
In this very way, when the moon rises at the end of the Śraviṣṭhās among those [asterisms],
its southern horn is uplifted and its northern horn sinks low.
One would see the kingdom, including the inner mountains and the great mountains,
as well as Vidarbha, Madra, and the Bharatas on all sides.
When the northern region becomes elevated, it destroys these districts: Sārāṇa and Vijarāṇa, as well as those situated on the ocean and in the south.
The Kaśmīras, Daradas, Darvas, Śūrasenas, Yayāvaras, and the Virājas of the Śālvas, as well as those who dwell by the western ocean.
When the [earth] is elevated toward the south, it destroys these regions;
a man kills the queen, and the western border perishes.
The Bāhlīkas, Yavanas, Kambojas, Śālvas, Madras, Uśīnaras, Godhas, and Bhadrakas, as well as the central region together with the Kurus.
The Saurāṣṭras, the Sindhusauvīras, the Vāneyas and the Siṃsakas,
the Kṣudrakas, the Mālavas, the Matsyas, and the Mlecchas along with the Pulindakas.
Soma, characterized by the human form, destroys those who subsist on weapons, those who live by walls, Brahmins who fight, and such people of the countryside.
Or, by its characteristic, it may be thick on the body but diminishes at the horns;
when the body is small, one should predict famine, fear, and disease.
When the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight is naturally deformed—
whether it is not fully emerged or is fragmented— one should predict the death of the king.
If the moon should enter the middle of the sixth lunar mansion, the king of the earth shall be slain;
specifically, the eastern half of the Avantis and the Magadhas.
The eighth day is supreme among the *kumāra* days; the tenth day is supreme for the king. Thus, during the waning of the fortnight, the twelfth day should be observed as the midpoint.
In that case, it slays the king and his very great army at the Five Rivers;
therefore, upon seeing such a portent, one should perform all the rites for the king.
And wondrous portents are seen during that appearance of the omen;
having reached the path of Vaiśvānara, it could even dry up the ocean.
The northern path among these— namely, the Kṛttikās, Maghās, Rohiṇī, and the two Viśākhās— is known as the Royal Road (rājavīthī).
If, having entered upon this path, the moon should turn back,
it should be known that the rains will not be excellent, and likewise for security and prosperity.
If the moon goes to the Gaja-vīthī or the Nāga-vīthī,
they say it is then the Govīthī, according to the word of Garga.
Kroṣṭuki indeed knows the eight positions of the moon:
The fourth, however, stands on a staff; the fifth lies on a staff;
the sixth should stand upon a sacrificial post; and the seventh lies on his side.
The eighth is downward-facing; learn now its fruit:
kings who administer justice with appropriate punishment rule over their own kingdoms.
The wielder of the plough devours the worlds and brings about the end of the age;
they say that when he rises high in the north, there will be an excessive plague.
One who stands with a staff should predict fear and disease for the ministers;
likewise, those who cut down spears, those who cut through knots, thieves of cattle, and adulterers [are to be so predicted].
When he stands with his staff raised, these [enemies] plunder the lands;
but when he lies down with his staff, one should predict fear for the Brahmins there.
If [the moon] stands upon a sacrificial post, one should predict fear regarding grain;
if it stands upon a green body, one should foretell the slaughter of cattle belonging to Soma.
If the body of Soma is black, one should predict the slaughter of Śūdras;
if the body of Soma is yellow, one should predict the slaughter of Vaiśyas;
if the body of Soma is red, one should predict the slaughter of kings.
In the bright fortnight of the moon, one should predict an increase in spiritual knowledge.
If, at the beginning of the lunar fortnight, the moon appears glossy, yellow, and golden-hued,
and is seen staying among the cattle, one should predict an increase in Brahmins.
When the moon, having equal horns, is drunk up while situated in a high position, and having entered the path of the Nagas, it is glossy; that [moon] is honored for all its qualities.
If one with a smoky appearance, standing upon a plow, glorious and marked by an auspicious circle,
is seen at the beginning of a lunar fortnight, it brings happiness to the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
When Ugradaṇḍī has reached the royal highway and possesses the luster of turmeric and saffron, one should look toward the cremation ground.
Soma, having the form of a child with his head hanging down, should be joined with Death;
when he stands holding a bow, resembling lac and blood.
Soma will incite a tumultuous and terrifying conflict in the world;
seeing two moons in the sky, one should declare that a great Brahman-murder has occurred.
If there should be two suns, then there will be a great slaughter of the kṣatriyas;
but having seen four suns risen in every direction, one should know that the destruction of the world is at hand.
When a white umbrella appears over the sun at the time of twilight, that is the sign of the end of the age, characterized by a slaughter of people with weapons.
The Sun should indicate the flight of the country and the death of the king when his white chariot appears at the time of twilight.
One should know that danger is imminent upon the appearance of such portents.
When the sun appears cut on all sides and split in two, the sun indicates the flight of the country and the death of the king.
One should declare security when [the moon] rests upon Vikukṣi; when it rests upon Sthālīpiṭhara, there is abundance.
When it is constricted, the world perishes; when it rests upon Vajra, there is famine.
For meteors fall during the day, the earth trembles constantly,
there are peals of thunder out of season, and the twilight has the luster of fire.
The occurrence of a fall of the stars, or of smoke and dust,
the appearance of a horn upon the sun, and the withering of grass and wood;
For kings there are indeed inauspicious; Mādhava pours down rain in a strange manner, and in the midst of twelve months, the king perishes.
One should know that on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there is a conjunction with the constellation Svāti for twenty-one days.
One should remain among cattle for seven days, among wild animals and birds for seven days, and among human beings for seven days; thereafter, one may arrange for what is auspicious.
(Pariśiṣṭa 51. Planetary Conflict) (AVParis 51.1.1) Oṃ! Some planets resort to men, while some planets reside in the luminaries and in the constellations.
How can one planet be struck by another? Having understood the truth, may the Blessed One explain it.
Thus questioned by the sages, the high-souled Garga spoke of the system of planetary conflict,
as well as their defeat and victory, and both the auspicious and inauspicious [outcomes], for the welfare of the world.
The Sun was born among the Kaliṅgas and the Yavanas; the Moon among the Aṅgas;
Mars in Avanti; and likewise Mercury in Magadha.
Bṛhaspati was born among the Saindhavas, Bhārgava in Mahārāṣṭra; Śanaiścara in Surāṣṭra, and Rāhu from the mountain peaks; Ketu was born in Malaya—this is the birthplace of the planets.
In whatever region a person was born, when that planet afflicts him, one should know that region will be struck by famine or by fear.
O Nagas, Divākara, Śanaiścara, Bṛhaspati, and Budha are stationary;
Prajāpati, Ketu, as well as Candramas, Rāhu, and Śukra are the movers.

When the citizen shall conquer the citizen, whether as an attacker or as one being attacked, and likewise when the traveler shall conquer the traveler, then the king, being a citizen himself, shall conquer the citizen, whether as an attacker or as one being attacked.
Ascending, piercing, scratching—on the left and the right—and the releasing of the reins:
thus the planetary conflict is fourfold.
One should predict a clash in a counter-clockwise [movement], and a battle when the reins meet;
in scratching, there will be the ruin of ministers, but in tearing, there is the destruction of people.

When all the planets meet in the sky, he who is most radiant is likewise declared to be the victor; however, whichever planet becomes glossy is the one joined by another, while the remainder shall be defeated.
Whether it is dark-colored, or has its orb of rays departed, or is rough, or lacks rays, or is emaciated;
or if it is overcome and fallen from its place, turning to the left—that planet is to be known as "struck" by another planet.

When Mercury, Mars, Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter move clockwise around the Moon, there is submissiveness toward the three [powers] and supreme happiness; in the opposite case, however, there is a great destruction of people.
All accumulations of wealth, gold, and silver, as well as those humans devoted to tranquility, self-restraint, and mantras— the Śakas,
Yavanas, Tukhāras, and Bāhlīkas— all go to their destruction when the Sun is struck down.
Then, if Soma is slain, one should know that the ruin of the king is certain;
and the protectors of the earth will each individually destroy the living beings.
When the moon is in a state of reversal, one should know that people will oppose one another, there will be terrible fear of hunger, and a dreadful fear of drought.
The Traigarta kings, together with their chief warriors, and those who dwell in the mountains and live by fire, shall suffer;
and there will be battles mixed with rains of blood and dust, as well as famine, upon the slaying of the Son of the Earth.
The citizens dwelling by the ocean, the foremost among merchants, go to their destruction;
yet the king who sets out becomes victorious, and during this bondage of Mercury, the Soubhyas fall into misfortune.
Astrologers who have long practiced austerity and reached certainty regarding their purpose, as well as self-controlled kings and their priests, shall prevail;
yet an outsider brings victory while the citizens face slaughter, and when the Guru is slain, the three worlds fall into terror.
The king whose prowess is renowned on earth, who holds sway over Vaṅga, Aṅga, and other lands along with Śūrasena;
and those warriors who have won fame on the field of battle—they all meet their destruction with their armies when Venus is afflicted.
Buffaloes, bulls, and those men who are smeared with ashes and red ointments, as well as those devoted to agriculture and cattle-rearing—
all these, beset by various fears, gradually meet their destruction when struck by the influence of Śanaiścara.

Whatever hypocritical demons among kings there may be— those who hide their sins while engaged in rituals and vows— and others such as Śabaras, Pulindas, Cedis, and Gāndhāras, they shall be afflicted if you, O Rāhu-slayer, strike here.

When the hosts of marchers experience being attacked, and if they are slain by one enemy after another, there will be battles mixed with a rain of blood and dust; however, through the affliction of the banner-star, famine occurs.
Whatever ill-omened sign there may be— whether occurring in the sky, born of the intermediate space, or on the earth—
all that shall be pacified by thunder, great clouds, lightning, and rain, as well as by oblations accompanied by ritual fees.
Those regions where the earth is shaken by the impact of hosts of planets, or where the moon and sun are eclipsed by the planets—
to those regions [shaken by the impact of hosts of planets], Parjanya brings peace with seven nights of rain.
In three months, the contact is considered monthly;
they say that for scratching it is a fortnight, and for piercing it is seven nights.
Those belonging to Agni, Vāsava, Vāyu, and Varuṇa—
all these are to be known as auspicious, according to the word of Garga.
(Pariśiṣṭa 52. The Compendium of Planets) (AVParis 52.1.1) Having paid homage to Atharvan, the Blessed Sage said:
"Tell me, what are the planets like, and how many are they?"
Then, having been questioned by Śaunaka for the benefit of the brahmins,
the Blessed One spoke of the number according to the doctrine of the Lotus-born.
Those who roam the quarters, those who move through the heavens, those who move upon the earth, and those who move through the sky;
those who wander by day, those who wander by night, and those who wander both by day and by night.
And those who wander there alone should move in groups;
and those who roam through other streets with wandering circles [of followers] should likewise do so.
I shall describe those planets in brief, by the hundreds and thousands, in their various forms and in their proper sequence.
Resembling cow’s milk or white water-lilies, endowed with intense physical forms, they move through the inner pathways— affectionate and possessed of vast splendor.
These, known as the Visarpakas, radiant and of great splendor,
are to be recognized as the eighty-four great planets who are the sons of Śukra.
White masses of solar light, as if casting off their rays,
and like shimmering orbs surrounded by beams, appeared in the sky.
For the most part, moving slowly in circular orbits on the southern path,
those fifty-five or sixty-six [planets] are known as the sons of Bṛhaspati.
Those which are white with a slight tinge of black, hairless, and without pupils—
these sixty planets, the sons of Śanaiścara, are named Kanakas.
It should be known that there are fifty-one thieves who are subtle rays;
they belong to Baudha, have the luster of the interior of a lotus, and possess a slightly pale radiance.
The Kauṅkumas, the Lohitāṅgas, and the sons of Vidrumatejas—
known as the Triśikhas or the Tribhāgas, numbering sixty— are located on the Northern Path.
Resembling various kinds of smoke, coarse, and with rays agitated by smoke—
there shall be one hundred and one comets, the sons of Death.
Dark-hued, with black borders and turbid forms, these thirty-three rays are the sons of Rāhu; they are the planetary obstacles (*graha*) known as the *tāmasa-kīlakas*.
Resembling fires of various colors, with spreading garlands of flames, the sons of Agni are of universal forms; they are recorded as one hundred and twenty grahas.
The sons of Vāyu, however, were the Aruṇas, seventy-seven in number, fierce,
driven by the wind as if wandering about, harsh, and with scattered rays.
Resembling clusters of stars and surrounded by circles of stars,
these are the eight planetary deities belonging to Prajāpati, known by their respective names as the Gaṇakas.
There are four subtle rays of form born from the stars, joined together;
they are named the "Lineages of Brahmā," numbering two hundred and four.
Resembling clusters of bamboo,
they are slightly veiled by rays that resemble the beaks of crows.
Releasing water as it were due to their moisture, and possessing a gentle appearance—
these thirty-two grahas known by the name Kaṅka belong to Varuṇa.
The rays are like headless trunks with hair made of gold, appearing as naked stars;
these sixty-nine headless trunks are known as the sons of Time (Kālaputra), and they are the ninety-six planets.
Arciṣmān, Prabhāsa, Romaśa, and likewise Viṣamāṃs; Asnigdha, Atikāya, Kiṃśuka, and Rājasāyaka.
O Rādhā, among these, the *ṛṣaka*, *kumuda*, *phanaka*, and *ghana* are to be known as those with white *ārā* spokes; they are the *parisarpaka* types.
For these sons of Bhṛgu, possessing great strength, move among the stars;
they have cool rays and very long, pale crests of flame.
Furthermore, there are sixty other exceedingly continuous *graha* spirits, the sons of Vāyu;
appearing with disheveled hair, they manifest with black and red rays of light.
But those who have become mixed should be known as being like those covered by dust;
they are to be known as the hundred and one sons of Dhūmaketu.
Others are exceedingly golden, with the luster of molten gold;
these sixty sons of Antaka are unaffectionate and move among men.
But those who occupy the northern portion of the Nakṣatra lineage are single stars, possessed of beautiful forms, large bodies, and endowed with radiance.
The sixty-seven sons of Vyālaka who were on all sides have been proclaimed by those who know the truth as being superior in name.
Those subtle rays which appear like a continuous stream—
whether as a single star, two stars, or even five stars— [are to be known].
The planets, established as your progeny, O Brahmarāśi,
traverse the entire sky when there is a decline of men.
Others appear as minute and red, with excessive hair;
they should be known as sixty-five, and are remembered as the Prājāpatya planets.
When halos appear around lamps and circles form around the planets,
those known as *kārmuka* are said to last for seventy-one years.
But fourteen other circuits, born of unrighteousness, appeared below with their crests pointing downward; they were discolored and possessed terrifying stars.
Resembling the openings of ears, those black ones in the form of stars are the *kīlakas*;
the sons of Rāhu, however, reside at the surface of the moon and the sun.
Vajra, Kavandha, Triśiras, Śaṅkhabhedin, and Śikhāvat; these sons of Rāhu are known by these names and possess equal splendor. They are the staff-like [planets].
Just as those who dwell near the orbs of light of the moon and the sun are seen to bring about the destruction of living beings because of their kṣatriya nature.
In that regard, those who dwell near the surface of the moon should be known as having meager results,
while those who dwell in the vicinity of the sun's surface are extremely fierce.
The twenty-four serpents and the thirty-two *grahas* are seen in the southern and other directions, moving at a low altitude with wandering orbits.
Only the five planets are seen in the form of stars, devoid of their usual luster; they are known to be yellowish-red when situated in the east and south.
In the southwest as well, two planets are recorded as yellowish-red;
however, in the northwest, one planet is recorded as yellowish-red.
In the northeast stands a single Sūryaka, shining with white and red luster; he who, at the junctions of day and night, appears like the sun in all directions.
Not far from Ravi, there was the affectionate Sa-varṣā for the sake of protection;
likewise, Yavakrīta, Uṣara, Ibhya, and Nārada were present on all sides.
Karṇa, the two sons of Raibhya—Cārvāvasu and Parāvasu—and Sarpiṇa, along with Sūrya; these seven are to be known as the immovable ones.
Svasthyātreyas, Mṛgavyādha, Ṛmucu, and Pramucu took the side of the eastern kings who were steadfast.
Prabhāsa, Candrabhāsa, the powerful Tathāgastya,
Dṛḍhavrata, Triśaṅku, Ajau, Vaiśvānara, and Mṛḍa.
Aruṇa and Danu are recorded as the stationary [deities] in the southern quarter;
likewise Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Kaśyapa.
The son of Ṛcīka and the heroic Bharadvāja—
these seven high-souled ones are remembered as the immovable ones in the north.
Accompanied by Śiśumāra and the high-souled Dhruva,
[there were] Pulastya, Pulaha, Soma, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras.
Hāhā and Hūhū are to be known as the supreme station of Viṣṇu;
the wise one understands that they are the regulators of those situated in the middle, at the end, and among the immobile.
One should observe all these fixed points in the directions;
they are endowed with radiance, white, glossy, and stainless.
When they are radiant, clear, and beneficial to living beings, one should know them as such;
but when they are lusterless, discolored, devoid of light, and impure, they are not so.
For things that are small and devoid of moisture do not come to fruition;
whatever is stable in the world flourishes when [the elements] are well-disposed.
When the fixed stars are not propitious, the stationary [beings] perish;
likewise, the Sun, Venus, and Mars [become unfavorable].
Rāhu, Soma, Śanaiścara, as well as Bṛhaspati and Budha;
likewise, those belonging to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and Varuṇa.
The Vāyavya, the Saumya, and the Brāhma as the eighth planet;
and the ninth should be known as the great planet Dhūmaketu.
The other planets are not the *yuga-grahas*; rather, those eight known as the *dig-grahas* are remembered [as such].
However, the *yuga-grahas* are seen upon paths accompanied by the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*).
The remaining planets moving through the sky are seen with their orbits disordered;
these, along with others born from the breath of Death, are to be known as the sixteen comets.
Like the *kūṣmāṇḍa* [vessel], it is completely severed; on the southern path there are twenty-seven, and exactly eleven are to be known as arising from the twelve Ādityas.
Those planets consisting of the element of fire have the sun as their radiance and gaze;
others, however, emerged from the wrath of Rudra at the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Eleven planets of terrifying form, bearing blazing goads, are there;
seven others belong to the Grandfather (Brahmā), while the remaining ones are the jarjara-planets that move transversely.
Emitting crests that are spread out like white cloth made of threads,
fifteen others are explained as being Śvetaketus.
Those sons of Uddālaka-Ṛṣiputra have wandering mandalas that move downward;
they all have white tufts of hair, are gentle, lovely, and possess slender radiance.
When the nectar of the city was being churned together with the eighteen moons,
comets resembling jasmine flowers are said to appear in the milk-ocean-like sky.
The planets will be devoid of rays, without crests, and of massive bodies; they will be without flames, resembling silver jars, gentle, and possessing cold radiance.
But there is one, consisting of the wrath of Brahmā, the soul of the universe, who seizes all things;
at the end of the four ages, the emergence of the worlds occurs from him.
Having departed from the path of the stars, the portions of the sky moving along its sides may either rise in the east or likewise move low in the north.
Whether they have risen above the horizon or are submerged in it, being overwhelmed by a lack of moisture,
all such planets are to be known as yielding results that are dull or unfavorable.
The ancestral rite (*paitṛka-karma*) of all is great, arising from the fortune of their progeny;
may they all utterly destroy whatever inauspiciousness they speak.
Their greatness of karma and birth, as well as their conduct and lineage;
likewise their forms, their qualities, those who consist of them, and those who are their dependents.
All [these] indeed bring about disease; they may strike by means of death, weapons, fire, or thieves, as well as by the destruction of livestock and crops, and by other causes.
Through fumigation, touch, staying [in the same place], and the occurrence of sunrise or sunset—all these comets destroy the fivefold [elements]; of this there is no doubt.
One should know that the fruit corresponds to the nature of the asterisms—whether they are mild, fixed, fierce, or swift; common or movable; and whether they are harsh or common and movable.
As instructed, according to their descriptions, and according to the assignment of their respective classes—
all these aforementioned great grahas shall slay [their targets].
Those who are born most terrible from Death, Time, the Sun, Brahmā, Tryambaka, Bhauma, Rāhu, and Agni;
The sons of Prajāpati, Dharma, Soma, and Varuṇa—
beginning with Pīta and the others— are to be known as the sons of the quarters, both mild and harsh.
The sons of Kaśyapa, Marīci, and the seer Uddālaka are to be known as having meager fruits; their origins are not from the nectar of immortality.
One should know that the heroic powers of those sons of Śukra and the other planets who have been proclaimed are indeed superior to those of their fathers.
Thus, this compendium of the planets of Nārada, Ātreya, Garga, and likewise of the teacher Uśanas, has been proclaimed in its entirety.
Possessing many hundreds of thousands and many hundreds of characteristics,
he who had obtained a boon from the gods spoke individually to all those present in the sky.
But when all this has arisen and fear has approached,
the king should perform a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) for the protection of his kingdom.
Then everything becomes peaceful, and there shall be happiness for all living beings;
the kings there, being joyful, protect the earth.

(Pariśiṣṭa 53: The Course of Rāhu) (AVParis 53.1.1) Om! Listen to the auspicious and inauspicious movements of this planet Rāhu, the son of the Asura, who approaches and seizes either the moon or the sun—the very embodiment of death.
But when Rāhu becomes desirous of forcibly seizing the moon or the sun during an eclipse, he then produces wondrous portents by which it is known that Rāhu is approaching.
Then the moon trembles when Rāhu becomes visible.
He is born pale or impotent, or his penis grows like that of a hare.
When the spokes within the city of the sun’s rays are marked by dark spots,
dogs bark loudly and terrifying winds blow.
If a meteor falls during both twilights, the milk of cows perishes;
likewise, on that day, the sap of milky trees also vanishes.
When glossy objects appear in the waters and crows form a circle,
and when the jackal howls upwards while Rāhu is visible;
The omens for an eclipse of the moon appear from the eighth day of the bright fortnight until the full moon; likewise, those for both [the moon and the sun] appear for the sun as well.
But when seized at sunrise, it destroys those people who know the Vedas;
it also destroys children with matted hair and those who wear saffron robes.
In the forenoon, it strikes down those who know the sacrifice who are in the prime of their youth;
all aquatic creatures and the lords of the serpents are also afflicted here.
Then, having reached the middle path, it kills Śūdras and thieves;
when surrounded, it kills the king; and as a "moon" (candra), it kills those who wander on foot.
A long-necked comet portends the destruction of women, the kṣatriyas, and the entire kingdom;
in this case, the people of Trigarta and those who bear the rod of punishment shall suffer.
When the sun rises eclipsed, or when it sets eclipsed,
one should predict terrible misfortune and lack of security throughout the three worlds.
For three years during the autumn, the grain that has grown does not ripen; in this time, the people subsist on roots and fruits rather than on summer crops.
It devours all luminaries and remains hidden for a long time;
it destroys prosperous kingdoms and the preeminent lord of the earth.
But if Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun at the end of the fortnight,
the earth becomes a river flowing with the mud of human blood, and Mādhava does not send rain.
If, having first grasped the sun, one then grasps the moon, that is the "moon-over-sun" (*somottara*); in that case there is destruction, for the deities do not prosper there.
The death of birds occurs when there is a breach; when it is wide open, there is the slaughter of the *rakṣasas*.
But when there is a breach involving a great serpent (*mahānāga*), the god does not send rain.
The color of Brāhmaṇas is white; that of Kṣatriyas is red;
the color of Vaiśyas is yellow; and that of Śūdras is said to be black.
Whichever caste the planet Rāhu moves through as he traverses the sun,
that planet afflicts the birth-constellation belonging to that caste.
When it is dark-colored, it pertains to the wind; when it is pale, it pertains to rain;
when it is yellowish, it produces a terrible outbreak of all kinds of grain.
When it is copper-colored, it serves as a weapon; when rough, it serves as a weapon for death. But when it has many forms, it produces a terrible fever in living beings.
Smoky-colored or fire-colored, this great planet causes fires among householders here in villages or cities.
When Rāhu, bordered by blue and red, moves against the sun,
the minister kills the king, or the king kills the minister, to his own destruction.
If Rāhu eclipses the lunar mansion of a king,
one should predict for him the loss of his kingdom, the destruction of his friends, and death.
When a planet, possessing a glossy color, radiant with flames, and full of luster, stands at a node,
or when it has risen quickly— declare that this indeed portends fear for all living beings.
If the moon moves clockwise, there is prosperity; if it moves counter-clockwise, there is conflict.
If its rays are divided, there is terrible fear; if it is eclipsed, there is the death of practitioners of mantra.
But when Rāhu, having displayed his forms, is no longer seen,
one should predict a terrible danger arising from the onset of weapons and famine.
But if the sun sets while the two [fires] have not yet been taken up, the twice-born shall not eat;
until they are seen again, he should perform recitations and oblations for them.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat; however, once they have been released, one may eat after bathing.
If they have not been released when they set, one should bathe and eat on the following day.
Then, after six [months], then again after six, or else after one and a half,
or after half a year, or after a month, there is then the seizure of the Sun.
Then for six [months], then for six, or again for three years;
the wise say that such is the course of Rāhu.
(Pariśiṣṭa 54: The Movements of the Comets) (AVParis 54.1.1) Oṃ! The venerable sage Bhārgava spoke first to the great seers:
"Listen to the movement of the comets and also their rising, just as it is."
I shall also declare the omens that have been taught for it; one who is skilled in the knowledge of portents should recognize all of them.
One of white appearance kills Brahmins; the red one kills Kṣatriyas; the yellow one kills Vaiśyas; and likewise, the black one kills Śūdras.
If a comet should afflict other [planets] and appear of a different color,
one should then predict the death of the king within six months.
A white [halo] would cause a confusion of weapons; a red one, however, brings fear from fire. A yellow one would cause fear of hunger, while a black one brings severe disease.
In whichever direction its head is located, that direction will suffer greatly;
if it is in the middle, there will be moderate suffering; but from the direction of its tail, victory comes.

The form of a spear leads to destruction and suffering; the form of a pestle likewise leads to suffering. That which is long and slender leads only to happiness, while that which is short and thick causes ruin.
The rising of comets is indeed remembered as being for the sake of destruction;
therefore, a wise person should perform a pacification ritual with the mantras of the Atharvans.
In the event of portents, one should cause the Mahāśānti rite to be performed with abundant sacrificial fees; it may be dedicated to Mahendra, to the Maruts, to the Waters, or even to the Viśvedevas.
When propitiated through various fire-oblations, recitations, and manifold kinds of gifts, those portents will undoubtedly subside into tranquility.
Wherever his head may be, rising from that place he should depart;
either leaving all his wealth behind, he shall be released from death, or he shall not.
Or, having given away the entire earth, a king attains peace.
(Pariśiṣṭa 55. The Characteristics of the Signs of the Seasons) (AVParis 55.1.1) Om! I shall proclaim the signs of the seasons in their proper order and according to rule;
how many sons each season may have, and what they should do when commanded from heaven.
All those months born of the earth, which were fashioned by the gods,
are bound by the rays of the sun and abide within the solar orb.
There are ten sons of Varuṇa, twenty sons of Sūrya,
twenty-four sons of Agni, and nine are remembered as the sons of Yama.
There are eighteen belonging to Kubera and twenty who are the sons of Vāyu;
this is the number of comets, remembered as one hundred and one.
One should designate those belonging to Varuṇa for the months of Śrāvaṇa and Prauṣṭhapada.
(When propitiated, those portents are pacified; of this there is no doubt—by means of various fire-oblations, recitations, and manifold kinds of gifts.
Thereafter, one should summon the clouds and make the earth full.
The rivers flow like madmen, impelled by the force of their waters.
Grain becomes cheap and calamities do not occur; this indeed is the characteristic that appears at the rising of the Vāruṇa asterisms.
In the months of Āśvayuja and Kārttika, one should point out the sons of the Sun;
now hear what their activities are like according to their characteristics.
Then the sun, with its blazing rays, burns up all foodstuffs;
likewise, cows die, and predatory beasts especially perish.
And there, among all those with fangs, a potent and terrible poison exists;
this is the characteristic that appears at the rising of the sons of the Sun.
In the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa, one should designate the sons of Agni;
now hear what their activities are according to their characteristics.
Fire burns the kingdoms and the green forests; then the regions, oppressed by fear, flee in every direction.
In some places security arises, and in some places fear arises;
for this is the characteristic sign when the sons of Agni rise.
Between the months of Māgha and Phālguna, one should point out the sons of Yama;
hear now what their actions and characteristics are like.
Soon there will be famine, accompanied by cries of "Alas! Alas! and a loss of consciousness;
there will be vomiting, fever, dysentery, exhaustion, and pain in the eyes.
At the rising of the sons of Yama, this is the characteristic sign that occurs.
Between the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha, one should point out those belonging to Kubera;
hear now what their activities are like, according to their characteristics.
With raised banners and altars, and with raised banners and archways,
the earth was then seen there to be filled with the smoke of sacrificial offerings.
Then Śakra, the lord of the earth, reached Triviṣṭapa;
thus do the wise consider it when the planet has entered the house of Kubera.
But at the rising of the Kuberas, this is the characteristic sign:
In the months of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha, one should designate the sons of Vāyu;
now hear what their activities are like according to their characteristics.
Great winds blow, signaling a great battle and great terror; the massive trees, gateways, and watchtowers are shattered.
Beautiful houses and the waters go to ruin;
this is the sign that occurs at the rising of the sons of Vāyu.
He who knows the seasonal course of these highly powerful planets beginning with Varuṇa,
as well as their results, possesses most excellent prosperity.
(Pariśiṣṭa 56: The Division of the Tortoise) (AVParis 56.1.1) Oṃ. One should designate the constellations Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and Saumya as the middle of the tortoise.
But for the remaining [nakṣatras], one should assign three [days] for each division of the asterisms.
Sāketa, Mithilā, Mekalālaya, Ahicchatra, Nāgapura, Kāśi, Pāriyātra, Kuru, and Pañcāla.
Then, having struck the Kosala country, Kauśāmbī, the banks [of the Ganges], Pāṭaliputra, and the region of Kaliṅgapura, he should strike at the very center of the earth's circle.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Māgadhas, Mahendraka, Gava, and Ambaṣṭhas.
If the head is struck, one should strike the eastern oceans as the corresponding parts.
The Khaśas, Bhadras, Samataṭas, Samavardhamānakas, Videhas, and Gāndhāras.
From Kosala, one should strike at Utośala, Veṇātaṭa, Sajjapura, Mādreyatā, and Tāmaliptā on the southeastern front.

The Āvantyas, Vidarbhas, Matsyas, Cakorabhīmaga, Rathas, Yavanas, Valayakāntis, Siṃhalas, Laṅkuṇas, Nāsikyakas, Karmayoṇīs, Mahi, Narmadā, and Bhṛgukacchas—these lie to the south-west; one should strike them down.
The Sahya mountain, Vaijayantī, Kuṇkuṇa, Nāsikya, Karmarāya, Mahī, Narmadā, and Bhṛgukaccha—these lie to the south-west; one should strike [the enemy] there.
He conquered Saurāṣṭra, Sindhu, Sauvīra, Mālava, and the Rāmarāṣṭra territories.
If the Ānartaga machine is struck at its tail, one should strike it again.
The Sārasvatas, Trigartas, Matsyas, Nāndīpālas, and Bāhlikas.
If [the omen] occurs in the northern part of the region extending from Mathurāpura, one should strike at those who have been struck.
One should strike Brahmāvarta, the Śatadru, the Himavat mountain, Mount Maināka, and likewise Kāśmīra on its northern side when it has been struck.
And likewise those from Nepāla, Kāmarūpa, Videha, and Udumbara.
Likewise, when [the enemy] has been struck in the northeast, one should strike the Avantis and the Kaikeyas.
(Viśākha, Kṛttikā, Puṣya, the two Pūrvaproṣṭhapadas,
as well as Bharaṇī, Maghā, and the two first Phalgunīs.)
If, at this time, the earth should tremble, or if there are thunderclaps and meteors, and if bodiless voices cry out and the deities shake;
If the sun is eclipsed here, or if the moon is obscured, one should recognize that as pertaining to Agni; and one should predict famine in such a case.
Likewise, cows yield little milk, and disease arises from fire;
at that time, cities, regions, and villages are indeed afflicted by fire.
Then those men who practice fire-rites and those who dwell by fire are afflicted;
likewise, fever born of bile and asthma afflict living beings at that time.
Furthermore, there will be terrible eye diseases, especially among men;
the rivers here will dry up, and the earth will not be rich in crops.
At that time, the earth suffers and the god does not send rain;
the trees are overspread with blue and red [fungi] and likewise become fruitless.
Famine, pestilence, disease, and likewise fear of foreign armies—
by these signs, the fiery [element] is to be known as having a flickering appearance.
Hasta, the two Aśvins, and Citrā are the asterism whose deity is Aryaman;
Mṛgaśiras is that of Brahmā, and Svāti is remembered as the Vāyavya maṇḍala.
If here the earth should tremble, or there be thunderclaps and meteors, and bodiless voices cry out, and the deities shake;
If the sun is eclipsed here, or if the moon is obscured,
one should recognize that as pertaining to Vāyu, and one should indicate that there will be insecurity.
Then a terrible rain of dust fell, and no ghee was to be found in milk; palaces, gateways, and other structures collapsed onto the surface of the earth.
The Madrakas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Kāmbojas, the Bālhikas,
and the Gandhāras shall likewise perish along with these [others].
Elephants, horses, camels, wolves, mongooses,
and servants— all these, as well as those who subsist by the use of weapons, are afflicted by disease.
In the beginning, the most excellent things perish among the multitudes, even those endowed with virtues;
and delightful houses crumble away on all sides.
There, exhaustion is intense and the brandishing of weapons occurs on all sides;
by these characteristics, the Vāyavya [weapon] is to be recognized by its flickering appearance.
Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, as well as Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Revatī, and that which has the Sun as its deity (Puṣya).
If, at this time, the earth should tremble, or there should be thunderclaps and meteors,
or bodiless voices should roar, and the deities should shake;
If the sun is eclipsed here, or if the moon is obscured,
one should recognize that as pertaining to Varuṇa, and one should predict abundant food in this case.
Likewise, the cows yield much milk, and the elephants bear fruit; all subjects are free from affliction, the forest regions abound in cattle, and the water is rich in milk.
All those who subsist on water attain supreme prosperity;
and here, beings moving through the air are seen on all sides, possessing a glossy complexion.
Kings lay down their weapons, and the Brahmanical and Kṣatriya orders flourish;
by these signs, however, the Varuṇa comet, appearing unsteady, is to be recognized.
Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, and the two Punarvasūs,
as well as Rohiṇī and the two Āṣāḍhās, are remembered as the Maṇḍala of Mahendra.
If here the earth shakes, or if there are thunderclaps and meteors, and if bodiless voices roar and the deities tremble;
If the sun is eclipsed here, or if the moon is obscured, one should recognize that as belonging to Mahendra; and one should predict great security in this case.
Cows together with their calves, women accompanied by their sons,
insects, predatory beasts, and whatever other sweat-born creatures there may be, all perish.
Brāhmaṇas were always devoted to the study of the Vedas and sacrifices;
Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas were intent on their own duties; and Śūdras were performers of service.
One hundred and twenty [stanzas] belong to Agni; ninety move for Vāyu;
eighty move for Indra; and seventy move for Varuṇa.
An earthquake of the Āgneya type ripens within two months;
that of the Vāruṇa type bears fruit immediately; and that of the Vāyavya type occurs after three months.
One should know that the fruit of the Māhendra sacrifice lasts for a month and likewise for half a month.

(Pariśiṣṭa 58: The Characteristics of the Burning of the Quarters) (AVParis 58.1.1) Om! Henceforth, learn of the burning of the quarters as they are being described—how the directions burn and what the fruit of their burning is.
Indra, Agni, and the Maruts themselves set the ten directions ablaze,
impelled by the Law of Destiny for the sake of the auspicious and inauspicious fate of the worlds.
When the flame of fire is seen after the sun has set, one should know that it is a conflagration of the quarters, according to the word of Bhārgava.
Arising from various passions and resulting in various kinds of fruits,
they are covered as if by dust, having resorted to the application of burning the quarters.
All the directions are burning for the sake of misfortune and its fruit,
if there is a burning even without a visible flame, provided the appearances are oily.
Those [omens] characterized by darkness, smoke, and dust, those surrounded by blazing birds and beasts,
and all those possessing blazing characteristics— even if they are real— are bringers of misfortune.
Likewise, those that are like gold, filaments, or lightning, as well as those that are auspicious,
rough, black, madder-red, or like the bandhujīvaka flower;
Burns that are white, red, yellow, and black in color are proclaimed to portend the destruction of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, respectively.
Red [omens] cause fear of weapons; yellow ones provoke diseases;
likewise, those with the color of fire cause great danger from fire and weapons.
