Those who are yellowish-brown, rough, and dark, or those who resemble the color of Varuṇa—
all these provoke hunger, disease, death, weapons, fire, and anger.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, however, there will be heavy rain and the flight of armies;
the twilight will be intensely luminous, or it will bring about the appearance of planets.
When the quarters are scorched, those who have devotion to specific regions suffer according to their respective directions,
as do those who hold authority therein and are indicated by the knowledge of omens.

When this great pacification (*mahāśānti*) is performed according to the prescribed rite and accompanied by ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), it shall quell all the terrible calamities born of conflagrations in every direction.
(Pariśiṣṭa 58b. Characteristics of Meteors) (AVParis 58b.1.1) Om! For meteors and the like have already been described, as well as those thunderclaps mentioned previously;
now I shall explain their specific characteristics individually.
Of the limbs belonging to the intermediate space, whichever limb is most highly honored—
that glorious limb characterized by the meteor (ulkā) shall be described in its entirety.
Those bodies which may be invincible due to firm faculties,
which are patient, pure, and devoted to truth and vows;
These shine forth, making the sky free from darkness with their radiance;
because they blaze here on all sides, the sky is difficult to behold.

O Bhārgava, when those [planets] have fallen further from the vault of the sky due to the exhaustion of their merit, they descend here upon the earth with their characteristic marks intact. Wherever they are observed as they fall there, [they leave behind signs].
In each and every such place, various kinds of fear arise among the people.
Having understood their relative strength and weakness through their form, color, radiance, moisture, dimensions, and configuration, their virtues and defects shall be explained.
The stars, the constellations, as well as meteors, lightning, and thunderbolts—
these are the fivefold conceptualizations, each succeeding one possessing greater power than the last.
Then, with a great, resonant, and far-reaching sound,
the long-eyed lady descended from the surface of the sky like a great wheel.
Blazing thunderbolts fall upon humans, deer, elephants, horses, trees, stones, paths, and houses, shattering the surface of the earth.
Suddenly, among those who had just appeared, there arose a sound that followed intensely after them, utterly shattering their composure and causing extreme agitation.
Spreading forth masses of flames and by nature appearing as suffering,
lightning bolts fall swiftly upon living beings and upon heaps of forest trees.
A meteor with a sharp point, a large head, and which increases as it falls—such is the *pauruṣī* by nature; learn now its various varieties.
Like a slender woman, it may be blazing, with a crest emitting sparks of charcoal,
illuminating the sky as if with golden armor.
By a great, clinging cloud that is yellow or pale, or smoky and reddish-brown, and which is dispersing;
Some resemble bamboo thickets, and some are like Indra’s banner;
some have the appearance of a rainbow, and some are arranged in circular formations.
They appear like parasols, they fall like wheels,
they stand like staffs, and they run like serpents.
Like peacocks moving through the sky with their plumage spread out,
one woman moves across the surface of the earth with her tail held high.
Others scatter sparks of light and run about like balls.
Likewise, followed by dancing spirits, jackals, and boars,
they fall upon the surface of the earth, both making sounds and remaining silent.
I shall now declare the individual results of these meteors,
which are indeed connected by a thread as if being carried along by the wind.
One is seen falling, another wanders in the sky;
surrounded by hosts of meteors, one descends to the surface of the earth.
But their common fruit shall now be stated in brief:
[they become] boars, ghosts, tigers, lions, cats, and wild boars.
A meteor that brings fear is similar [to those previously mentioned], as is one resembling a low-caste serpent;
likewise, those shaped like a trident, a spear-head, a javelin, a double-edged sword, a mallet, a blade, or an axe.
Those resembling rain, smoke, trees, and so forth are censured;
those resembling a lotus, a conch, the moon, a vajra, a serpent, a fish, or a banner are auspicious.
They have the appearance of the śrīvṛkṣa, the svastika, the whirlpool, the swan, the elephant, and glowing embers; they are crooked and yet swift-moving.
Without the space for a tail— whether it be short or excessively thin—
the ten intervals of the bow and the tail itself are clearly visible.
A transformation of a meteor is to be understood as that which is designated by the term *dhiṣṇya*;
however, that which is of white color or has a delicate form, [is of another kind].
That which resembles a lotus fiber or appears like a streak of smoke is called a transformation of a meteor; it is known by the name "star" (tārakā).
Thus, these five kinds have been proclaimed by Śaunaka as the characteristics of those of meritorious deeds who fall while descending from heaven.
If these [meteors] fall upon the head of Indra, there will be fear for the king;
if they fall upon the images of the deities, there will be danger for the king and the kingdom.
If there is agitation at the city gate, there will be a destruction of people; if at the threshold of Indra (*indrakīla*), there will be a loss of life;
and if there is damage to the temples of Brahmā, there will be calamity for the Brahmins.
When there is damage to the trees of a shrine (*caitya-vṛkṣa*), there is great danger for those who have been honored;
at the gate, one should know it indicates the exhaustion of life, while in the house, it portends danger for the master.
One should know that danger for cattle-owners lies in the cow-pens, for farmers in the threshing floors, for kings in their own houses, and for those devoted to them in their [respective] dwellings.
When there is an affliction caused by the seizing of hopes, for the ascetics residing in that region,
[the omen] facing downward portends the death of the king, while one facing upward portends the death of Brahmins.
A [line] moving horizontally portends the death of the king’s wife; one resembling a thorn-bush portends the ruin of a merchant;
one resembling a bamboo clump portends the destruction of the kingdom; and one resembling Indra’s banner portends the death of the king.
An elephant resembling Indra’s bow [is assigned] to the Indra [direction]; a city arranged in a circle to the [Vaiśravaṇa] direction;
ministers are situated in the form of a wheel; and the domestic priest has the shape of a parasol.
A meteor followed by peacock feathers portends the exhaustion of water;
a meteor that dissolves in the sky drinks up the clouds.
If those [stars] that emit sparks run about in every direction and move like balls,
there will be danger to the kingdom.
Those meteors that fall from the vault of heaven surrounded by clusters of firebrands,
following after one another, bring fear to the king and the kingdom.
Those [omens] that follow the path of hungry ghosts, those that follow boars, and those that have the form of carrion-eating fire or venomous serpents— these cause the destruction of people.

When there are shouts, slapping sounds, and cries, accompanied by the resonance of singing and musical instruments during the falling of meteors, these should be understood as bringing fear to the king and the kingdom.
When the winds of twilight are harsh and accompanied by sounds, moving contrary to the natural direction, or when they reach the middle of the sky, or when they cause [clouds] to move back and forth;
A white meteor destroys by its head; one with the luster of blood, by its middle;
a yellow one, by its two sides; and a black meteor, when joined with a tail, kills.
White [light] would slay the gods and kings; blood-red light, the Kṣatriyas;
yellow, for the destruction of Vaiśyas; and that which is other than white would slay the Śūdras.
Falling, they are not perceived; their action is revealed:
wherever there are thunderbolts upon the earth, there the onset of fear does not exist.
Other lightning flashes fall accompanied by stars, moving against the wind; they are undesirable, whereas those occurring otherwise are desirable.
The stars and lunar mansions should be understood as yielding their results slowly after a long time;
yet, for the most part, even their falling portends misfortune.
Whichever way the portents fall excessively, in that very direction the king should march; that is called the divine path.
Having performed the great pacification regarding omens, and especially regarding a falling meteor,
one attains success and is liberated from the fault of the meteor.
(Pariśiṣṭa 59: The Characteristics of Lightning) (AVParis 59.1.1) Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of lightning,
as well as the variations in its color and form, and the auspicious and inauspicious regions [it portends].
Always pure, one should await the fourth and fifth [lunar days];
for during the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the appearance of lightning is invariably a wondrous omen.
A person [can know] excessive rain, drought, as well as existence and non-existence,
and the ripening of all crops by observing lightning.
If lightning flashes in the eastern quarter and the wind blows from the northeast,
one should predict abundance of food, security, health, and freedom from calamity.
If both [planets] should be in the southeast, there will be danger from weapons, fire, and rain;
in the south, there will be poison, enemies, as well as the fear of disease and death.
The youngest [year] is equal to the Nairṛta year, characterized by much distress;
the middle one brings abundance of crops, while the Vāruṇa year is filled with disease.
In the northwestern direction, there will be flies, stinging insects, and mosquitoes;
in the northern direction, one should know there is danger from excessive water, while in the northeastern direction, there will be abundant prosperity.
In the northeast, there will be freedom from calamity and an abundant, delightful harvest of grain;
however, when the winds blow in a contrary direction, one should predict a great abundance of calamities.
One should predict the absence of calamity when the winds blow favorably;
however, if the auspicious river flows in an unfavorable direction, it portends what is undesirable.
If there should be a great drought, it results in a bountiful harvest;
if it rains poorly at first but beautifully afterwards, it flows auspiciously.
In that case, they say there will indeed be good rain, yet the crops do not flourish;
however, when all [the rivers] flow turbid, one should predict a calamitous rain.
When there is frequent lightning, there will be danger from abundant water;
when they display a beautiful [lightning] accompanied by lightning and thunder, [it is auspicious].
The clouds recognize that as a good rain for the eastern and northern directions,
if the water-bearing clouds are seen in the east during the early rains.
If they turn clockwise and are auspicious, one should predict a good rain;
however, if they belong to the fire element, there will be excessive rain and the crops will perish.
One should predict irregular rain, disease, and death among the Yāmyas;
among the Nairṛtas, there will be much distress, yet it shall yield roots and fruits in abundance.
One should predict a mediocre harvest from rainfalls associated with the western quarter;
where Indra pours down rain in the northwestern quarter, there shall be the first [best] rainfall.
In that case, there will be excessive rain; one should sow only a small amount of seed.
However, if the clouds were filled with color and moisture during the previous rains, [the harvest will be good].
Where gentle clouds rain down, there all the water-bearing clouds shall rain.
Thus, this clear characteristic of lightning observed during the previous rains has been fully proclaimed exactly as it was understood from the sounds of the rain.

Even in auspicious matters, the Great Peace (mahāśānti) is prescribed for the sake of removing obstacles; in inauspicious matters, it is for the sake of prosperity. Therefore, the rite of pacification (śāntika) applies to all.
(Pariśiṣṭa 60: The Characteristics of Thunderbolts) (AVParis 60.1.1) There are eight types of thunderbolts; among them, Indra is praised.
One should indicate that through the eastern [thunderbolt] there will be rain, crops, and the prosperity of the king.
In the northeast, there will be abundance; likewise, in the north, there will be gain of land.
In the southwest, however, there will be fear of thieves and also affliction for horses.
In the west, there is danger for the king, and those born of the water are afflicted;
in the southwest, there is great danger for crops, cattle, women, and the various assemblies.
If it is in the south, there will be oppression by a king; one should also predict a shortening of life.
If it should be in the southeast, one should know that there is danger from Ānarta.
The sound of a thunderclap extends for a league;
one should know that fear exists everywhere wherever it penetrates.
In times of fear, one should perform the Raudrī or the Abhayā mudrā, which bestows fearlessness;
by means of these, portents are pacified and ultimate happiness shall prevail.
(Pariśiṣṭa 61: The Characteristics of Halos) Om. Now, therefore, the characteristics of halos shall be explained, just as Vṛddhagarga formerly spoke them to me, O observer of noble vows.
By the command of the Self-born, the stainless one brings about transformation.
White, dark-grey, tawny, and black—these are the established colors;
these four are declared to be manifest in the clouds, glossy and highly auspicious.
O Nārada, when these four halos are glossy,
one should predict rain during twilight if they possess these colors.
When clouds resemble gold, blue collyrium, ariṣṭa fruit, lightning, or a serpent, and when they have a luster equal to molten silver— in all three of these cases, the cloud rains.
When the twilight is submerged [in darkness], this portends good rain;
however, those clouds which are the opposite of these bring the fear of drought.
Clouds shaped like boars, crocodiles, camels, wolves, herons, as well as donkeys and rabbits, portend danger during the twilight.
They were the color of molten gold, and there was a vast destruction of people;
they stood amidst dogs, donkeys, jackals, vultures, and crows, making a great noise.
Those facing forward declare that a battle will occur during the morning and evening twilights,
wherein the warriors mounted on horses and elephants shall fight like men.
In the clouds are seen those forms resembling nooses and goads,
as well as those appearing like elephants, striking one another.
When kings, engaged in battle and causing uncertainty, are being devoured by flesh-eaters— vultures, jackals, and crows— they fight on with resolve.
When clouds resembling peacocks, watchtowers, lotuses, the moon, or blue kāśa flowers are seen during the twilights, a heavy rain is imminent.
Accompanied by lightning and a rainbow, and accompanied by thunder, clouds resembling crests of fire are seen during the twilights; a heavy rain is imminent.
Seeing a rainbow that is dark-necked, bordered by blue and red,
accompanied by lightning, and discolored, one should know it to be a bringer of rain.
If the sun should ever reach its rising or setting while the iron bar is three-colored, or while there are three-colored clouds;
A great danger has arisen for those of royal lineage upon the earth;
one should know it will bring about the destruction of the world if the god does not send rain.
If the sun were to rise in the form of a fish through a semblance of likeness,
that Āditya with his radiant rays would utterly consume the earth.
Having seen this great form when the sun has risen, the light becomes clearly manifest; this is the unmistakable sign of immediate rain.
Driven by their own momentum, the clouds— driven by the force of the wind— cover one another, roar, and counter-roar against each other.
In that fourfold battle of clouds moving through the sky, three phenomena arise; listen as I describe them to you.
When the clouds are thundering, the elephant trumpets in response;
one should direct him toward that quarter where the sound of the thunder is perceived.
When clouds take on various forms, with weapons resembling Indra’s bolt,
and when the thundering of crashing lightning occurs in whichever direction those cloud-elephants appear;
When armies clash and arise with mutual intent to slay one another,
the king who directs his army toward that direction conquers that direction.
In seizing, covering, roaring, and counter-roaring,
this very rule is to be understood, as is every determination.
It is impossible to describe that extent in its entirety,
like the jewels produced from the clouds within the ocean.
The twilight is said to extend for one *yojana*, while thunder extends for two *yojanas*.
A halo (*parigha*) spans five *yojanas*, and a secondary sun (*pratyāditya*) spans three *yojanas*.
There are six types of thunderclaps, as well as lightning; halos are twice that number [twelve];
there is also a conflagration extending for a *yojana*, and meteors possess immeasurable power.
The ten concluding rites are completed according to their measure;
however, the intermediate limbs should be understood in brief.
(Pariśiṣ�ṭa 62: Characteristics of Earthquakes) (AVParis 62.1.1) Oṃ. The wise Garga declared that there are four types of earthquakes:
fire, wind, water, and the fourth is said to be Indra.
We shall explain their forms and modifications in due order,
knowing which a wise and steadfast person may point out the various results.
If the earth should tremble within seven days,
there will be battles among kings that bring about the fear of death.
There will be conflict among kings and deaths will occur;
the sun and the moon will appear copper-colored, and deer and birds will turn yellow.
And may all directions possess a radiance equal to the rising sun;
one should know that this, endowed with such characteristics, is shaken by fire.
Regarding this, there is an instruction according to the words of Śaunaka:
"Gold, fine gold, and whatever else is found in the house."
Having abandoned all this, one must undertake the collection of grain;
for fire may consume the kingdoms, as well as the villages and cities. Furthermore, battles take place here, with flesh and blood for their mire.
Kings fall into conflict with one another, and the god does not send rain here.
Thus, for those who tremble, this shaking of the fire is censured.
"If the earth should tremble," so it is said.
An exceedingly fierce, abundant, and terrible wind arises,
dragging along gravel both in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should know that this [place], endowed with these characteristics, is shaken by the wind;
one should provide protection against weapons by means of a rampart and likewise a moat.
At that time, one should not travel to the village; rather, having recognized oneself, one should protect it, for here battles increase, with mud made of flesh and blood.
Kings indeed come into conflict and deaths occur;
the earth drinks the blood of thousands of princes.
For a month or for twenty nights, the god does not rain there;
after two months have passed, there shall be abundant water.
In this case, it corrupts what has been bitten, and wounds that have healed become aggravated;
among these very tremors, however, that which is shaken by wind is considered censurable.
When the earth trembled.
Great clouds, raining down, approach from all sides;
and crocodiles, porpoises, tortoises, and sea-monsters appear.
When clouds shaped like mountains are seen swallowing the moon and the sun,
one should know that this phenomenon, possessing such characteristics, is caused by the agitation of water.
One may sow seed upon mountains, as well as in saline or arid soil;
there the seed sown prospers, whereas elsewhere on the earth it perishes.
I have brought forth flowers, roots, and fruits;
and there, aquatic beings also attain growth.
One should predict security, abundance of food, freedom from disease, and timely rain in this place.
When the earth trembled.
O King, a deep-thundering cloud approaches,
glossy like collyrium and resembling a truly massive mountain.
Terrifying all the directions, it rains swiftly;
moreover, there shall be Indra’s bow, lightning, and thunder.
There shall be good rain, security, health, abundance of food, and supreme joys;
indeed, the subjects, being gladdened, shall rejoice in the bliss arising from sacrifice.
Among these earthquakes, the shaking caused by Indra is indeed praiseworthy;
one should discern all things, both auspicious and inauspicious, through these characteristics.
During these three types of earthquakes, Atharvan, who is skilled in the scriptures,
should perform the Māhendrī or the Amṛtā pacification rite, accompanied by sacrificial fees.
During the Indra-kampa, however, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform oblations according to rule with the mantras dedicated to Indra;
thereafter, for the sake of the primary purpose of the ploughing, he should likewise offer oblations and recite prayers.

(Pariśiṣṭa 63: Characteristics of Portents of the Lunar Mansions and Planets) (AVParis 63.1.1) Om! Now I shall further declare the various kinds of halos surrounding the lunar mansions and planets, which result in manifold outcomes.
He [created] those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, and Kubera—red, pale-white, and dark-blue;
and those belonging to Pāṇḍu, Babhru, Pīta, Anīla, Anala, and Yama—pale-yellow and tawny-brown.
O Bhārgava, he spoke of the halos belonging to Prajāpati, to Rudra, and also to Nirṛti— those that are variegated like a lion, spotted, or pigeon-colored.
These nine colors of the planetary orbs are the sources of their deities;
they attain multiplicity through the mutual interdependence of their qualities.
Having taken up subtle particles of cloud-dust and having combined them with color,
Mātali, by the command of Pitāmaha, fashioned the chariot into a circular form.
He obstructs the luminaries for the sake of the auspicious and inauspicious destinies of the worlds;
having understood his form and quality, the excellence or defect of that [luminosity] is proclaimed.

When the nature of the constellations and stars, as well as that of the surrounding region, becomes settled and then departs, it is traditionally known as a *pariveṣa* (halo or atmospheric phenomenon).
When the sun’s rays are held firm, when the gentle orb is clear, and when it is glossy, uniform in color, full-bodied, and its characteristic marks are manifest;
When the two eyes are red, when the razor has descended, when there are rays and a yellow halo,
from the onset of dusk until midday, and until the disappearance of the stars.
When there is thunder accompanied by a mass of clouds and a halo appears,
one should know that even outside the rainy season, a great danger has arrived.
When the orb [of the sky] is naturally overcome by black mist and darkness,
when it is strewn with atmospheric portents and filled with inauspicious sparks;
In a rugged place free from moisture, where the turbid clouds have been dispersed,
one frequently attains a vision during the three junctions of time.
Or when two or three constellations have risen, or even when half a constellation has appeared;
or when wild beasts and birds are gazing on with blazing eyes and making sounds.
One should recognize that when a halo appears around kings and others,
there will be terrible danger from thieves, weapons, fire, and death within seven nights.
With a form variegated by smoke, madder-red, crimson, yellow, and black,
it appears on one side as a turbid orb in its appearance.
There, completely enveloped by a fine net,
it repeatedly undergoes both dissolution and reformation.
That halo should also be known as being composed of wind; with the sun appearing dim and faint, it yields little fruit, yet it increases the occurrence of wind and rain.
Now, if wind and rain do not cease for three nights,
the appearance of water, fire, and thieves will arise.
If a meteor appears within the halo during the double-halo phenomenon,
there will be danger from the commander-in-chief with two [halos], and danger from the crown prince with three.
When three or more circles are maintained, there will be a siege of the city;
for therein the stars, planets, and moon are obstructed.
After three days, one predicts rain; after a month, one should speak of a conflict, as well as the flight of generals, princes, and the army.
When there is a halo around the red-bodied planet [Mars], and when there are portents involving weapons and fire,
stationary objects, farmers, and minor grains are likewise afflicted.
When Saturn is eclipsed, it produces wind and rain;
indeed, Rāhu certainly afflicts the kingdom as well as the embryos.
When the moon is eclipsed, it brings forth diseases;
there is also terrible fear of hunger, asthma, fire, the king, and likewise death.
When the banner of Ketu and that of Śikhin are both eclipsed in the sky,
they together portend a battle between two planets that have been eclipsed.
In three [of these], one should recognize the fear of hunger as well as the withholding of rain;
by four, the king perishes along with his ministers and his domestic priest.

One should know that it is like the end of a cosmic age when the five classes of birds have descended; one should slay the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras on the first lunar day and the subsequent days.
From the fifth [day] onwards, during these three [periods], he destroys villages, cities, and the treasury;
on the eighth day, he destroys the crown princes along with the commanders of the army.
On the ninth, the tenth, and the eleventh days, there will be trouble for kings;
on the thirteenth day there will be an upheaval of the army, and on the twelfth day the city will be besieged.
On the fourteenth or fifteenth day, the king’s wife,
the domestic priest, the minister, and the king himself shall slay one another.
One should recognize a siege of the city when Jupiter is surrounded;
then ministers, scribes, and even immovable things are obstructed.
One should also recognize that there will be rain when the planet Mercury is eclipsed;
furthermore, travelers, the Kṣatriyas, and the royal faction shall suffer.
The son of Bhṛgu, when served [as an omen], makes the price of grain dear;
likewise do halos around the stars and planets, and exclusively those of the lunar mansions.
One should predict the rising of a great planet or the death of the king when [the halo] is red,
yellow, black, copper-colored, dark, green, or dawn-red.
One should know that there will be fear for the social classes from hunger, weapons, disease, rain, fire, death, crops, wind, and water, according to the specific class that is affected.
The pigeon-colored and the variegated bring fear from animal births;
those as white as a peacock’s throat, a conch shell, the moon, a pearl, or cow’s milk are auspicious.
Clouds resembling the scum of madhūka oil, dark as dūrvā grass, and free from the appearance of ill omens— resembling oil or myrobalan— are indicative of rain.
Those resembling smooth, pure water, or appearing like mirrors, when worshipped, bring good fortune;
whereas those that are brown, rough, harsh, resembling turmeric or dawn-red,
fragmented, blood-red, short, or discolored, do not bring auspicious results.
One should recognize the halos of those who are traveling, those who are stationary, and likewise those who move by crying out, according to their outer, inner, and middle positions.
One should know that defeat belongs to those whose portion is intensely red, dark, turbid, or lusterless; whereas victory indeed belongs to one whose portion is glossy and white.
By whichever cloud-color each respective portion is colored, one should know that to be its fruit; this has been proclaimed regarding prosperity and other such matters.
"These openings are said to be great and pure;
through these gates a king may travel upon paths free from thorns."
The birth of all beings is for the purpose of [experiencing] the effects of the rising of the planets through the outpourings of the clouds of time; the remainder is characterized by portents.
Raudrī, accompanied by Dakṣiṇā, is proclaimed as the pacification for portents;
however, in the case of a combination [of such events], it should be understood that Vaiśvadevī and likewise Abhayā are to be employed.
Having personally mastered the Atharva-utpātahṛdaya while remaining free from affliction,
one should employ this great pacification which destroys all defilements.
(Pariśiṣṭa 64. Signs of Portents) (AVParis 64.1.1) Oṃ! Those which Aṅgiras proclaimed in the past, and those which the seer Vedaśarman taught—I shall now fully declare those portents of three kinds.
Wherever a transformation of the natural state arises,
one should recognize that in every such case it is characterized by a portentous omen.
The terrestrial, the atmospheric, and the celestial omens of portents—
just as they have been described in the case of disturbances among the constellations, so too are they [to be understood] according to the rule.
Among those hosts of portents, listen as they describe the thunderclaps arising from the subterranean realm and the earthquakes.
Those belonging to Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu cause the earth to tremble day and night like a wheel, for the sake of indicating the auspicious or inauspicious fate of the worlds.
I shall describe the characteristics and the results of those tremors,
as they were proclaimed by the renowned Uśanas to the inquiring Nārada.

If an earthquake occurs within seven days of its onset and is of the nature of Vajradhara, the sky will be filled with thunderous sounds and dense clouds shaped like svastikas extending to the very horizon.
With clouds resembling Indra’s bow as weapons, trembling with flashes of lightning like lattice windows, shaped like nooses, fish, and cities, and terrifying as mountains and serpents;
They frequent the very edge of the sky, where the lightning flashes like their own sun;
at the extremity they are well-sheltered, and there the winds are both cool and warm.
With streams flowing like sprouts, possessing the luster of blue lotus petals and resonating with sound, Varuṇa himself would cover the sky and cause it to tremble.
With the falling of stars, the burning of the quarters, and the crashing of thundering meteors, the sky—its paths set ablaze—seemed as if it were crying out "Alas! Alas! in distress.
Or if, within seven days, fire erupts from the earth,
that will be a fiery earthquake, bringing fear to the king and the kingdom.
The sun in the sky was as if devoid of light, yet it was not truly without brilliance;
the quarters of the horizon did not shine, like women overcome by sorrow.
When the winds blow with a roar, harsh, dragging along gravel,
and when an earthquake occurs within seven days that brings extreme terror, it is caused by the Maruts.
Earthquakes occurring in the directions of Indra and Varuṇa should be understood as bestowing abundance and security;
earthquakes born of the regions of Vāyu and Agni bring fear to the king and the kingdom.
In whichever direction the earth cries out with a distorted sound,
in that very direction there shall be fear together with those in authority.
Thunderclaps and earthquakes have been described together with their various types;
hereafter, I shall explain the remaining characteristics of portents.
To the east, south, west, and north, as well as in the city of the Gandharvas,
it appears in the directions with red, yellow, and black colors.
The misfortune or even the death of the king, the commander-in-chief, the crown prince, and the royal priest should be understood in their respective order.
Fear from Varuṇa and others should be understood according to the specific colors [of the quarters];
and when the intermediate directions are discolored, suffering for those who are discolored should be known.

When [the moon] is constantly visible, it brings fear to the king and his kingdom; furthermore, distress for those holding official appointments should be understood according to the prescribed rules.
(1) Engaging in sexual intercourse with those of incompatible species, (2) giving birth to other beings, and (3) the appearance of extra hands, feet, eyes, or heads.
Anointing with oil during sexual union, movement that is devoid of purpose,
and the mutual association of beings who are incompatible;
The movement of the immovable and the lack of movement in the moving; the speaking of that which is unspeakable and the speech of that which is soundless.
The sight of fire without a flame, the reversal of cold and heat,
the floating of iron and other metals in water, and the non-flowing of waters upon water;
The appearance of flowers out of season, the fivefold and fourfold qualities of the crops,
the yoking of plows, and the activities of the lights [are described].
The trees and springs were filled with various excellent deities;
the quarters of the sky were shrouded in the darkness of smoke, and the beasts and birds were ablaze.
The sky is shrouded by *rajas* and *tamas*, the moon and sun are obscured,
and there is a blazing glow of redness upon the garments, flesh, and waters.
Suddenly, there was the cracking or even the flaming of gate-towers, battlements, mountains, palaces, and houses, as well as earthquakes and the emission of smoke.
Violent winds blow incessantly, dragging along gravel; and circles of clouds, joined together, appear blue, red, and yellow.

When the flagstaffs, Indra-piles, and sacrificial stakes, along with dry shrines and the like, as well as the trunks, branches, and sprouts of trees, are cut or broken; [in such cases, the following applies].
And the sounds of songs, mṛdaṅga drums, and musical instruments,
accompanied by gandharvas, shall arise in the path of the sky.
Seeing shadows where there are no objects, hearing cries during the dead of night, and the inverted movement of creatures that roam by day and by night.
Rain without clouds, thunder without clouds, and the falling of flaming meteors during the day that produce sound but lack smoke; these are portents.
Furthermore, the appearance of the moon or the sun within dust, stones, and the like,
as well as frequent halos surrounding the sun and the moon that are turbid, [portend misfortune].
Peacocks, cuckoos, and other such creatures experience intoxication out of season;
likewise, there is the departure of forest deities and mountain deities.
The settling of forest-dwelling beings in cities and villages,
the arising of things that have not yet come to be, and the destruction of those already arisen.
If this portent born of calamity arises in the territory of a king,
that territory shall perish and the king along with it shall be destroyed.
Furthermore, whatever region the heretics, the twice-born, and the gods abandon,
or toward which they feel aversion, that region also perishes.
The dancing of granaries, the shaking of heaps of grain,
the creeping of mortars, and the entering of pestles.
The movements of royal ladles and likewise of earthenware vessels,
as well as the burning of cold objects— these sounds are indeed the subsequent [omens].
The eating of dung by wretched beasts and birds,
and the loud braying of domestic animals with dejected bodies;
The eating of sand, charcoal, or grain, as well as rains,
and the behavior of cranes and crows at the city gate [are signs of misfortune].
There shall be mutual devouring among cats, fish, marrow-eaters, and creatures known as "small"; and the nights shall all be of equal duration.
In whatever region aversion to meat, crops, and food, as well as the cessation of ritual activities, is observed, one should predict the danger of famine there.
The gliding of weapons and flames, the movement and filling of pillars,
and the appearance of umbrellas, garments, and banners upon anthills.
A halo around the sun, such as from clouds or a rainbow, as well as halos around the sun and moon;
a crimson color like lac, and the discoloration of all [the planets].
Showers of skin, flesh, blood, bones, fat, marrow, and bone-marrow fall upon him; and cloudless showers [fall] with a luster like that of silver and blood.
There shall be striking down, shaking, destruction, lightning, and the falling of thunderbolts;
and there shall be the avoidance of the gods and others stepping upon one's head.
The procreation of women and men, the growth of grass and other plants,
and the speech of non-human beings— all these are like those of humans.
In whatever region there occurs the smell of fat and blood from elephants, deities, and horses, in that place there will be great fear of weapons and conflict.
The flowing of blood and tears, the acts of laughing and staring,
dancing, instrumental music, singing, and speech accompanied by cries of lamentation.
There was the trembling of the deities as well as their blazing, the drying up and transformation of the waters, and their acting like human beings.
The splitting and quivering of the king, as well as deformities and eruptions on the earth; earthquakes and laughter, as well as weeping and shrieking.
The pedestal, the insignia, the parasol, the sword, the arrow, the stake, and the water-pot;
the blue-tipped [hand] and the red-palmed [hand]; the rising sun and the moon.
There are various manifestations such as the moon, the sun, and meteors, as well as two suns and two moons;
rivers flow against their currents, and arrows travel backward.
The breaking of teeth occurs for men, elephants, and horses; likewise, the breaking of parasols occurs for men, elephants, and horses, accompanied by the breaking of tortoises.
The digestion of meat and oil, the leaking of oil from a shrine,
the breaking of Indra’s banners and flags, and the howling of carnivorous beasts.
A battle between a cat and an owl took place near the king’s palace;
the sky was covered with dust, or else with pollen and darkness.
The sky has the radiance of red fire, and birds and deer are ablaze;
moreover, whirlwinds at the twilights move counter-clockwise with flickering flashes.
Circles and assemblies of beasts and birds were seen on all sides;
the quarters of the sky were everywhere agitated by flesh-eating predators howling aloud.

If rain occurs after three nights, when the moon and sun have disappeared during the day, and if it is seen out of season accompanied by terrible thundering and long-lasting [clouds], [it portends disaster].
Vajra and the others, the sons of Rāhu, as well as trees and birds,
remain within the mandala of the Sun and the Moon.
Or they appear in the sky, or the mountains tremble;
the sun and moon would be eclipsed, and likewise the stars would flicker incessantly.
The barking of jackals, the frequenting of milk-trees by cats,
and conflict with donkeys, blazing owls, and howling creatures;
Lion-thrones, parasols, water-pitchers, and likewise couches,
suddenly tremble, break apart, slither along, and shriek.
All these signs of portents are terrifying to kings;
one should understand them for the sake of the country, according to the words of Garga.
Halos surrounding the staff-like twilight, dust, solar halos, and the like;
and clusters of circles with yellow and reddish-glowing radiance in all directions.
Carnivorous monkeys roar and shriek at the gate,
while crows take delight in pecking at the ground with their beaks.
The garland withers excessively, and the fragrances smell like a corpse; such are the signs of a portent appearing among garments, foods, and edibles.
Honey, clarified butter, and curd shall flow from trees that have burst open;
and dogs shall howl and cry out in the cremation grounds.
In whatever village or city this portent is seen,
one should know that there will be great terror in that very village or city.
The appearance of blossoms on the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha* trees,
as well as white, red, yellow, and black rainbows, [are auspicious omens].

Thus, there shall be the downfall of those of inferior complexion and the destruction of the temples of the gods; it is the ruin of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras when kings act with such conduct.
If there is a flow of coarse matter from the sacrificial firewood, that will bring about very great danger;
if there is a flow of ghee, milk, or fruit, there will be a depletion of ghee, milk, and water.
If there is a mutual breach when fermenting liquor, the kingdom will fall into ruin;
if blood flows from a cow's horn, there will be the destruction of cows and Brahmins.
When one sees fruit upon fruit and flowers enveloped by flowers,
there will be miscarriages among women, or war, or even the death of a king.
Where the great serpents with hoods, the maṇḍūlas,
and the scorpions devour the frogs, there the king is struck down.
There was a falling of snow and a rising of fierce winds, with distorted and wondrous sights;
the sky was like black collyrium-colored clouds, tawny with the falling of stars and meteors.
Variegated births from wombs among women, cows, goats, horses, deer, and birds,
as well as the transformations of leaves, sprouts, and creepers, are auspicious in the cool season.
Thunderbolts, lightning, earthquakes, the sounds of portents at twilight,
halos, dust, smoke, and the sun appearing or setting red— these are the omens.
From the trees, there is the emergence of the essence of food, oil, honey, flowers, and fruits;
and there is the increase in the cries of cows and birds—these are auspicious signs in the month of Madhava.
Turbid with the falling of meteors and torches, the orbs of the sun and moon turned tawny,
and the world was struck by wind, smoke, dust, and sparks that burst forth without fire.
Having seen the twilight colored red, yellow, and crimson; the sky like an agitated ocean; and the drying up of the waters of the rivers during the summer, one should predict auspiciousness.
The appearance of Indra’s weapon, halos, lightning, and the sudden sprouting of withered plants; the sudden alteration of colors, and the bursting of the earth.
The swelling of rivers, streams, and wells, as well as the crossing by boat or raft and the rapid flow of waters during the rainy season, do not bring fear.
There were the wonderful sounds of celestial women singing and of gandharvas in their aerial chariots,
and the sight of planets, lunar mansions, and stars in the sky even during the day.
The sounds of singing and instrumental music in the forests and on mountain ridges, the growth of crops, and the emergence of flavors— these are recorded as the auspicious signs of autumn.
The presence of cold winds and frost, the crying out of wild beasts and birds,
the sight of beings such as *rakṣasas* and *yakṣas*, and non-human speech;

In the winter season, the quarters, the elephants of the directions, the forests, and the mountains are obscured by blazing smoke and dust; the clouds, the moon, and the sun are high in the sky, and these are considered auspicious.
For these are seen to be the very nature of the seasons; when occurring in their proper season, they bestow auspiciousness.
Even portents seen at other times than the season become givers of auspiciousness when they occur in their proper season.
Whatever verses are uttered by the insane, whatever is the behavior of children,
and whatever women speak— therein there is no transgression.
She speaks first among the gods and afterwards goes among men;
she speaks without being prompted, for this Sarasvatī is indeed truth itself.
All these portents whatsoever should be understood as occurring sometimes for the death of a king, or for the destruction of the country, or for the approach of Rāhu.
When there is a downpour from dark clouds, or for the rising of the planets,
or when fear has arisen from one's own army or from an enemy army;
In the kingdom, in the commander of the army, in the son, or in the city, or in the domestic priest, or in the minister, in the vehicle, in the wife, or in the king— they perish.
Having recognized that these [omens] had arisen, the king, together with his army and vehicles, should prostrate before his preceptor and say: "O Blessed One, pacify them for me."
"Tell me all the fears born of portents; what may I do for you?
Thus was he addressed by the king, who was full of faith and desiring his own welfare.
Having observed the omens and having first performed the purificatory rite,
one should employ the Great Peace (*mahāśānti*), which destroys all calamities.

One should perform the Raudrī Mahāśānti, which pacifies all diseases and destroys the effects of portents, with faith and with abundant sacrificial fees— with faith and with abundant sacrificial fees.
(Pariśiṣṭa 65: Signs of Immediate Rainfall) (AVParis 65.1.1) Om. Now, therefore, we shall explain the signs of immediate rainfall within the supplementary section on characteristics.

When the sun— whose surface is smooth and stainless to behold, radiant, exceedingly brilliant, with thick rays resembling the fire of Indra— was about to rain immediately, and when the quarters of the sky were pure, and the mountains, colored like the eggs of crows and shrouded in dense dust, appeared as if submerged in lakes, and when the hosts of stars seemed to have descended low, appearing clear, vast, glossy, serene, and joyful to the sight; (AVParis_65,1.2) When the sun— whose surface is smooth and stainless to behold, radiant, exceedingly brilliant, with thick rays resembling the fire of Indra— was about to rain immediately, and when the quarters of the sky were pure, and the mountains, colored like the eggs of crows and shrouded in dense dust, appeared as if submerged in lakes, and when the hosts of stars seemed to have descended low, appearing clear, vast, glossy, serene, and joyful to the sight;
When the wind is favorable, auspicious, cool, and gentle, there is a verse on this matter:
The wind that blows from the east is the bringer of clouds, while the other is the destroyer of clouds; the northern wind generates rain, and the southern wind indeed pours down rain.

In the clouds, which took on the forms of darkness, sea-monsters, serpents, elephants, crocodiles, sharks, porpoises, conchs, trees, tortoises, waves, fish, buffaloes, boars, the elephants of the quarters, clusters of night-lotuses, water-jars, buds, chaplets, arches, whirlpools, svastikas, *vardhamānas*, *ravauḥ*, silver, *madrāṇis*, banners, horse-tails, various aquatic creatures, birds, and quadrupeds;
and which were as soft as the petals of night-blooming blue lotuses and day-lotuses.
In those resembling pearls, crystal, silver, lapis lazuli, collyrium, bees, and serpents;
and in those possessing the luster of honey, milk, the smoke of palāśa wood, dūrvā grass, silver, gold, and coral.

In times when mountains appeared doubled or tripled, possessing roots and towering peaks, amidst great whirlpools with the rattling sound of moving chariot wheels, resounding with the roar of ocean waters, echoing with the blast of agitated drums;

in times resembling the filaments of a lotus, or like the dark throat of a peacock amidst a bed of water-lilies, or like masses of clouds, or like clouds rent asunder, or like times when the roots of things are severed; in times comparable to gold or red arsenic.

One should predict immediate rain within half a yojana of this place, which is filled with waters containing gold, beautified by its interior regions, stirred and spread by southern breezes, and where the sounds of thunder deep as the roar of clouds resound within its caves.
On this point, there are two verses:
At sunrise and sunset, clouds containing embryos within the sun appear as if ablaze amidst the variegated and uneven extremities of the sky.
Five jeweled couches for the Maruts, like gold,
rain down wherever they are observed.

Upon seeing a dense mass of clouds rising at sunrise or setting at sunset, and observing that the ocean-born creatures, mountains, and auspicious signs appear like lapis lazuli, blue lotuses, lotus petals, smoke, moss, red lead, and cranes; and when the winds, accompanied by lightning, have intensified with deep and resonant sounds, and the trees on the earth have grown with thickened trunks and branches— one should predict immediate rain.
On this point, there are two verses:
With clouds resembling the stainless luster of gold from a fire that blazes within,
and resembling the radiance of blue lotuses, beryl, and collyrium;
Wherever trees with spreading branches are seen, as if sprouting blue rays of light, there rain will surely fall.

And the twilight, resembling a mass of fire, the sun, blue lotuses, the nectar of the sun, molten gold, the rising sun, yellow orpiment, blue lotuses, clarified butter, honey, bandhujīvaka flowers, japā flowers, kiṃśuka blossoms, and heaps of flame;
likewise, it illuminates the quarters with the colors of molten gold, coral, crystal, and lapis lazuli, while the various beasts and birds become tranquil.

Why is it that the twilight, garlanded with rays, is now so glossy and dense? Having seen the twilight, with its clear, smooth, and glossy halo and its encircling wreath of cloud-trees, along with mock suns cast by the red-eyed ones, this region has become like a place frequented by the five classes of outcasts together with buffaloes, bulls, boars, elephants, and hosts of aquatic creatures. On this point, there is a verse: (AVParis_65,2.3) "O King, the sky is filled with clouds resembling the bodies of elephants; the earth is covered with dust raised by the hooves of horses; and the quarters are darkened by the smoke of fires kindled for the sake of the *pāyasa* offering. (AVParis_65,2.4) "The sun, having reached the western mountain, appears like a red lotus; the moon, though rising, does not shine; and the fire, though fed with oblations, does not blaze. This is the time for the *pāyasa* sacrifice. (AVParis_65,2.5) "The sky is filled with clouds resembling the bodies of elephants; the earth is covered with dust raised by the hooves of horses; and the quarters are darkened by the smoke of fires kindled for the sake of the *pāyasa* offering. (AVParis_65,2.6) "The sun, having reached the western mountain, appears like a red lotus; the moon, though rising, does not shine; and the fire, though fed with oblations, does not blaze. If one's head is severed, or likewise if one's palace or blood [is lost],
there shall nevertheless be great generalship, long life, and the acquisition of wealth.
For cutting the ear, one incurs the loss of ornaments and knowledge;
for cutting the hand, one loses a son; and for cutting the arm, there is the arrival of wealth.
The chest yields a thousandfold gain, and likewise does the cutting off of the feet;
by the cutting off of the chest and the generative organ, one bestows absolute happiness.
Likewise, the appearance of umbrellas, mirrors, fruits, turbans, white garlands,
as well as the appearance of fish, meat, curd, milk, and blood;
The previously mentioned illustration applies likewise to spears, hooks, banners, umbrellas, swords, bows, and pure waters.
The killing of animals to be ridden by pigs or donkeys, even if it be but a single animal; likewise, the killing of a vehicle drawn by men, or of a cow that has been set down [to rest].
Furthermore, seeing things that should not be seen, approaching women who should not be approached,
and the sight of or climbing upon fruit-bearing trees that yield milk— these are [inauspicious].
Seeing or touching poison; filling one's lap with grain;
and waking a weeping person who is being attacked by bandits.
For the twice-born, the acquisition of curd and meat results from eating meat;
and for eating what is unfit to be eaten, there is the wearing of white garlands and unguents.
The killing of wild beasts, blood appearing on the hand,
the acquisition of wealth, and meeting with friends and well-wishers are to be understood as portents of gain.
One obtains [the fruit], of this there is no doubt; such are the words of Bhārgava:
white flowers, virgins, curd, cows, Brahmins, and a bull.
The deities, royal officials, white houses, friends, fruit-bearing trees, the stars, and pure water— these are auspicious.
Auspicious words regarding bricks, women wearing white garments,
a sky with clear stars, and a fire with flickering flames.
If a man sees trees, shrubs, and creepers flowering in his own house and awakens at that very moment, one should predict prosperity for him.
A man who sees women dressed in white shall be favored by Śrī;
even one whose limbs are smeared with poison and blood attains joy.
A man whose limbs are radiant obtains land, as does one whose limbs are increasing;
likewise, a man who is surrounded by his kinsmen and weeps piteously [obtains it].
One afflicted by grief attains satisfaction, and one who is dead shall obtain life;
wearing white garlands and garments, he is dissolved while being cremated.
He who sees in a dream a fierce stranger shall obtain wealth;
likewise, one who sees an ivory peg, a lute, a garland, or collyrium [shall obtain it].
The man who sees gold, or likewise obtains a woman, or sees birds flying away, or those situated in a lotus pond;
A man who mounts an elephant in rut obtains another's wife;
a man [who does so] with iron fetters obtains a maiden as his woman.
He who, having tied a new garland of blue lotuses,
awakens while the door-panels are joined together, likewise [dreams] of a handful of blue lotuses.
If one obtains a water-jar or even a mirror, it foretells the arrival of a son; the same applies to obtaining a pond, a grove, a well, a city, or a pleasure garden.
And from the filling of the water-jar, one should predict rain after crossing the eyebrows;
if the ear, being flattened, black, or naked, urinates.
If one whose flesh is raw vomits or dreams of rain, one should predict rain; likewise if one dreams of a sow, a buffalo, an elephant, or a female bird.
When one gives birth in a dream, one should then predict an abundance of food;
likewise for beds, seats, vehicles, houses, villages, and cities.
One should predict prosperity for those in whose dreams [these things] dissolve:
a bull, a man, a tree, an elephant, a mountain, or a house.
By ascending [this vehicle], a man attains prosperity, especially through white [garments];
likewise, the deities, the twice-born, cows, the ancestors, the *liṅgin*s, and the planets [are propitiated].
Whatever they say regarding a man in a dream, one should declare that to be exactly so;
crossing over rivers, lakes, and oceans signifies the crossing over of sorrow.
Having drunk human blood, a man obtains his natural state;
however, if the moon, Indra’s banner, or the sun fall, there is danger for the king.
One should predict agitation during the agitation of the great ocean and Mahendra;
and from the falling out of hair, beard, and nails, the arising of grief is indicated.
It would be fortunate to become a worm, according to the words of the jackal;
for one meets destruction at the hands of flesh-eating beasts with fangs during a conflict with spirits.
One should recognize the onset of fever from blows with weapons or fists;
whatever object is radiant, that shall bring happiness.
Whatever is seen as contrary in a dream, one should point that out to the person; when seeing those who have already given birth, one should indicate their place of residence.
Likewise, when seeing shoes, strength-giving items, or an umbrella in a house,
or when surrounded by one's own kinsmen laughing or even dancing;
He who, having mounted a chariot yoked with boars, donkeys, camels, and black quadrupeds, should travel while the axle-tree remains unbroken;
With disheveled hair, she is carried away either by the south or by the west;
a maiden who has come from the south dwells in the Kālikā family.
And when one is led away by men specifically with nooses in their hands,
there will be misfortune for the deceased among those who have been cast out and are in distress.
Of oil-cakes, sesame seeds, salt, and measures of a *karṣa*,
as well as of those with grown beards and nails, and of garments that are ill-fitting.
Likewise, there is the sight of those clad in discolored garments, as well as those who are deformed,
and the sight of reptiles, beasts of prey, and enemies.
Or for all those who are black [in complexion], except for kings, twice-born men, and bulls,
there shall be seeing, going, sorrow, and the feeling of pain.
If one sees oneself playing with lotuses or water-jars,
or if one carries away lotuses in a dream, one will suffer the amputation of a hand.
When it is severed, grief is certain; when the rope is cut, he dies.
Grief is death for one who has been swept away by the current, but for one perishing in the current, there is no death.
The appearance of severed teeth, arms, or heads, or of fragmented objects,
portends the destruction of one's brother, father, or son.
If in a dream one's bed, a branch, or even a bolted door should vanish, that person's wife perishes.
If a chameleon, a wolf, or even a tawny man climbs upon one's bed, his wife also becomes corrupted.
If one kills a white, yellow, or red snake in a dream,
or cuts off the head of a black one, his son shall perish.
For a prince, a thief, or one who is a royal servant, dreams shall yield fruit according to what has been declared regarding these [categories].
When there is gain from those things, there should be growth; when there is loss of them, there should be virtue.
When there would be loss from the gain of certain things, there should be virtue from their gain.
But he who, having seen something auspicious in a dream, subsequently sees something that is not honored—
whether it be auspicious or inauspicious— shall obtain the fruit of that which comes later.
Dreams occurring in the first watch of the night bear fruit within a year;
those in the second, within eight months; and those in the third, within half of that period.
If the cows are released at the end of a month, however, the cooking must be done immediately at dawn; thus the times for the night have been declared separately for these five stages.
Giving according to one's ability to Brahmins, rites for peace and prosperity such as the Sviṣṭakṛt,
and attending upon the Aśvattha tree in the morning destroy bad dreams.

Attendance upon the *aśvattha* tree, the gift of a vessel of sesame seeds, touching a cow, the satiation of Brahmins, the performance of pacifying rites, and the performance of auspicious rites— these destroy bad dreams.
They should perform the purchase of goods, the giving of gold, the worship of deities, and attendance upon the assembly of their preceptor;
furthermore, the sight of the twice-born, bulls, cows, horses, and kings, as well as the recitation of histories and auspicious rites, should be observed.
Having seen these inauspicious dreams, one should rise quickly in the morning and thoroughly cleanse the face with water from the confluence of rivers.
Having consecrated the water with the *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, the *śaṃtātīya*, and the *mayobhuvaḥ* verses, one should diligently wipe the face according to the true principle.
O you who are not a living being, depart to the beyond; we know your perception, O dream!
[We offer] bright mustard seeds, clay, fuel, flowers, and curd.
Having paid homage to a cow, a goat, gold, a living being, a maiden, and a virtuous Brahmin,
the king should proceed toward his charming friends.
When the king, who knows the ritual injunctions, desires to set out on a journey,
he should then have him consecrated with auspicious and gentle mantras.
Then, wearing white garments, restrained in speech, and with his senses controlled,
the king should lie down for that night on the ground and consecrate it with mantras.
"For the illustration of the objects seen in a dream is indeed otherwise.
Having spoken thus, the king, with a restrained mind, should then go to sleep.
Having observed auspicious dreams, the lord of men should then proceed;
however, if the dreams are inauspicious, he should then undertake a rite of pacification.
One should perform the *māhendrī*, the *amṛtā*, the *raudrī*, or even the *aparājitā*;
or one should employ the *kauberī* or the *ādityā* accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
When a lord of men touches the moon and the sun with his two hands, or even swallows them,
he crosses the salt ocean and rivers with his arms, as well as the mire of distress and darkness.

If a king perceives here within himself the conditions for fire, death, or increase at an improper time, he should not cut down men, horses, trees, or mountains, nor should he destroy elephants that roam his palace.
And if the king wanders the earth with his secret spies, encompassing it along with its cities;

or if he weeps— and having seen such signs as these— he should set out for the enemy's territory with a joyful heart.

He sleeps, conquers, eats, rejoices, laments, dances, and laughs with songs;
he becomes delighted and obtains a maiden, if the king, seeking victory, should possess statesmanship.

If a king is mounted upon a camel, a donkey, a boar, or a monkey; if his crown, armlets, garments, and insignia have been snatched away and he is naked; if his horses and elephants are slain; or if his banner has fallen—then he should not advance.
If a king is unconquered by his enemies, yet is mocked by those enemies who are intoxicated with pride;
and if he becomes difficult to behold due to his fierce appearance—
then...
Such a person as that should not march against others.
Having seen auspicious dreams, the king, consecrated by those reciting prayers, becomes endowed with favorable omens and freed from the multitude of portents.
Accompanied by allies, well-armored, and attended by those skilled in interpreting omens, the lord of the earth should set forth at an auspicious hour and under a favorable constellation.
Anointed with oil, he eats *kṛsarā* drenched in oil;
and he who enters his mother and the blazing fire.
Whether a man should fall from a palace or from a mountain peak,
or whether he sinks into pits of mud or perishes in water;
He who uproots a tree, he who looks upon a king's servant,
and he who approaches a female monkey at the mouth of a young girl— [these shall be punished].
Or if it emits [the sound] from the throat of one whose throat has become blood-red,
or if one who is discolored is bound by nooses, he shall die.
Whosoever’s splendor ascends into bell-metal or a vessel of bell-metal,
that man shall be slain by the sword in no long time.
Having first ascended the tip of a sacrificial post, he then ascends the tip of a boat;
in no long time at all, he ascends the tip of a stake.
Whether it be a shaven-headed ascetic wearing saffron robes, or even one clad in white or red garments,
if they mount [the patient] in a dream, disease mounts that person.
If a dog, a python, a monitor lizard, a hyena, a porcupine, or even a chameleon,
a ruru deer, a tiger, or a leopard should climb upon him;
If in a dream a serpent, or one with fierce matted hair, or even one clad in white or red garments, approaches a person, disease shall likewise approach that person.
With his limbs smeared with the ashes of the earth and remaining entirely unclothed,
he beholds the assemblies of his kinsmen and their festive gatherings.
Traveling on difficult roads, frequenting marshy lands,
and the anointing of the limbs with sesame oil, cow-dung, and mud.
Gold, gems, pearls, ornaments, and silver—
either the sight of these or their entry [into the body] causes the onset of diseases.
Singing, dancing, laughter, as well as the performance of marriages,
joy, delight, and the witnessing of calamity.
A man whose limbs are smeared with old ghee shall meet his death;
thus have been declared the various great portents previously mentioned.
Likewise, five types of meteors are known, as are nine types of halos;
eight kinds of portents regarding the burning of the quarters have been proclaimed, and likewise eight kinds of lightning.
There are four types of earthquakes and likewise eight kinds of thunderclaps;
twenty-two varieties are recorded as being known among the phenomena such as meteors.
Many great portents have been proclaimed in connection with the rites for pacification (*śānti*);
desiring pacification, the lord of men should perform all of them according to the prescribed rule.
Then the king, terrified by fear, should choose an Atharvan priest who is learned in all the scriptures; he, being thus chosen by the high-souled one, shall act for the sake of pacification.
The lord of the earth should properly grant security to his subjects;
immediately thereafter, he should perform worship of cows, and especially of Brahmins.
In a temple of the deities, one should immediately cause milk-cows to be milked upon the ground;
and one should constantly smear it with ointments and worship it with flowers and incense as prescribed.
With various bright lamps arranged in all directions,
as well as with offerings of oblations consisting of milk-rice and cakes.
With various kinds of heart-pleasing foods prepared in every direction—
at that very time, in a peaceful cow-pen or near a body of water—
Having emerged from the city, or else in a pure place, being composed in mind,
one should choose auspicious rites for averting portents that are known by those who understand the reality of pacification.
Sixteen or eight [priests] are chosen, and they must be purified by preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*); other excellent brahmins, numbering one hundred, shall perform the auxiliary functions (*aṅga*).
Seated comfortably at sunrise and sunset, they should perform their recitation without weariness;
they are called "members of the assembly" (sadasya) during the recitation of the sacrificial rite.
Among them, the most excellent one— a knower of peace, a witness, captivating to the mind,
and an expert in all rites— should also bring [the materials] with reverence.
Having purified the ground according to the rules and having constructed a pavilion there,
he himself should duly prepare the altar and the sacrificial vessels.
Thus, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti), preceded by the churning of fire, which destroys all calamities.
Having performed a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) accompanied by various kinds of food, garments, and abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should present a choice cow as an offering.
Having likewise given a house, an ornament, a parasol, an ox, a horse, or an elephant adorned with bells and ornaments;
One attains great happiness and achieves the fulfillment of one's purpose;
one achieves the fulfillment of one's purpose.
(Pariśiṣṭa 69. Atharvavedahṛdaya) (AVParis 69.1.1) Om. Having approached the omniscient one of tranquil mind, the sages—free from envy—questioned Bhṛgu, the best among the knowers of Brahman.
For many desires indeed exist in the world, each established with different means;
tell me, without doubt, which one among them alone is truly supreme.
I shall explain in brief that by which everything is bestowed;
although this is an exceedingly difficult question, I shall nevertheless speak.
For the sake of accomplishing all goals, the *Āṅgirasa-śruti* is beneficial; blazing with its own splendor, it illuminates the heart of the followers of the Atharva Veda.
I shall describe his power hereafter according to the rule;
for I know certain signs that are difficult to accomplish.
He whose teeth erupt at an improper time, who is devoid of hair,
or has excessively long hair, as well as one who has deficient or extra fingers;
He may also be born with two tusks; his ritual practice shall be that of his own Vedic branch, and he should perform whatever is prescribed in his own branch or the Atharvaṇa rite.
Whether he has two heads, three eyes, one eye, or two noses; whether he lacks a hand or some other limb for the sake of his purpose—he is indeed not [merely] Atharvaśiras.
Having performed the preliminary rites, being pure in soul and honored by the one to be initiated,
he— having sipped the water of peace— should sit near a tree of peace.
One should perform the fire-oblation with fuel-sticks from the *śānta* tree, as well as sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets; by this, the Atharvan priest causes the noble family to rejoice.
If he does not obtain the Atharvan [text], he himself should perform the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblation ten times over, as well as the *sāvitra* recitation.
If one is born with deformed limbs, with an extra limb, or even with missing limbs—
an extreme marvel for the family— then the Atharvan priest shall bring it to pacification.
In whatever kingdom a king is born with limbs and face resembling those of a monkey,
a camel, or an elephant, that kingdom shall indeed perish within six months.
Or else, monkeys and the like are born from another [species] with bodies identical to their own;
or a flower, or even a fruit, produced on one tree grows upon another tree.
Then, desiring peace for himself, he should seek out the best of the twice-born, a master of the Atharva Veda;
he should have him perform a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) for both the kingdom and the city.
When the loss of the kingdom is imminent, or indeed in the Mahāraurava hell,
or during famine, or pestilence, or even in the fear of drought.
The entire kingdom might perish through locusts, rats, and the destruction of crops;
or the land might suddenly become waterless, or a great river might fail to dry up.
Likewise, when other unmentioned terrible calamities have arisen, the twice-born Atharvans should perform pacification; for they are the physicians in these matters.
Even a scion of royalty, though worthy of sovereignty, does not obtain a kingdom;
a twice-born man, though reciting and even hearing it, does not acquire sacred knowledge.
Even one desiring to establish a sacred fire should not perform the consecration nor build a dwelling;
nor should one desiring to marry a maiden, nor one desiring objects of pleasure, seek a husband for a sacrifice.

Whether she be barren, or one whose children have died, or an unfortunate woman who gives birth only to daughters, or a woman who has borne once and never again conceives a fetus— [for these, this rite is prescribed].
Even when the time for birth has passed, or even when the fetus is throbbing, she who does not bring forth, or she who gives birth to many sons, [should perform this rite].
A farmer conquers a farmer, and even one who lives by weapons may conquer;
likewise, one may conquer a celestial being in legal dispute, or attain good fortune pertaining to all beings.
Now, when one desires to dispel such fears as these, or seeks the very fruits that have been described,
one should at that time go for refuge to a twice-born man who is radiant with the excellence of the supreme *Aṅgirasa* mantra.
At night, one should observe a tree with two shadows, or an evil dream that portends misfortune;
by day, one should observe the planets, earthquakes, and similar phenomena.
Now, the wonders of flames are proclaimed, as well as those distinguished by meteors and the like;
furthermore, there are the wonders of dreams and other wonders which those who know the truth declare occur within households.
In these cases, one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) involving the *amṛtā* mantra accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
or the *raudrī*, the *vaiśvadevī*, the *abhayā*, or the *aparājitā*.
With cows, land, gold, garments, food, sesame seeds, or auspicious fruits,
[one should offer] together with shoes and an umbrella, and provided with the teacher’s ornaments.
Or, whoever should perform the practice as prescribed according to the rules,
all these portents arising from calamities will be dissolved by means of the Great Peaceful Rite (*mahāśānti*).
In whatever king's realm an Atharvan who has mastered the *śānti* rites resides,
that kingdom prospers and remains free from calamity.
In whatever king's realm that [protection] is absent, his kingdom is oppressed by various fears and sinks like a cow in the mud.
Therefore, a king should especially and constantly honor the Atharvan who has conquered his senses with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality.
One should constantly perform rites for peace, worship the planets and constellations,
and carry out acts of "milking the earth" in the temples of the deities.
One should cause the ritual satiation of cows to be performed according to the rules at crossroads, in cow-pens, at sacred fords, and in waters;
this destroys all defects.
Proclaiming thus at all times, the king who has conquered his senses attains infinite happiness and enjoys the entire earth.
Even when death has arrived, the best of the twice-born, having studied the Atharvāṅgirasa and being firm in his vows, should bring it to peace.

A wise man, possessing the purity of mantras and ever radiating splendor and brilliance, having obtained a sacrificial fee through the performance of pacification rites from a king, a wealthy person, or anyone else, [should proceed].
If a householder, finding his family in distress, takes up another means of support and abandons the former,
he should recite the *Saṃhitā* three times after eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and perform a *kṛcchra* penance for purification.

Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred thousand times, ten thousand times, one thousand times, or even more, a fire oblation (homa) consisting of a tenth part of that number should be performed according to the nature of the faults.
He who is pure and free from pride, who does not fail to honor even the most excellent of the twice-born,
and who is utterly devoid of envy— he alone should undertake this rite for peace.
"Wherever Aṅgiras of such a kind accomplishes whatever rites are to be achieved, there nothing shall be deficient; so was it spoken by Bhṛgu."
A wise Atharvan priest, knowing this entire *Atharvahṛdaya*, should perform all this— whether by means of the brief rite for pacification or with the *Gāyatrī*— for the sake of the body.
Those twice-born ones who, even though they have studied it, do not know the *Āṅgirasa-śruti* nor the *Atharvaveda-hṛdaya*, are not considered knowers of the Veda.
One who knows the *Atharvahṛdaya* is considered the supreme Atharvan;
this [text] should not be given even to one belonging to the Atharva Veda who harbors hatred toward his teacher.
A twice-born man who, out of delusion, teaches a text belonging to another Vedic branch, perishes;
however, he who understands the Atharvaveda-hṛdaya and recites it with devotion attains liberation.
Atharvan, there is nothing wondrous for him; peace alone shall always prevail.
Peace alone shall always prevail.

(Pariśiṣṭa 70: The Bhārgavīyāṇi) (AVParis 70.1.1) Oṃ. In ancient times, having duly honored the wise one, the learned sages questioned the undisturbed Bhṛgu, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
O Sage, you have not yet spoken of the pacification of the various portents that arise in manifold ways throughout the three worlds; tell us this without doubt.
Bhṛgu replied to the brahmins with a focused mind: "Listen without doubt to the triple method for pacifying portents as it is being told."
In this regard, I shall describe the Brahmins who are capable of pacifying ill-performed rites:
those learned in the Atharvāṅgiras Veda and conversant with the rules for all ritual actions.

Endowed with non-violence, truthfulness, courtesy, purity, and faith; possessing knowledge of the Śruti and Smṛti, and following the conduct of the virtuous; and being possessed of noble lineage, good character, and [appropriate] age.
Among them, one who is preeminent, tranquil, the best of the twice-born,
highly learned in the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras [mantras], exceedingly pure, and esteemed by the virtuous [should be appointed].
"The king should appoint that Brahmin as the *brahmán* priest and one who knows all the Vedas as the *hotṛ*.
When this was said, the sages spoke to Bhṛgu, who was free from all taint."
The officiating priests of those who protect the earth are proclaimed to be the Great Peace;
for is it not so, O learned one, even when [the king] has declined or fallen away from his own duty?
In that case, when a rite for pacification is performed, whose fruit of pacification would it be?
Even an unrighteous king should first perform a libation for Brahmins.
Then, having performed the great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*), which protects the king on all sides,
he, surrounded [by his retinue], should go to the purifying [bath] for the purification of the twice-born.
In that case, there is a twelve-day vow, subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits.
For three sets of three days, one should subsist on milk, roots, and auspicious fruits;
then for three days, the wise man should remain without food—this constitutes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Likewise, ninety-nine men who are free from blemish and desirous of service are capable of performing that ritual for three days, even if they have not been previously instructed.
Having performed even the beneficial *kṛcchra* penance, they should perform the ritual with concentrated minds;
being pure in soul and free from envy, they should do so through Vedic recitations and fire-offerings.
Thereafter, among the household priests, he shall obtain that divine ritual procedure,
beginning with the guest-offering for the planets and the sacrifice to the quarters in every respect.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rules under all the lunar mansions,
one should then establish Padmasambhava with the great propitiatory rite of Amṛta.
On a Tuesday, those who are wise should perform a *lakṣahoma* sacrifice with the Sāvitrī mantra;
they should also give to the Brahmins whatever gifts each one desires.
Beyond this, one may give according to one's desire cows, land, gold, horses, jewels, grain, garments, chariots, and elephants.
Whatever may satisfy the Brahmins, or whatever may be appropriate for each individual, all that should be accepted; this is remembered as the rule for giving.
And he should give a village, a cow, or a pair of garments to the teacher;
having honored him with ornaments, he should satisfy him with a pleased mind.
By this procedure, the preceptor should pacify terrestrial portents;
this very same procedure is to be understood as applicable even to portents occurring in the sky.

This, however, is the specific distinction regarding the Sāvitrī: one should perform ten hundred thousand oblations with a mind concentrated on the sacrifice, and one should also offer a "blanket of ghee."
Twelve cows, accompanied by a hundred gold coins, should be given to the preceptor; when that is bestowed, it pacifies even the most extraordinary calamity from the sky.
In the case of divine and miraculous events, it should be performed accompanied by a *koṭihoma* sacrifice;
furthermore, a thousand cows must be given as the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor.
This procedure has been correctly explained for warding off divine calamities;
through it, the prosperity of the people is increased by means of abundance and security.
In all *koṭi*-homas, the fruit depends upon the specific material used;
