listen as I declare it for the purposes of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and subjugation (*abhicāra*).
One desiring peace should prepare sacrificial fuel-sticks from trees of gentle nature;
with fuel-sticks of *arka*, *kāśmarya*, and *nimba* trees, one effects the destruction of enemies.
Especially with the fuel-sticks of the *durnāma*, the *kaṇṭaka*,
and the *ambu* plants, as well as those of trees that are broken or split, the fruit [of the rite] is the destruction of enemies.
By means of oblations of *bilva*, *padma*, and *utpala* flowers grown in a pure place,
a person always obtains all their desires.
The Hotṛ priest should commence the rite for peace with offerings of sesame, rice, barley, and so forth, as well as curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, wheat, and śāli rice.
Ghee is traditionally held to be the pacifier of all oblations;
therefore, ghee deserves to be poured as an offering in every substance.
A wise man should perform rites for peace while wearing the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder;
however, in all ancestral rites, he should begin with the thread worn over the right shoulder.
When honey, clarified butter, curd, or milk are being consumed; when ointments, mechanical vehicles, weapons, dwellings, or armaments are present; [in these cases, one should not recite the Veda].
In a mirror, in a vessel of food, in jewels and pearls,
in ornaments and other such things, as well as on a bed and in seats;
There may be the sight of crows, owls, and pigeons, or of honey,
or the arrival of other inauspicious beasts and birds.
And of white flowers, of the multitude of reptiles, of fat, blood, and flesh, and of bones, marrow, and hair; (5)

And if, without any apparent cause, there is a sudden clashing together in sight of one's nails or ashes, or if there is a change in the flavors of tastes, or an odorless stench arises without a reason; [then one should know that death is near].
Wherever the shape of a lotus flower is seen in honey, clarified butter,
kṛsarā, or milk-rice, there is a depletion of both wealth and lifespan.
When, in clarified butter or in honey-mixed curd, the shape of a lotus or even a svastika appears, one should then predict death.
If a defect should be observed in the milk, rice, or sacrificial oblation, a man should give that to one learned in the Vedas; thus he shall pacify his mental state.
Wherever one might see a portentous marvel, there too one should perform [the rite];
or else, with supreme meditative concentration, one should perform the Vāruṇī pacification.
Or even among those of other forms who perform rites of pacification in this place,
one should know that their lifespan, wealth, or merit shall be inexhaustible.
When there is trembling, flaming, falling, quivering, or rising up—
specifically among great crowds of people or among elephants and horses— one should know that there is great danger.
There they fight among their kinsmen; that will undoubtedly bring them fear.
Even there, they will be deprived of their stores of wealth, their livestock, and even their knowledge.
But those men who do not employ the ritual actions for the purpose of pacifying portents will quickly perish, along with their lineage and their retinue.
A meal should be prepared for a thousand or ten thousand Brahmins,
and the deities should be propitiated with offerings of oblations and flowers.
And the wise man should perform the rite of pacification according to the proper rule;
when this is done, all fear perishes at that very moment.
The sages spoke to Bhṛgu concerning the nature of the auspicious and the inauspicious;
he replied to them regarding the person who takes refuge in the year.
In the cold, hot, and rainy seasons, and at all times when free from afflictions,
the person known as the year is said to be without calamity.
If it is free from portents such as thunderclaps, earthquakes, and fires in all directions, yet is joined by comets or by solar spikes (*ādityakīlaka*).
Or by other wonders intended for the destruction of the world, which cause turmoil through ruin;
then this person of purified soul prospers in happiness.
If, moreover, he should be possessed by many kinds of wonders for a year, the wise should quickly perform the pacification of that [possession].
In this regard, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification (*śānti*) which destroys all sins,
by means of which a teacher (*ācārya*) learned in the divine tantras may obtain the fruit [of his practice].
First, having purified his self, he should perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*);
thereafter, he should perform the sacrifice to the deities according to the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Having performed a sacrifice to the planets, and thereafter to the lunar mansions, he should then worship the seasons,
the seasonal periods, and the lords of the hosts of Mahādeva.
One should worship the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, as well as Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa, along with Viśveśvara, Viṣṇu, and the one of wondrous deeds.
One should perform the great pacification (*mahāśānti*) according to the prescribed rite for Sūrya and Candramas, Agni, all the hosts of planets, as well as Vāyu and the two Aśvins.
The wise one, honored by the gods, should perform [this]; in this way, the affliction is pacified.
It may be white, or reddish-brown, or yellow, or indeed blackish-tawny;
listen to all that regarding how these four kinds of portents bear fruit, as told by me in brief.
For when there is a defect in the clouds, a white [halo] portends harm for brahmins, while a red one immediately destroys the king;
if it becomes yellow, it destroys the class of vaiśyas, and indeed, when there is a blackish-brown defect, it affects the śūdras.
Where the seed sprouts and yet the fruit fails due to negligence— this indeed is called a most extraordinary destruction for a married couple.
From failing to honor those worthy of honor, from honoring those unworthy of honor, and due to the defect of the internal organ— because of these causes, peace does not arise.

Therefore, he should appoint as chief attendants learned brahmins who are experts in the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, who are free from passion and envy, and who are skilled in their duties.
Having been deliberated upon by the learned and further determined by the wise,
the discerning person should perform the ritual action in accordance with the proper place and time.
One who knows the injunctions should not perform one action when another has been enjoined;
nor, having begun a rite, should one stop anywhere in the middle.
A wise person should never engage in the confusion of duties;
however, even when performing such an act, he should not produce excessive fault.

Having observed many faults here in the case of performing otherwise, one who possesses right resolve does not reach completion; [thus, the acts of intention, speech, and physical action are rendered ineffective].
Having observed the portent in its entirety, one should then commence the rite of pacification;
for a man who acts without careful examination does not obtain peace.
Just as a physician, having determined that a disease is caused by wind or bile,
may achieve success in his treatment once the appropriate medicine has been administered.
Therefore, one should investigate until a miraculous effect has been produced; for both the non-existent and the existent, as well as for the agent and the instigator.
But a rite being performed with deficient qualities may cause calamity;
especially would it destroy the performer along with his retinue.
Since both the scriptural authority and the observed result have been seen, one should therefore practice virtue;
when that virtue has been performed, all prosperity will surely be attained.
By performing oblations with *aśoka* flowers combined with honey and milk,
a Brahmin attains through his meritorious deeds the supreme station of a Gandharva.
O best of the twice-born, whatever desire one strives for, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, one obtains that very thing without effort; this is the truth.
(Pariśiṣṭa 70b. Gārgyāṇi) (AVParis 70b.1.1) Om. Having bowed to Brahmā, the best of poets, who was seated upon a grass mat, Gautama, having bowed his head to the god, questioned him.
O best of gods, please explain to me with due discipline the portents that appear for the harm of living beings, as well as the means for their pacification.
Having heard those words of his, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
being supremely pleased, spoke regarding the remedy for all calamities.
Listen, my child, to the summary of the twelve chapters as it is being recited in its entirety according to the proper method, concerning that which is proclaimed by the disorders of wind.
And because Vāyu is powerful, supreme, and the source of all wonders,
I shall therefore first proclaim him according to the prescribed rule.
When vehicles go unyoked without men,
or when those that are yoked do not move, there is great danger for the lords of men.
Kettledrums, clay drums, and tabors resound even without being struck;
and though struck, they do not sound; or else, mountains that are immovable begin to shake.
If the sound of musical instruments should be heard in the forest as if it were coming from the sky,
or if it is heard within one's own house, the body will suffer distress there.
And great sounds are heard, as well as the resonances of singing and music;
there the body is afflicted, or a very great disease may arise.
Or if the ladle ever falls from the hand into the cooking vessel,
or if the pestle falls, or if the winnowing basket is shaken;
The mingling of langurs, an eclipse of the sun and moon,
or a woman suckling another woman— these portend a tumultuous danger.
When pillars, palaces, and trees shake,
and when beds, seats, and vehicles move on their own, the death of the king is certain.
And a terrible wind blew out of season, dragging along gravel;
it was as fearsome as the end of an aeon, felling trees and houses alike.
For seven days or even for a fortnight, it binds [the world] with extreme cruelty;
if it does not rain for three days, there will be a terrible danger from weapons.
In the Vāyavya [rite], the king should worship Vāyu with seven [verses];
for these three verses beginning with "dvāv imau" should be recited by the self-restrained twice-born.
A fire oblation accompanied by abundant food and sacrificial fees should be performed with great care;
for the sake of pacification, one should offer it specifically toward the northwestern direction and incorporate the mantras of Vāyu and Savitṛ.
One should apply [the ritual] in this same way at the beginning, the end, and the middle;
one should give a sacrificial fee to the guru for the sake of achieving pacification from the wind.
If twin flowers or twin fruits are produced,
or even many lotuses— kumuda, utpala, and padma— on a single stalk;
Those with many heads or two heads, as well as those with other types of sprouts,
or even barley or rice, portend the death of the master.
If one should observe diversity among the fruits and flowers on a single tree,
or their displacement or alteration, there will be the arrival of a foreign army.
(There is no fifth section in the manuscripts.
(AVParis_70b,6.1) If plants or creepers bear fruit or flowers out of season, or do not bear fruit according to the proper seasons, there will be danger to the people.
Furthermore, in the case of an exchange of grain, he foretells misfortune;
either the sesame seeds will be devoid of oil, or they will become like liquor-oil.
The king shall cause flowers or fruits that have become unnatural to be treated as unrefined;
in the case of a transformation of grains, he shall cause the field together with its crop to be confiscated.
One should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Sūrya when flowers and fruits are deformed, and likewise an animal sacrifice;
one should also offer a pap to Kṣetrapati and one to the Earth when the crops are deformed.
The propitiatory rite for Sūrya should be performed according to the rules with the mantras dedicated to Sūrya;
the embryo is consecrated by reciting the two verses beginning with "uccā patantam."
In the event of a deformity in the crops, one should interpose the *Bhauma* Anuvāka;
then, after twice-born men have eaten with ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should honor the performer [of the rite].
In those regions where trees impelled by the gods are seen—
whether weeping, laughing, or exuding many fluids;
When branches, being healthy and in a windless place, release their fruit and flowers without agitation, and young women display them as such, it is called "laughter."
Displaying all manner of fruits and flowers out of season,
a terrible and horrific fourfold danger will swiftly break forth there.
Wherever the god sends rain upon serpents, fish, or birds,
there shall be damage to the crops or great fear shall prevail.
Likewise, where the rain-cloud pours down liquor, honey-essence, clarified butter, oil, or curd,
there small creatures are born.
When meteors and stars fall upon the sacrificial hearths and it rains glowing embers,
one should predict a terrible fear of disease in those regions.
When iron arrows, spears, and swords repeatedly burst into flames,
one should predict a terrible danger from weapons in those regions.
When a man, a horse, or even an elephant is set ablaze in any place,
the attendants there perish and the leader shall likewise be destroyed.
Where a sacred tree suddenly exudes various juices—
whether individually or all together— I shall now describe its characteristics.
In ghee, honey, and milk; likewise in ghee, milk, and water;
in honey, water, and yet again in ghee and milk.
Wherever this most terrible great portent occurs among the trees— namely,
mutual strife over liquor and spirits, or the falling of weapons upon blood— [there is danger].
In [a dream of] oil, the principal [ministers] are slain; in [a dream of] food, one should predict the fear of hunger.
If fruit or a flower is seen on a tree out of season, [the same result follows].
It is certain that [the child] will be born in the tenth month; in the case of a king, there may be a reversal of this.
Where there is flower upon flower, there likewise shall be fruit upon fruit.
One should recognize a leaf upon a leaf; therein lies manifold danger, where a sacred tree is completely covered with white cloth.
At that time, one should predict a terrible and intense fear for the Brahmins;
and from others clothed in red garments, a great danger for the Kṣatriyas.
For Vaiśyas, [the banner] is with yellow garments; for Śūdras, with black garments;
with blue ones for the destruction of crops; and with variegated ones for deer and birds.
If, for ten months or more, the winds become harsh and discolored,
or if the deities in one's kingdom chatter or laugh;
If they gaze ahead or even toward the east, one should know there is great danger;
likewise, if the bodily signs laugh, close their eyes, or become distorted.
Within a month, one should recognize that there will be great danger here and there,
wherever one beholds a painting, or where one repeatedly sings or makes gestures.
One should predict the death of the king within these eight months,
wherein there are various signs as well as sacred shrines.
If they should cause excessive transformation there, one should know that a great danger exists;
it may be the uprooting of houses, or likewise of lakes or forests.
One should know that there is great danger where fires blaze up in the open air,
and where trees display blossoms and fruit out of season.
They may emit milk, fat, liquor, blood, honey, or water;
or they may suddenly wither away while free from disease, or having become dry, grow once again.
They rise up and sit down; I shall explain that further hereafter.

If it laughs, there will be the destruction of the body; if it strikes with a weapon, the warriors perish. If it is agitated, it portends the ruin of the country; and if it bears fruit, it signifies the loss of artisans.
The death of children occurs when there is fruit and flowers on young trees;
unseasonable fruit and flowers cause the division of one's own kingdom.

One should know that a decline in milk-yielding cows occurs during the flow of milk; a sign of famine during the flow of fat; a decrease in draft animals during the flow of wine; and one should predict battle during the flow of blood.
If there is a flow of honey, disease will arise; if there is a flow of water, it will not rain.
If those who are healthy wither away, one should know this to be a sign of famine.
If a tree falls of its own accord, there will be a division; if it falls while weeping, there will be a loss of food.
If it makes a sound, there will be a loss of wealth; and the same applies to shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants.
If water flows from trees that have been worshipped, one should predict the death of the king;
having covered those trees, one should adorn them with perfumes and garlands.
And here, food accompanied by honey and clarified butter should be given to the Brahmins;
likewise, an umbrella and a banner should be offered, as well as the supreme leaf-oblation.
Thereafter, one should [perform] the piercing of the two breasts with mantras combined with medicinal herbs,
as well as offerings, oblations, and singing and dancing on all sides.
Likewise, one should offer perfume, garlands, incense, and lamps,
as well as various kinds of food and drink, as an offering to Rudra at night.
And the ripening in the tenth month is according to the word of Śukra;
likewise, what Bṛhaspati and Āditya declare is exactly so.
And here, one should perform the Raudrī rite, which destroys trees and portents;
indeed, one should give a gold coin (niṣka) and land as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) there.
Women who give birth out of season, as well as offspring born after the [proper] time has passed; those who give birth to twins, and even those who give birth to double sets of twins.
When non-human, deformed offspring are born of a woman—
whether with excessive limbs, lacking limbs, or with deficient limbs.
If [the omens] resemble four-footed animals or birds and possess half-human features,
one should predict the destruction of that region and its lineage.
A fetus that has not reached maturity, or even a woman with two or four feet, may be born ruined or deformed; that portends danger.
Those [omens] should be quickly abandoned in foreign lands by those seeking merit;
and here, peace should be established by Brahmins who are exponents of the Veda.
If a mare, a female elephant, or a cow gives birth to twins,
or even if the offspring is deformed, the king will die within six months.
Offspring should be abandoned in foreign lands from their herds;
otherwise, they will destroy the herd and the city of their master.
When they go into non-human wombs— even among living beings—
whether as donkeys, camels, horses, elephants, or birds, that is not good.
Whether they become intoxicated at the wrong time or remain sober at the right time,
it is not good if elephants, camels, horses, or birds [behave] like Śiva.
Now, if a bull should drink from a bull, or a cow from a cow;
or if a bitch suckles a cow, or a cow a bitch.
Whether it be among the animal realm or among humans, there may be the arrival of a foreign army; if non-human beings speak through human creatures, [this shall be known].
If a woman should give birth to quadrupeds, birds, or serpents, the king will die within a month, whether through convulsions or by crying out in distress.
In the animal realm or among humans, there may be the arrival of a foreign army;
or that which is mobile may become stationary, or that which is stationary may become mobile.
When that reversal of the birth-place occurs, there will be the arrival of a foreign army;
yet by practicing renunciation, exile, or giving gifts, even after such [calamity], auspiciousness will quickly arise.
The domestic priest should sacrifice with a vessel of cooked food or with an animal;
he should perform the sacrifice with the Prajāpati-mantra, providing abundant food as the sacrificial fee.
In that case, the performance of rites for Yama is seen first;
thereafter, a king seeking the welfare of his subjects should cause a *prājāpatya* pacification to be performed.
The group of deities has been declared as peaceful at the beginning, the end, and the middle;
in that region and for its king, there shall be health and auspiciousness.
Wherever wondrous and diverse portents are seen on all sides,
even that most prosperous region will very quickly perish.
When portents appear in royal palaces— on the mansions, banners, and archways— there is great danger for the king.
The sudden collapse of palaces, gateways, watchtowers, doors, and palace chambers is recorded as a portent of the king's death.
The falling or even the breaking of the banners of the kings of the gods,
or their being frequented by flesh-eating beasts, [or] by those who have fallen away and are devoid of rays.
When all the quarters of the sky are thrown into confusion by the falling of planets and constellations,
and both twilights are ablaze, one should know that there is great danger.
If the earth suddenly cracks, or if it becomes riddled with fissures,
or if it trembles excessively— in all such cases, that portends fear.
The paths do not carry them, for they are filled with fear by the winged demons of the Rākṣasas;
the forms of Rākṣasas are seen, yet there is no protection even within their homes.
When Piśācas, or Rākṣasas, or those resembling them have entered,
that city will soon be destroyed by a plague among its people.
But the seasons have become inverted, the Brahmins act contrary to the Dharma, and the constellations are disjoined; such is this manifestation of fear.
Where those unworthy of honor are honored, and those worthy of honor are not honored,
and where there is a persistent refusal to give to those who deserve honor— such is the manifestation of danger.
The powerful do not honor or revere the Brahmins, nor do they show respect to the gods;
furthermore, through unrighteousness, they take no delight in their own duties.
In a conflict, elephants, men, and horses that are divided, full of crookedness, lacking enthusiasm, truthful yet devoid of truth, will be defeated.
Devoid of moral conduct and proper behavior, fond of liquor, meat, and falsehood,
and abounding in naked heretics, they will exist when destruction is imminent.
One should offer great oblations, great propitiations, and very abundant foods,
[dedicating them] to Prajāpati, Mahendra, or even Mahādeva.
One should employ the Māhendrī hymn in the place of the Aindrī, and the Raudrī hymn in the place of the Raudrī;
the lord of men should give eight hundred cows to the Brahmins.
But one hundred *niṣkas* should be given to the preceptor; in this way, there will be well-being for all creatures.
Otherwise, through drought or excessive rain, or through famine, there will be fear.
Unseasonable rain portends disease; excessive rain, as well as lightning and thunder without clouds occurring suddenly, portend danger.
Or if a thunderclap falls from a cloudless sky, it portends the death of the king;
likewise, if it rains violently out of season, or fails to rain during the proper seasons.
When there is cold in the heat, and likewise heat in the cold,
the state of things is seen to be transformed, not according to its own nature as defined by the season.
One should declare: "There shall indeed be ill-health for the subjects."
When the subduer of Pāka rains continuously for seven nights out of season,
the death of the leader of that region is certain.
Where blood rains down, there shall be fear of weapons;
where marrow, bone-fat, or flesh rains down, there shall be fear of a plague among the people.
If there is a rain of embers and dust, that city will perish;
likewise, [a rain of] fruit, flowers, leguminous grains, or gold portends danger.
Living beings are distressed and deformed; even straw brings about destruction.
There are whirlpools in the openings and monkeys, which cause the excessive growth of crops.
If, whether by day or by night, a white rainbow should appear in a cloudless sky—
whether seen in the east, west, north, or south— [it portends a specific result].
Even a place that is very prosperous perishes through famine.
If, even when the sky is cloudless and clear, the shadow of the sun is not seen, or if it appears contrary to its course in a cloudless sky, there will be danger to the country.
When there is an abnormality regarding rain, the Sun, Indra, Vāyu, and Parjanya are to be worshipped;
the sacrificial fees consist of foodstuffs along with gold, grain, and cows.
A Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed, which destroys all portents;
and a white horse, endowed with all auspicious marks, should be given to the preceptor.
Either a hundred gold coins (niṣkas) should be given, or a hundred cows.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on abnormalities of the digestive fire, as spoken by the blessed Śukra.
Where fire blazes without fuel, or where it suddenly makes a terrible sound,
or where it blazes even with fuel present, it shall afflict the king along with his kingdom.
If curd, meat, or even *dūrvā* grass should spontaneously ignite,
or if anything that is dry catches fire without a flame, the death of the king is certain.
A palace, a gateway, a door, a rampart, a house of Kāśyapa,
as well as a bed, a seat, a vehicle, a banner, a parasol, and a fly-whisk.
If one should burn [the site] without fire, or even consume it with lightning,
the death of the king will certainly occur within seven days.
Where there may be darkness at night, or dust and smoke arising without fire, one should know that there is great danger.
If a flame is seen at night or by day, even when there are no clouds, or if the appearance of the celestial bodies themselves should be observed during the night, it is considered ominous.
The collapse of ancient buildings and their frequent, repeated blazing, as well as other sudden occurrences, are seen there; in such cases, one should declare a danger from fire.
If smoke should arise in temples such as palaces without fire,
or if fire should appear without smoke, it is likewise a source of extreme terror.
If weapons blaze, or if they bend down or rise up,
or even if they emerge from their scabbards, there will be a tumultuous battle.
If quadrupeds, birds, and humans suddenly burst into flames,
or if trees or even mountains do so, one should know that there is great danger there.
On beds, seats, and vehicles, and upon coverings of hair, fire is seen to appear suddenly; there too, danger from fire shall arise.
Weapons and missiles roar; they bend down or rise up;
or arrows together with bows [appear]; there shall be a tumultuous battle.

The fire should be offered oblations with fuel-sticks of *kṣīra-ṛkṣa* trees, mustard seeds, and clarified butter, using its own specific mantras; and in this rite, gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, the king should feed the twice-born with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter;
he should cause a sacrificial fee to be given to them according to his ability.
One should have the rite for Agni performed there with the three verses beginning "Agni on the earth";
one should give a sacrificial fee to the teacher consisting of a gold coin (*niṣka*) and a beautiful horse.
Gārgya said: "I shall proclaim in its entirety the characteristics of portents:
where there should be an earthquake, or where a divine image should laugh."
Wherever the deity wanders, there one should predict death;
or else, the thundering of wells and portents shall arise.
Rivers may even flow upstream;
after six months, one should recognize an impending assault by a foreign army.
Fruit and flowers out of season, cold and heat occurring at the wrong time,
and rivers overflowing when it is not their season— these indicate that people desire another master.
Where the immovable becomes movable, or the movable becomes immovable,
the king perishes, or else the country itself perishes.
If one should see stars during the day, or if there should be a white bird [seen then],
or if one should see a rainbow at night, one should predict the ruin of the country.
When one sees a hare, a jackal, a boar, or likewise a deer in the middle of the site, it is certain that it is empty.
The various species of wild forest animals go of their own accord to the king's palace;
that place, however, becomes empty, with its walls and gate-towers broken down.
On city walls, in houses, on ramparts, at gateways, or even in cow-pens—
wherever honey is seen, what fruit indeed belongs to whom there?
[The boundary] whose path has been lost to time, overgrown with grass and creepers...
That region, abandoned by humans, shall become the domain of wild animals.
When one sees [the moon] facing the sun, whether in a city or even in a temple,
the king, though equal to Śakra, will perish within the year.
If a stone is used to cross a pond, a well, a lake, or a river,
there will surely be a collapse of the king's rule, as well as fear of thieves and disease.
If one should burn with something other than fire flowers, garments, and ornaments intended for the king, a bolt will certainly fall upon him there.
When that [state] is abandoned through falling away, even for a wise person, this [misfortune] may sometimes occur;
the wise person employs his intellect and speech for the destruction of fire, wind, water, death, disease, demons, and decay.
There, one should perform the great pacification, the nectar-like universal medicine.
(Pariśiṣṭa 70c. Bārhaspatyāni) (AVParis 70c, 22.1) Om. Gautama, firm in his vows, questioned Bṛhaspati, who was seated on the Himavat mountain bringing happiness, out of a desire for discipline.
How is this fire to be examined so that it may be auspicious for the performance of mantra-rites?
You, indeed, must reveal your true nature for the discernment of what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Bṛhaspati replied to that Gautama.
White, fragrant, lotus-colored, smokeless, with a sound like a drum, unattached, with an undisturbed crest, rising smoothly, and turning to the right.
When being offered oblations, the fire should be blazing, possessing radiant luster, and bestowing happiness;
where the fire is thus, it is certainly a sign of success in rites of pacification (*śāntika*).
Appearing in the form of a svastika, a vardhamāna, a śrīvatsa, and turning clockwise, she is seen in the form of a flame; she is indeed Śrī, facing in every direction.
When the fire, being offered oblations by the Hotṛ priest with a serene mind,
produces a smooth and auspicious sound, one should interpret that as a favorable sign.
Blazing and resembling jewels, secure and deep-sounding like a drum—
such smoke is auspicious for men, bringing about the accomplishment of their own goals.
A fire that has a smooth sound, little smoke, and is large and white in color; or one whose flames are compact and whose form is beautiful—such a fire brings about success.
But when the fire touches the oblation with the tips of its flames from all directions,
then the king quickly crushes the kingdom of his enemy.
Where singing is heard that is steady, stable,
and melodious, and where speech during oblations is clear and auspicious, it leads to success.
During the fire oblations, the hearing of the sounds of the cuckoo, the peacock, the vulture, and the *kurala* bird, as well as circumambulation from left to right, are praised.
The *śatapattrā*, the *rudantī*, and likewise the *cāṣasya nandana* and the *rambhaṇa* of cows are praised in sacrificial offerings.
Instruments sounding like lotuses and beryl,
and cows with calves of the same color, are praised when seen during a fire offering (*homa*).
The sacrificial fire, resembling a blossoming lotus, possesses bright flames; its rays are perfectly even, glossy, and well-ordered.
Where it roars deeply, that is the foremost sign of accomplishment:
unbroken fruits and flowers, and a pitcher of water overflowing.
Having seen or heard [such signs], one should predict the accomplishment of the rite:
flames resembling a seat, an umbrella, a banner, or an elephant.
Praiseworthy, radiant, and resembling diamond earrings,
the glorious fire moves in a clockwise direction, captivating the mind of the performer; for one who possesses such a fire, victory will surely and swiftly be achieved by the lord of men.
If the smoke from honey, milk-rice, and clarified butter poured upon the ground by clouds becomes fragrant, it shall be a sign of victory for the lord of the earth.
The forms of a conch and a svastika, as well as the form of a wheel, a mace, and a garland of heads— if these are seen, that indeed is the mark of victory.
Fire that resembles the color of clarified butter, has a smooth sound and a great roar,
or possesses variegated flames and is serene, is certainly a sign of success.
When wild beasts and birds of the forest enter the city,
or when domestic animals leave the town and go fearlessly to the wilderness;
Whether they are night-wanderers by day or day-wanderers by night,
or whether they are situated in the middle of the city during the day, they shriek horribly and without fear.
If a jackal howls at the king’s gate or the city gate, it foretells something inauspicious;
furthermore, when deer and birds abandon the forest and take up residence in the city, [it is a sign of calamity].
In the months of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa, that city becomes empty;
having abandoned it, lions, along with deer, mice, boars, and ruru deer depart.
Seeing that they have entered the city, that town becomes empty;
and even the beasts, deer, and birds utter cries of lamentation.
Where hawks, vultures, cranes, and crows— all moving in circles—
screech with a terrifying sound, even that place quickly perishes.
When many dogs howl loudly at night and, though being beaten, do not depart, then dwelling there is not pleasing.
Upon seeing balls of food for donkeys, antelopes, and jackals at the palaces, flagstaffs, halls, walls, gates, and archways, one should abandon the city.
If a deer faces east during the twilight with an unpeaceful cry, it foretells the destruction of the villagers, starting from the village headman and his attendants.
If a jackal, having come from the forest, should howl at the village gate with a loud and piercing cry, it portends the destruction of the village.
If a pigeon enters a house, or especially if an owl enters a royal palace, that house should be abandoned before long.
Suddenly, many vultures, crows, and owls, along with cranes, fall upon the walls of the house, the palace, the archway, and the banner.
Moreover, O King, when honey is produced in these locations— specifically in a lotus pond or an anthill— the king shall die within six months.
If a deer, a beast, a bird, or even a pig cries out,
and if it stands up and listens, that man shall perish.
Having repeatedly seen many terrifying crows, mice, cats, dogs, and insects, one should predict destruction through famine.
Dogs, howling with jackals as they wander through the middle of the city,
or [the sight of] bones of the dead and so forth, cause terror among the people.
If a dog, having taken up a piece of wood or even a horn, should run through the middle of the village by itself, they say that likewise there will be great danger.
The domestic priest, however, should perform the supreme *kāpotī* pacification rite;
he should recite therein the hymn beginning with "O gods, the dove... (*devāḥ kapota*).
In the insertion (*āvāpa*) and in the interlocking (*vyatiṣaṅga*), the offering is made afterwards;
one should give a desired sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or whatever by which the teacher is satisfied.
The images of the deities dance, they shine or blaze;
they tremble or weep, they perspire or laugh.
They rise up, sit down, run about, or drink;
they move or cast about their limbs, weapons, and banners.
They speak with their faces turned downward, or they move from place to place;
they sow fire, water, oil, blood, milk, and fat.
They chatter, or sigh, or writhe, or weep; or where one observes various movements with their limbs or gestures.
Wherever these sudden transformations are clearly seen in the shrines,
temples, and sacred monuments, there one finds no pleasure in dwelling.
Either the king’s misfortune occurs there, or that very fault is dissolved; or else, something is brought about there through death by hunger or by weapons.
May those who have set out on great festivals to the temples of the deities,
as well as those who are weary on the even path, find success through recitation and burnt offerings.
When a solar eclipse occurs unexpectedly at midday, and likewise for one involving a neutral planet,
it is seen as a portent for the destruction of either the king or the realm.
Where the elements have been established and the bases of the ritual mark are present,
there the terrible [obstacles] are pacified, and the recitation and fire-offering become effective.
Either the temple or the lotus may crumble or fall;
or, struck by a wind-thunderbolt, there shall be danger to the chief of the city.
Whatever sign exists among the twice-born regarding the duties of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
those same signs are found in the domestic priest concerning the horse-treadings and the fire-vehicles.
The [consecration] of cattle should be known as originating from Rudra; that of kings as originating from the World-Protectors (Lokapālas);
and that of regional rulers (Māṇḍalika) should be known as belonging to Skanda and Viśākha.
The worldly [mantra] should always be known as belonging to Viṣṇu and to the Viśvedevas;
that of the Senāpatis belongs to Gaṇeśas, and that of the ministers is Gāndharva.
The servant of the gods [is worshipped] by the servants of kings; the wife of the gods [is worshipped] by the wives of kings.
Kāśyapa [is worshipped] in a mechanical palace, and Vāstoṣpati [is worshipped] while stationed in the city.
Among maidens, [the rite] born of maidens; among youths, [the rite] born of youths;
and the ritual of drinking as prescribed for the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and nāgas.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the single chapter on the "Comprehensive Collection of All Things," as spoken by the Blessed Bṛhaspati.
That exposition which has been proclaimed in twelve chapters— listen once more to it in summary, as it has come down through tradition.
When the sun, defeated, its orb eclipsed by Rāhu, discolored, distorted by twilight, and devoid of luster, goes to its setting,
one should then know that the destruction of the noble Brahmins is imminent.
When the sun rises together with Rāhu already eclipsed,
then the fruit of dharma is exhausted and the people enter the Kali age.
When the moon rises together with Rāhu, not yet released from his grasp,
then the fruit of dharma is exhausted and the world enters the age of Kali.
When the moon sets together with Rāhu without having been released, one should know that there is danger from that; death shall enter the people.
Though not being struck, the kettledrums resound again and again;
weapons and mounts blaze with an inauspicious and terrible radiance.
When there is an agitation of the winds, the quarters of the sky are permeated with dust, and the twilight is followed by thick clouds;
if the twilight appears in five colors, they portend dangers for the king.
Where it thunders though there are no clouds, and where the sky appears as if covered by thickets of shrubs,
the kingdom will quickly flee, lasting for fifteen years.
If lightning strikes or manifests from a cloudless sky,
or if a thunderclap falls even when there are no clouds, it portends the death of the king.

If, during the day, a line of Mahendra or a rainbow of Mahendra appears among the winds, then those foremost of the twice-born who know the meaning of the scriptures declare that there will be fear for the circles of kings at night.
When at night a rainbow appears together with a halo, increasing in size throughout the night,
and likewise a meteor falls while disintegrating, then there is danger for the circles of kings.
The elephants discharge blood from their trunks, and the hairs of the horses blaze;
the swords and the celestial signs blaze as well, portending the king’s [impending] fate.

The falling of great mountains, the shaking of the earth, and likewise the terror of human beings; the birth of deformed creatures and speech with fierce words—these beasts and birds utter when there is great danger.
If smoke or fire arises from a parasol, a house, a chariot,
or a banner, that king— his treasury depleted of men— shall meet with destruction and the slaughter of his people.
When rivers, with their own vast and spreading waves and masses of water, carry away trees from their own banks,
if they then flow against the current, there will be destruction for the king and his kingdom.

But when the rays of the sun are obscured by dust or smoke during the day, they say that he shall have no residence within the realm; it is said that there will be the destruction of the prosperity of the hosts.
The blazing of the fire is extinguished, and likewise the fuel does not burn;
these portents announce fears for the king.
The falling of rocks from mountain peaks, the falling of branches from the trees of the city,
and likewise the falling of the trees at sacred shrines— these portend fears for the king.
Cows with unweaned calves wander through the city gates, uttering fierce cries;
and elephants with lotus-stalks tied to them appear, portending fears for the king.
Where palaces, gate-towers, and the like fall down, as do trees, banners of Indra, and horses;
for them, they predict auspicious results, and likewise, they indicate that Saumya and others will shine forth with great splendor.
Looking upward at the city settled there, at sunrise indeed the jackals howl most fiercely; and vultures, rising up in circles, wheel about, signaling that danger has come upon the countryside.
Where a thunderbolt falls like a staff, where the earth trembles with sparks, and where there is a cessation of the sun;
and where the moon becomes deformed and unpeaceful—there, within a month, a most terrible danger arises.

Where there is the provocation of blood from sacred trees and the appearance of headless trunks as vehicles during the twilights, there is an increase of Rākṣasa lords among the people and great danger for the king.
When rain falls as showers of dust, and thereafter a shower of yellow orpiment falls from above,
and after that it rains showers of stones, then the power of the king perishes.

A forest-dweller [sees] a flock of deer and birds living in a village; a village-dweller [sees] a gathering of vultures at the edge of a forest; or there may be a gathering of vultures at the palace gate or within the city of a king.
Wherever there is the birth of women with many forms, such as faces like those of donkeys or young camels—at that place one who desires life should not remain, for it is corrupted by portents.
The gods suddenly depart from their vehicles, or they fall upon the ground into the forests;
some abandon their stations and cry out, while others have their limbs mangled by blood.
Through extremely fierce multitudes of portents, the destruction of the kṣatriya power arises,
as well as the affliction of the worlds resulting from disease, thieves, and fire.
The fires are in a state of intense agitation, producing terror; the quarters of the sky are ablaze; at midday, the firmament is studded with hosts of planets and scattered with flocks of vultures;

there is constant foulness due to thunderclaps and showers of dust, as well as a terrible earthquake; and the falling of tears from the gods—these portend fear for kings and the destruction of the kingdom.

When the jackal, having released its flame toward the sun, howls with its face turned upward while surrounded by flocks of crows and vultures, those who know the Vedas declare that there is then cause for fear.
The elephants cry out with their trunks extended, and the horses cry out with their teeth bared; the women also weep at the gathering. Then there shall be fear, rooted in the signs heard.
But when garments from the wish-fulfilling trees fall upon the head with a brilliant rain,
one should know that by observing such a fall as it truly appears, it portends fear for the kingdom and the king.
When vehicles such as carts and the like move while unyoked,
one should know that a great danger has arisen in the countryside.
Just as they are always seen, so should one recite them;
there is no transgression of them at all as long as the rite of pacification has not been performed.
One should know that the destruction of the women of the countryside occurs when the elephant-king and the domestic priest [are afflicted];
one should employ recitation, fire-oblations, and rites of pacification during such portents.
One should especially render [the person] immortal, according to the word of Bṛhaspati;
one should perform a hundred-thousand-fold fire-oblation, or recite the Vedic Saṃhitā;
and one should employ gifts of gold in the rite for pacification.
(Pariśiṣṭa 71: Auspicious Omens from the Teachings of Uśanas) (AVParis 71.1.1) Nārada, standing before him, questioned Kāvya Uśanas regarding divine, atmospheric, and likewise terrestrial portents.
And likewise when there is a reversal of the seasons, as well as of beasts and birds;
when there is the speech of non-human beings, or a transgression by stationary objects.
In the case of a reversal of the female organ, the discharge of flesh and blood,
the failure of the fire to ignite, and likewise in the case of crawling after a vehicle;
And likewise when weapons blaze, when a shrine grows dry vegetation,
and when the images, temples, or paintings weep or thunder.
When there is the appearance of wells or ponds in fire or thunder,
or when there is the raining down of fish, snakes, birds, or juices;
Especially when weapons blaze or roar,
when flowers and fruits appear on trees out of season, or when they sprout prematurely;
When palaces, mountain peaks, celestial chariots, and city walls tremble, and the sounds of singing and musical instruments arise without any apparent cause;
And whatever other portents of a distorted nature arise,
O Bhārgava, explain their fruit and their timing according to the truth.
To that inquiring Nārada, the wise Aśana properly began to explain the three kinds of portents.
When it becomes excessively hot during the cold season, or excessively cold during the hot season,
one should know that there will indeed be danger in those regions after nine months.
In a place where it rains after three days have passed since a drought began,
there shall be the execution of the principal person in that region.
If cuckoos and peacocks should experience their season of passion out of time, or if they should even engage in mating, one should know that there will be danger for the people of the countryside.
One should designate as forest those regions where the ruru, the raudra, the pṛṣata, and the hariṇa deer are seen.
Likewise, on the seventeenth lunar day, the principal leaders are slain;
and in that very region, a great danger arises.
Cows, horses, elephants, dogs, donkeys, camels, monkeys, serpents,
mongooses, birds, beasts of prey, boars, buffaloes, and deer.
In whatever regions these creatures utter human speech,
in those regions the king shall perish in the sixth month.
Wherever portents of unnatural form are indeed seen here and there,
in that region there will swiftly arise, within six months, the greatest danger.
Whenever and wherever one moves upon a seat, a bed, or a vehicle,
its owner encounters terrible fear from the opposing side.
Where granaries, armories, stones, wells, and mountains move about and speak in distorted forms— these are portents.
Indeed, much is born; in that region, there will be intense and great fear for three months. But during the remaining period beyond that time, the result will be mild.
Whether in a region or in a village, if there should be a confusion of castes (*yonivyatikara*),
then after a year has passed, great danger arises there.
In whatever region a cow, a horse, or even a mare gives birth,
one should predict the death of the king within that year.
Where a human woman gives birth to various grass-eating animals,
there a great and intense fear arising after six months will surely occur.
The knower of the treatise should here predict the arrival of a hostile army;
moreover, vast and deformed battles will break out in this place.
If a human woman gives birth to a serpent or even a bird,
that region shall become unstable for more than six months.
A woman who gives birth to a camel, or even a monkey,
or any other moving creature whatsoever, or even any stationary thing;
Afflicted by disease, the stroke of weapons, and famine,
that land quickly suffers, and the king therein perishes.
If a non-human woman gives birth to a human, or a human woman gives birth to a non-human,
one should know for certain that the arrival of a foreign army is imminent.

If a woman gives birth to one who has four eyes or two heads, or whose limbs are deficient or redundant, and who is endowed with secondary sexual characteristics [of the opposite sex], [that child is a *pāṇḍaga*].
Within two years, the king perishes there where a camel,
a bull, a horse, or an elephant is born.
Within a fortnight or a month, great danger shall arise for the king from that quarter;
or else that region shall encounter peril arising from a foreign army.
Where women commit such a perversion of the female organ that a cow gives birth [to a male calf] or other such anomalies, there the kingdom perishes.
In whatever regions these [beings] dwell, one should know that there is great danger;
therefore, the king should quickly banish these creatures.
If a mare should give birth to a horned foal anywhere,
one should predict the death of the king within a year.
According to the *Śāstrasamuccaya*: "If a buffalo gives birth on a Wednesday in the month of Māgha, or a mare by day in Śrāvaṇa, or cows in Siṃha, they bring death to their master."
When a woman gives birth to donkeys, bulls, camels, horses, dogs, pigs, or mules, or even to Rākṣasas or Piśācas, [it is an ill omen].
In that place, grains, crops, and wealth are destroyed;
a fourfold, terrible fear swiftly breaks out there.
For indeed, the principal [leaders] are slain together with their followers at the eighth month;
one should predict diseases in those regions for three years.
In whatever region fire blazes suddenly without fuel and without being kindled,
the king of that country, along with his entire realm, shall perish.
In whatever region Maghavan rains down a shower of flesh,
there bones, blood, marrow, and fat certainly exist.
The arrival of a hostile army should be recognized as a great danger;
moreover, vast and deformed battles arise therein.
Where the god rains down charcoal, sand, or grain,
there a terrible fourfold danger will swiftly arise.
Wherever the god sends rain upon serpents, fish, or birds,
there shall be damage to the crops and great fear shall prevail.
Wherever the rain-god pours down liquor, honey-wine, clarified butter, oil, milk, or curd, there famine and disease arise.
When meteors and stars fall upon the sacrificial hearths and it rains glowing embers,
one should predict a terrible fear of disease in those regions.
When a man, a horse, or even an elephant is seen blazing in any place,
one should know that after ten months there will be a total upheaval of the kingdom in that location.
When iron arrows, spears, and swords repeatedly burst into flames,
one should predict a terrible danger from weapons in those regions.
The sacred trees of the caityas break apart and cry out discordantly;
they laugh, creep forward, sing, and weep.
An invasion by an enemy army will swiftly descend upon them;
or they shall perish along with their chariots, and their leader shall be slain therein.
Where a sacred tree suddenly exudes various fluids—
either individually or all together— I shall now describe its characteristics.
If [the poison is] in ghee, honey, milk, or likewise in ghee, milk, water, raw honey, or oil, there will be most dreadful diseases.
In the case of *surāsava*, there will be mutual dissension; in the case of blood, the falling of weapons;
in the case of oil, the principal figures are slain; and in the case of food, one should predict the fear of hunger.
If a tree bears fruit or flowers out of season,
one should know that in the twelfth month there will be a reversal of fortune for the king.
Where there is a flower upon a flower, or likewise a fruit upon a fruit,
or a leaf upon a leaf— one should know that there is danger from the local people in that place.
Where a sacred tree is completely covered by a white cloth,
one should predict a terrible, swift, and intense danger for the Brahmins.
Great danger for the Kṣatriyas arises from others clothed in red garments;
for the Vaiśyas, from those in yellow garments; and for the Śūdras, from those in black clothing.
If the clouds are dark blue, there will be damage to the crops; if they are variegated, it will affect wild animals and birds;
and if they are discolored, severe diseases will prevail for up to ten months.
In whatever kingdom the deities wander about or laugh, and when they gaze upon the fortifications, one should know that there is great danger.
They laugh, they close their eyes, they sing, and they perform contortions;
wherever there are the scents of flesh and blood, there is great danger.
If one observes [the king] looking at something variegated, singing, or moving about repeatedly during these eight months, one should predict the death of the king.
Where there are variegated signs as well as sacred shrines that cause excessive transformation, one should know that there is great danger there.
If a well, a pond, a lake, or even a mountain blazes up in various locations, one should know that danger has arrived.
If they should laugh or cry out, or if a dog should bark like a cat,
then the king of that region will suffer terrible affliction.
In whatever place the sound of conchs, flutes, musical instruments, and drums is heard most intensely, there the king's punishment is inflicted.
In the realm of that king where the subjects are constantly agitated and go to ruin,
one should predict destruction there, not merely from portents.
In whosever kingdom there is a constant decline of cattle,
one should know that danger is imminent before long.
In the realm of whichever king a river flows carrying mud,
wood, grass, stones, dead fish, and likewise crocodiles;
In that region, one should predict the presence of intoxicants, honey, meat, clarified butter, oil, milk, and curd, as well as fear arising from the arrival of another king.
In the realm of whichever king a river might flow upstream,
there shall be fear for the eight months from the local people, who will have weapons in their hands.
Wherever a well roars, or whenever it bursts asunder,
or if blood or pus [is seen], one should predict that there will be danger in that place.
The weapons rush forward and strike back with violence;
from the quivers, arrows suddenly gush forth and roar.
By their very nature, bows become full and blaze forth;
in that region, a fierce and terrifying battle takes place.
When trees are seen bearing flowers and fruits out of season within someone's kingdoms, their destruction is foretold.
Where trees and young creepers that bear fruit and flowers should appear even out of season, one should know that there is great danger in that place.
Where palaces and celestial mansions indeed blaze forth,
and even solid structures crumble, he for whom this occurs will die before long.
Musical instruments resound in the forest and are constantly heard in the sky;
at that time, the king should dwell there, having gathered [the people] from the ten directions.
In whosever house the sounds of singing and musical instruments are heard,
yet he dies unexpectedly and his wealth is utterly lost.
Conch shells, flutes, lutes, kettledrums, clay drums,
and horn-shaped drums were seen being played even in places where they had not been struck.
Having thus gathered his burden, he should then proceed to another district;
for that region is frequented by wild beasts, and the wind arises there.
If drums sound without being struck and musical instruments play by themselves,
and there are holes in one's house, that person quickly encounters danger.
The falling or even the breaking of the banners of the king of the gods,
and the entry of carnivorous beasts, will bring suffering to the king.
If the death of the foremost horses and elephants should occur suddenly,
one should recognize therein the imminent arrival of another king.
When the *aśvattha* tree flowers, the *kṣatriyas* and *brāhmaṇas* suffer; when the *udumbara*, the *vaiśyas*; and when the *nyagrodha*, the *dasyus* likewise.
A white rainbow portends the destruction of Brahmins; a red one, the destruction of Kṣatriyas;
a yellow one at night, the destruction of Vaiśyas; and a black one, the destruction of Śūdras.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or the withered regrowth of a shrine tree,
one should recognize that there will be suffering for the region, and a person of high rank will be slain therein.
When the sacrificial post for Indra breaks, or when the animal being immolated should escape,
one should then recognize that suffering has befallen the king.
When there was an inauspicious omen concerning Pitāmaha, Vāsudeva, Soma, Dharma, Aryaman, and also Mitra, which brought fear to the Brāhmaṇas.
Whatever forms are seen in Bṛhaspati, or in Śukra, or in Pāvaka, or in Pākaśāsana, one should know those same forms to be present in the domestic priest (purohita).
That omen, which has been set in motion among kings, should be understood as pertaining to Mahādeva, Kubera, as well as Skanda and Viśākha.
Whatever sign is seen suddenly is proclaimed as a portent.
Wherever the chariot of the gods or of kings sinks down, one should recognize that there is imminent and extraordinary danger for the king.
Whatever fear is seen regarding Someca, Vāsudeva, Varuṇa, or Pākaśāsana, that indeed should be known as arising from the *bhāṇḍādhika* *kana*.
Whatever omen occurs in relation to Vāta, Prajāpati, and Viśvakarman, that shall be known as a regional omen.
Among maidens, the fruit belongs to the maidens; among boys, it belongs to the boys born [at that time]. Likewise, among all servants, one should determine the fruit according to the scripture.
Whatever Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Bhadrakālī, Mahābalā,
and Vīramātā may declare, that shall be the danger to the king’s queen.
Of these, there is one and likewise another; whatever other female deities there may be, one should designate them as the causal signs of women and of the principal [deities].
That omen which appears among the Gandharvas is seen elsewhere as well;
it brings fear to army commanders and causes terror for ministers.
Among the Rakṣasas, Pannagas, and Yakṣas, as well as in the sanctuaries of the Liṅga,
[the deity] is established among men according to their form and according to their karma.
In the right limbs of the bodies, in the dwellings of the deities,
and in all the members of women— the fear of both shall be equal.
Just as portents occurring on one's own body are interpreted by those who contemplate fate,
so too should all things, whether auspicious or inauspicious, be reckoned everywhere in that same manner.
The Yakṣas, such as Māṇibhadra and others, and the Gandharvas, such as Citrasena,
should manifest that fear to the chief ministers.
In whatever regions auspicious or inauspicious signs are seen among the deities,
those regions shall perish, or else the king shall perish.
Where Brāhmaṇas are being slain— whether in a village, a kingdom, a city,
or royal capitals— that is the sign of impending non-existence.
Where the king does not protect the weak who are being oppressed,
there the rod of divine punishment swiftly falls upon the king.
One should have the fire-oblation and the recitation performed over the parasols, banners, and flags, in temples, houses, gates, watchtowers, and palaces.
Wherein there are primary and modified genders,
as well as deities, rivers, trees, shrubs, and great plants.
If the army itself is not seen, along with its elephants, horses, and foot soldiers,
or if they appear with missing limbs or deformed limbs, one should predict total destruction there.
Where pillars, trees, or banners emit blood-water,
or where they smoke or blaze, there indeed is the death of the mantra-practitioners.
If one should know [the omen] regarding the Mistress of the World (*jagatsvāminī*), if it occurs in the sky, it pertains to the celestial realm;
if it occurs in the intermediate space, it pertains to the atmosphere; and if it occurs on the ground, it pertains to the crops.
Divine calamity falls in eight ways: upon the wife, the vehicle, the son, the treasury, the army commander, the city, the domestic priest, or the king.
In the event of portents, one should perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite— dedicated to Mahendra, Amṛta, Rudra, or the Viśvedevas— with abundant sacrificial fees.
By this, terrible calamities are pacified and security and prosperity arise;
there, joyful kings protect the earth.
(Pariśiṣṭa 72. Great Marvels) (AVParis 72.1.1) Now we shall explain the great marvels.

When one’s birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) or action asterism (*karmanakṣatra*) is afflicted by a planet, struck by a meteor, eclipsed, cast down, or scorched by smoke— asterisms that have swift ripening, are unfailing, and are terrible—
at such times the king should immediately perform the great *amṛta*-pacification (*mahāśānti*), especially on the eighth lunar station (*sthāna*) of the moon, [with the *vajra*].
And when a pillar is possessed by a deity,
or when one who is multicolored, multiform, horned, sun-like, or staked down is struck by meteors— wondrous portents arise— and he becomes blind, sighs, laughs, and wanders about.

In laughter, speech, sound, noise, and in the latent impression (*vāsana*), when Vaiśvānara has not yet blazed forth, there are ashes, bones, stones, and embers in the atmosphere; and in a rainbow at night, it is indeed a streak of light in a cloudless sky.
If the moon and sun should be eclipsed within one's kingdom; or if hostile enemy populations situated beyond the borderlands [should appear];

or likewise, if crows, pigeons, herons, vultures, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and beasts of prey should cry out, hoot, sing, or howl at night upon the wheels, banners, houses, dwellings, and tops of palaces, or if they vomit forth, roar, or flash lightning over ponds, wells, and water-reservoirs.

In chariots, machines, elephants, carriages, musical instruments, and so forth, the appearance of firebrands, embers, smoke, or flames is a portent concerning the king, whether it occurs in a primary object or a secondary one.
Likewise, the falling of an owl, a chameleon, or a hawk; the breaking of the royal parasol, the banner, the wheel, the staff, or the tusk of the king.
When a female elephant is in rut, when a village has given birth [to twins],

and when a royal chariot with the king mounted upon it has its axle broken— after seven nights, this destroys the king's domestic priest, minister, commander-in-chief, wife, elephant, queen, prince, or even the king himself;
yet he who knows thus shall prosper.
One hundred and twelve cows, milch-cows, a bronze vessel, clothing, gold, a neck-ornament, a horse—these are the sacrificial gifts.

Peace is not ordained for kings until the divine calamities have arisen; peace performed at the wrong time results only in further omens. Therefore, one should perform a rite of pacification specifically directed toward the source of the danger.
In an assembly of serpents, during a disturbance caused by wind, upon the appearance of water or its movement;
during the sighting of a bow-shaped halo, twilight halos, comets, solar eclipses, lightning, thunderbolts, iron clubs, or circular halos around the sun or moon;
during a rain of dust, a rain of stones, or a rain of curds, honey, clarified butter, milk, marrow, or blood— (AVParis_72,3.4) ... [rain of] marrow and blood.

It rains (AVPariś 72.3.5). When the rays have diminished, there are two paths and two tracks at the waning of wealth; when Soma has waned, they are the illuminations of that waning which fill what was not full. Immediately after the latter part of the night, there is the burning and smoldering of the quarters, irregularity of the planets, mounting, and encroachment; there is a city of Gandharvas, the agitation of the Maruts, and the disjunction of Soma from the lunar days, divisions of time, moments, asterisms, planets, and so forth.
Rivers flowing upstream; flocks of crows gathering upon palaces, archways, and banners; the mounting of wolves onto carts; cats washing themselves; the hooting of owls;

the distorted cries of hawks, vultures, and other birds arising from both human and non-human sources; the lamentations of women, children, and the elderly; and when a sacrificial post is ablaze, or when a foot is broken, or when objects lack their proper substances, or when there is one tree with two shadows, or no shadow at all.

From this point forward: when a shadow suddenly falls; when a sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), a pillar, or a post falls; when trees that are growing fail to grow, or when their leaves fall without being severed; when dry branches appear on trees; when smoke, dust, or water suddenly manifest or move about;

when there is the breaking of many weapons; when Indra-pikes, gate-towers, watchtowers, banners, and the like break; when things that are appropriate are cut off, while inappropriate things flourish; and when there is a firm breaking of these.

In the case of the regrowth of what was dry, in a house, in an anthill, at the place of one's bed, upon the growth of a *darbha* stalk, in enmity with a friend, in affection for an enemy, and likewise upon the cutting down of an image of a deity;
when there is a loss of royal favor toward the citizens, servants, and others—there are verses on this matter:
"But when the moon, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), becomes deformed by a transformation..."
Whether unscarred or cut, one should predict the death of the king.
Clouds shaped like weapons, white in color and form, as well as those of five colors and resembling staffs;
When the orb of the moon becomes dark in the midst of the sun,
that should be known as the Śaṅku planet, which is most terrible.
In that case, one should recognize it as the king’s death, which brings fear to all beings;
there, one should perform the great pacification, the immortal universal medicine.

(AVParis_72,4.1) Now, in whatever region there occurs a confusion among cows, Brahmins, charioteers, astrologers, and physicians, or likewise among wandering mendicants, performers, forest-dwellers, and students— that one should know to be a portent.

(AVParis_72,4.2) Wherever there is a confusion of ritual acts, a confusion of sacrifices, and a confusion of legal procedures, and where dharma is oppressed by what is not dharma— that one should know to be a portent.

If among them there is that for which no expiation is known—that which is unknown and not prescribed—one should offer oblations in the middle with the *Puruṣasūkta*. And while those [oblations] have not yet been performed as expiations, great portents appear;
they are called "divine" in the temples of the gods. Then they laugh, sing, weep, shriek, perspire, smoke, blaze, tremble, open their eyes, close their eyes, and lick what has been smeared.
When these [omens] flow forth or revolve,
one should know that upon their appearance or occurrence, there will be the arrival of another king, or a violent upheaval, fear of drought and weapons, famine, death, the ruin of the subjects,
and the destruction of the ministers and the king.
Regarding all of those, it is said that one who knows the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases should approach the Lord at the crossroads.
"Oṃ, I take refuge; I take refuge in Bhūḥ; I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ; I take refuge in Svaḥ; I take refuge in Janat"—thus one should take refuge.

Having cooked milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the milk of eight hundred tawny cows (*kapilā*), or, if tawny cows are unavailable, having cooked milk-rice with the milk of a hundred milch cows, and having placed the fuel-wood (*idhma*) facing eastward and strewn [the sacrificial grass] around it...
One who has been pacified should offer oblations with *barhis* grass accompanied by the troop of Rudra.
One should offer clarified butter as an oblation; one should offer milk-rice as an oblation; one should present white flowers; one should attend upon the Brahmins with a meal.
One should give those very cows for his satisfaction, or a kingdom for a limited time. To the performer [of the rite], one should give a thousand cows and an excellent village.
Now, when this fire arises upon a bed or upon a garment,
it is called a most extraordinary omen that brings about the destruction of all men.

In this case, one who desires a kingdom or wealth should perform the great *brāhmī* pacification (*mahāśānti*), accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), plentiful food, and many ritual materials, and which is well-conducted with excellent gifts; he should thus honor Bṛhaspati.

The divine gods create miraculous wonders before the onset of obstacles for the sake of awakening; likewise, they create hindrances to the tasks of people in this world crowded with activities and filled with the various social classes.

One should perform the task with divine power and bring about peace by prostrating before the gods; thus one is liberated from affliction and obstacles. If there is something undesirable in heaven, he shall not do it again.
One should observe the movements of all beings upon the earth, in the intermediate space, and in the heavens, as well as the cries of beasts and birds.
If, whether in a village, a family, or even a country, among kings, ministers, or likewise among the twice-born,
the disposition of the animals becomes abnormal or distorted, one should know that to be a portentous marvel for that region.
A division among ministers occurs when there are various heads on a single body; if there are one or two heads, there will be a dual kingship.
If a headless trunk arises without hands or feet, a minister dies; if a headless torso (kavandha) is born, the king shall perish.
If among the sacrificial animals there should be one with an extra limb or one lacking a limb, or one that is deformed and misshapen;
and likewise, if among the women there should be one who is deformed and misshapen—one should know that to be a portentous marvel for that region.
If a *vidūlaka* is born without a nose or without lips,
or if a *vidūlaka* is born without form or with a deformed shape;
If one who is not blind should eat from a lower vessel and so forth, or if a *vidūlaka* is born,
this is indeed called a great marvel that causes the destruction of the kingdom within the realm.

Once he has been bathed with water, made fragrant and scented, and his life has departed, one should offer him, anointed with ghee, into the fire. Having offered ghee with the *raudra* gaṇa-mantra, the high-souled one should likewise bring about his welfare (*śiva*).
